statement: Information architecture design principles are technology- and vendor-independent, so they remain useful even as specific technologies, tools, and software packages change.

Frame the design subject abstractly as an 'information environment' rather than as a 'website,' because doing so lets the same semantic-structure design principles apply across channels beyond the Web.

Because any interactive product contains information, information architecture is relevant to anyone responsible for defining how interactive products and services work, regardless of their job title.
Deliver an information experience that is familiar and coherent across multiple interaction channels, from the Web to smartphones, smart watches, and other devices.
Avoid grounding information-architecture guidance in specific software packages, because such product details change too quickly to retain long-term value.
Good information architecture makes whatever an organization wants to share easy to find, navigate, and understand.
Information architecture is a design discipline focused on making information findable and understandable.

Information architecture lets you frame design problems through two perspectives: that information products and services are perceived by people as places made of information, and that these environments can be organized for optimum findability and understandability.
Successful software applications tend to outgrow their original problem-set boundaries by accumulating features over time, which causes them to lose clarity and simplicity.
Decoupling information from its physical container also decouples it from the contexts in which it is accessed, so the same information is now consumed across many devices and situations.
Design for the wide variety of contexts in which users access information, aiming for experiences that stay consistent and coherent regardless of where or how the information is accessed.
When a single tool spans many content types that each carry different and incompatible organization schemes, its search results become harder to interpret because they mix media types.
Structuring information well requires a systematic, comprehensive, and holistic approach that makes it easy to find and understand regardless of the context, channel, or medium the user employs.

Gaining a coherent view of an information system requires stepping out of product-development detail to look at the whole in the abstract, and information architecture serves as a lens for gaining that perspective.
Findability techniques that were effective at late-1990s information scale, such as curated hierarchical directories, become ineffective as the volume of information grows.
condition: at large and growing information volume

statement: Digital information artifacts are part of a system that can gather usage metadata such as highlights, annotations, and reading patterns, and provide additional functionality based on that metadata.

People interact with information environments through language—labels, menus, descriptions, visual elements, content, and their relationships—which frames the information and shapes whether people understand it.
Design cross-channel coherence by defining abstract semantic structures that can be instantiated differently per channel, rather than designing a single specific artifact instance.

Across channels the semantic structures should stay consistent and familiar even though each channel's capabilities and limitations differ, and achieving this requires abstracting the structures away from any specific implementation.
condition: when an organization serves users across multiple channels

statement: The same underlying information structures and rules can be expressed through many different physical or interface forms; the semantic structure, not the physical form, is what defines the thing.
Practice systems thinking: define the semantic systems that individual artifacts such as apps, websites, and voice interfaces operate within, not merely the individual artifacts.
You cannot design products that work coherently across interaction channels without understanding how those channels influence and interact with one another and with the surrounding systems.

Effective information environments balance structural coherence (high-level invariance) with suppleness (low-level flexibility), so a good information architecture is defined at both the abstract and the low-level-artifact levels.
Maintaining a systems-level view alongside day-to-day design work helps ensure you are solving the right problem rather than building the wrong thing well.

Information architecture is the structural design of shared information environments—the synthesis of organization, labeling, search, and navigation systems within digital, physical, and cross-channel ecosystems.

No single definition can fully capture information architecture, because language and representation are inherently imperfect—no document, label, or definition fully conveys meaning, and no two readers interpret it identically.

Information occupies the messy middle between data (structured facts and figures that yield specific answers) and knowledge (what is in people's heads); information architecture concerns information of all kinds plus the metadata that describes content objects.

Structuring means choosing the appropriate granularity for the information components and how they relate; organizing means grouping them into meaningful, distinctive categories that create the right context; labeling means deciding what to call those categories and the navigation elements that lead to them.
Findability is a critical success factor for overall usability: if users cannot find what they need through some combination of browsing, searching, and asking, then the system fails.
An information architecture must balance the needs of users with the goals of the business, and efficient content management with clear policies and procedures is essential to it.
Information architecture cannot be reduced to numbers alone because of inherent ambiguity and complexity, so practitioners must also rely on experience, intuition, and creativity.
Effective information architecture design rests on three interdependent variables—users, content, and context—and cannot be designed in a vacuum from content alone.
Users, content, and context are all moving targets that vary along many dimensions and change over time, so an information architecture must be re-evaluated as they shift.
Resolve difficult information-architecture questions by deconstructing them into users, content, and context; the honest default starting answer is often 'it depends.'
Every information ecology is unique, so information-architecture solutions must be matched to their specific situation rather than copied from best practices or from competitors.

First understand the business context (which is often tacit, undocumented knowledge held in people's heads), then align the information architecture with the organization's goals, strategy, and culture.

Understand the contextual constraints each channel imposes—for example, smaller screens force shorter labels and navigation menus and are used at different times and places—and when a service spans channels, plan how those channels overlap and interact.
condition: when a service will be used via more than one channel

statement: Define 'content' broadly to include the documents, applications, services, schemas, and metadata that people need to use or find in a system; even a task-oriented ecommerce site has content that customers must be able to find.
Survey content along its distinguishing facets—ownership, format, structure, metadata, volume, and dynamism—because that unique mix drives the need for a customized information architecture.

Who creates and owns the content—centralized authoring, distribution across departments, licensed from vendors, or produced by users—strongly influences how much control you have over all the other content dimensions.

Content structure can follow a document paradigm (the whole document is the smallest discrete unit) or a content-component/digital-asset approach that uses structural markup such as XML or JSON to manage and access content at a finer level of granularity.

The extent and quality of existing metadata—whether documents are tagged, how consistent the tags are, and whether a controlled vocabulary or user tagging is in place—determines how much you are starting from scratch for information retrieval and content management.
Remember that 'users' are people—human beings with desires, needs, concerns, and foibles—and design the information environment for those actual people.
Differences in customer preferences and behaviors translate into different information needs and information-seeking behaviors, so different user segments require different designs.
Learn who is using your system, how, and what information they want by studying users in the real world; these questions cannot be answered reliably in brainstorming meetings or focus groups.
Information architecture starts with people and the information need that brings them to the product—not with taxonomies or search engines—and no goal is more important than satisfying users' needs.
Each type of information need causes specific information-seeking behaviors, so understand those needs and behaviors and shape the design to correspond to them.
Distinguishing among users' information needs and behaviors and determining which are their highest priorities tells you where to invest design effort and resources.

Reject the 'too-simple' input-process-answer model of finding: it is mechanistic, ignores the context before and after the interaction, assumes an ignorant user, and wrongly assumes there is always a single right answer.

Treating finding as a data-retrieval problem measurable by time, clicks, or pages to the 'right' answer is a misconception that has wasted millions on search-engine panaceas, because for messy textual information there is often no single right answer.

Four common information needs recur: known-item seeking (you know what you want, what to call it, and where it is), exploratory seeking (open-ended learning through searching and browsing), exhaustive research (leaving no stone unturned), and refinding information found before.
Searching, browsing, and asking other people are the three basic building blocks of information-seeking behavior.
Users integrate searching, browsing, and asking within a single finding session and iterate as their needs change, so design the information architecture to support both integration and iteration.
When users berry-pick, support easy movement from search to browse and back—let them search within categories found by browsing and browse categories found by searching.
condition: when the berry-picking model fits your users

statement: Support the 'pearl-growing' need for 'more like this' by letting users move from one good document to similar ones—via similar-pages commands or links to documents sharing the same keywords, citations, or user tags.

Corporate portals often follow a two-step model—first find the right subsite, then find information within it—and seeking behavior and the appropriate information architecture differ between the portal and the departmental subsites.

Learn users' information needs and seeking behaviors with real research methods—especially search analytics (mining query logs to diagnose problems with search, metadata, navigation, and content) and contextual inquiry (observing users in their natural settings and asking why).
Combine multiple user-research methods to cover as many bases as possible, favor methods that expose users' direct statements of their own needs, and use focus groups only with great care.

Understanding what users actually want helps you prioritize which architectural components to build and gives you data to counterbalance non-user drivers of design such as budget, time, politics, entrenched technologies, and designers' personal preferences.
People understand things only in relationship to something else, so context—the frame around information and where that frame sits—changes how the information is perceived.

Designing an information architecture is a form of placemaking that alters how people perceive and understand information; aim to create environments that are understandable, usable, and able to grow and adapt over time to meet users' and the organization's needs.

People experience information environments as types of places, picking up semantic cues such as navigation structures, headings, and images that tell them what kind of place they are in and how to interpret its content.

An information environment must accommodate both what all such environments need to be usable by people and what is specific to its type and distinguishes it from others, just as a bank building must satisfy general usability and bank-specific requirements.

Information architecture defines compositions of semantic elements—navigation labels, section headings, keywords—together with the design principles, goals, and guidelines that capture the intended feeling of the place.

Because information environments manifest in many different forms, the semantic structures information architecture produces are more abstract than the products of other design disciplines, and coherence between instances is achieved by consistent use of language and a consistent order among the linguistic elements.

First-level navigation order plays a large role in defining the conceptual boundaries and overall perceived form of an information environment, much as a building's primary structure defines its physical form and adaptability.

Digital information environments evolve typologies: the information structures of bank websites tend to resemble those of competing banks, and the same is true for airlines, universities, hospitals, newspapers, and online stores.

Conforming to an established environment typology helps users because it signals what kind of place they are in and lets them reuse learned behaviors and expectations, so a product's understandability and ease of use are greatly affected by how closely it hews to the norm.
condition: when operating in a space characterized by common environment types

statement: Against a standard structure, small differences such as particular word choices or tone help an information environment stand out and define the brand—provided they do not go so far afield that they lose the user.
exception: if the differences go too far afield and confuse or lose the user

statement: The layers of an information environment change at different rates: page layout, visual design, and interaction mechanisms change quickly while the underlying semantic structures change slowly, paralleling Stewart Brand's shearing layers of buildings.

Information architecture primarily defines the relatively long-lived semantic structures; users become accustomed to those structures and can become disoriented if they change too abruptly, so avoid abrupt structural churn.
Given the dynamism of digital environments, graceful adaptability and extensibility are even more important for information architecture than for building architecture.

Maximum flexibility is not the ideal for an information architecture, because suppleness usually invites ambiguous language that harms clear communication; aim for a middle ground that accommodates change yet stays clear and crisp in its objectives and affordances.
Achieve the balance between flexibility and clarity by setting off parts of the environment that change at different rates as obviously separate but related subenvironments of the whole.

Information architecture aims to balance the needs of the user, the organization that owns the environment, and society as a whole; when the right balance is struck, the result is coherence and understandability across products and services.

A carefully designed organizational structure helps users understand a new or unfamiliar environment by grounding it in concepts the target audience already understands and is emotionally engaged with.

A good organizing structure accommodates organic growth and change within a coherent whole, letting new items be added to existing categories while users still accept the changes because there is an overall method to them.
Carefully chosen labels for the people in an environment—such as 'guests' and 'cast members,' or 'buyer' and 'seller'—help define and constrain how those people are expected to act within it.

Even while keeping consistency between channels, tailor the information architecture to the specific information needs of each channel's current users, because different channels serve different needs.
condition: when the same service is delivered through multiple channels

statement: Finding and understanding are not really separate goals but flip sides of the same coin: the context an environment sets information in influences how people find information in it, and vice versa.
A well-designed information architecture is invisible to users, which is a paradoxical and unfair reward for information-architecture success.

Most interactive information environments share four component systems—organization systems, labeling systems, navigation systems, and search systems—plus the largely invisible systems of thesauri, controlled vocabularies, and metadata that shape the environment behind the scenes.

When examining a page, distinguish information architecture—the organization, navigation, search, and labeling systems—from visual design, information design, and interaction design, because much of what appears on a page is not information architecture.

In top-down information architecture, designers posit a structure that anticipates and answers users' key questions (where am I, how do I search, how do I get around, what is important and unique, what is available), and the environment's form is produced to support that centrally defined structure.

In bottom-up information architecture, structure inherent in the content itself—through chunking, sequencing, and tagging—lets answers to users' questions (where am I, what is here, where can I go) rise to the surface and support searching and browsing.

Chunk content into clearly defined units placed in a logical sequence (for example a recipe's title, ingredients, then directions) so users can recognize what the content is and understand how to use and move around it before reading it in full.

Design for bottom-up use, because users increasingly bypass a site's top-down structure—arriving deep inside it via web-wide search, ads, and social-network links—and then want to jump to related content without learning the top-down structure.
Evaluate a site's bottom-up information architecture with a navigation stress test that checks, from an arbitrary entry page, whether the page answers where am I, what is here, and where can I go.

Much of information architecture is invisible: search-system configuration decisions—what is indexed, what appears in each result, how stop words are handled—and manual interventions such as editor's-choice or best-bets results are integral information-architecture decisions that users never see.

Information-architecture components can be categorized as four systems—organization, labeling, navigation, and searching—or alternatively as browsing aids, search aids, content and tasks, and invisible components; grouping them different ways helps examine them from different perspectives.

Browsing aids present users with predetermined paths and include organization systems (taxonomies/hierarchies), general and local navigation, supplemental navigation such as sitemaps and tables of contents, indices, guides, walkthroughs and wizards, and contextual navigation.

Search aids accept user-defined queries and return matching results, comprising the search interface, query language, query builders, retrieval algorithms, search zones, and the presentation of search results.

Content and tasks embed information-architecture components that help users find their way, including headings, embedded links, embedded metadata, chunks, lists, sequential aids, and identifiers such as logos and breadcrumbs.

Invisible information-architecture components operate in the background and feed other components—controlled vocabularies and thesauri enhance queries with synonyms, retrieval algorithms rank results, and best bets are preferred results manually coupled to a query by editors and subject-matter experts.
Organization and labeling are related but distinct: you organize content into groups and then label those groups, and each group can be labeled in different ways.
The way we organize, label, and relate information influences the way people comprehend that information.
Classification systems inherently reflect social and political perspectives and objectives, so information organization is never neutral.
Digital media let you apply multiple organization systems to the same content, escaping the physical single-arrangement limitations of the analog world.
Classification systems are made of language, and language is ambiguous—single words carry many meanings—so using words as category labels risks users missing the intended meaning.

Beyond agreeing on labels and their definitions, you must also agree on which documents to place in which categories, which is especially difficult when organizing abstract concepts such as subjects, topics, or functions.

The heterogeneous nature of information environments—varying granularity, formats, media, and dynamism—makes it difficult to impose any single structured organization system, so a one-size-fits-all approach to heterogeneous content is difficult and often misguided, a fundamental flaw of many enterprise taxonomy initiatives.

Do not classify documents at very different levels of granularity side by side, and do not handle differing formats the same way, because each format has uniquely important characteristics that need distinct treatment.

Labeling and organization systems are intensely shaped by their creators' perspectives—as when a site is organized by internal divisions or org charts—so to design usable organization systems you must escape your own mental models of content labeling and organization.
Use a mix of user research and analysis to learn how users group information, what labels they use, and how they navigate, rather than imposing your own organization.

No single organization system fits all users, and it is impossible to create a perfect one, but recognizing the role of perspective, understanding intended audiences through user research and testing, and providing multiple navigation pathways lets you organize information far better.

Because information organization has inherent power to shape understanding and opinion, designing information architectures involves organizational politics; be sensitive to the political environment, remind colleagues to focus on what works for users, and make compromises where needed to avoid serious conflict while managing the impact on the architecture.

As the Internet gives users the freedom to publish information, it burdens them with the responsibility to organize it, and exponential content growth creates a need for innovation in content organization.

Organization systems are composed of organization schemes (the shared characteristics that drive the logical grouping of content items) and organization structures (the types of relationships between items and groups), and both strongly affect how information is found and understood.

Isolate the design of the organization system—focusing solely on grouping information—before designing navigation and labeling, because doing so avoids implementation distractions such as the navigation UI and yields a better product.

Exact (objective) organization schemes—such as alphabetical, chronological, and geographical—divide information into well-defined, mutually exclusive sections that are easy to design, maintain, and use, but require the user to already know the specific name of what they are looking for (known-item searching).

Chronological schemes suit date-driven content such as press-release archives, but users often also want to browse by title, product category, or geography or to search by keyword, so a complementary combination of organization schemes is often necessary.

Ambiguous (subjective) organization schemes divide information into categories that defy exact definition and are harder to design, maintain, and use, yet they are often more important and useful than exact schemes because users do not always know what they are looking for or how to name it.

Ambiguous organization supports a serendipitous, associative mode of information seeking by grouping items in intellectually meaningful ways decided by someone other than the user, which helps users make new connections and reach better conclusions.

The success of an ambiguous organization scheme depends on the quality of the scheme and the careful placement of individual items within it; rigorous user testing is essential, and ongoing maintenance may require dedicated staff with subject-matter expertise.

Most information environments should provide some topical access to content, and when designing a topical scheme you must define the breadth of coverage because you are defining the universe of present and future content users will expect to find there; topical groupings are cultural constructs that can vary over time, not fixed.

Task-oriented schemes organize content into collections of processes, functions, or tasks and are appropriate when you can anticipate a limited number of high-priority tasks users will perform; they are common in apps and transaction-focused sites but are rarely used as the sole organization of a whole site.
condition: when a limited number of high-priority tasks can be anticipated

statement: Audience-specific schemes make sense when there are two or more clearly definable audiences and value in customizing content for each; they can be open (allowing cross-audience access) or closed, but they carry the peril of personalization because users may not fit neatly into one audience, so these educated guesses must be revisited over time.
condition: when there are two or more clearly definable audiences and value in customizing per audience

statement: Use caution before adopting a metaphor-driven global organization scheme: metaphors must be familiar to users to succeed, and they carry unwanted baggage and limits—users import real-world expectations, and services with no real-world corollary force you to break the metaphor and introduce inconsistency.

A pure organization scheme's power derives from its ability to suggest a simple mental model that users grasp quickly, and fairly small pure schemes can be applied to large amounts of content without sacrificing integrity or usability.

Blending multiple organization schemes into a deep hybrid causes confusion and does not scale, because users cannot form a mental model and must skim every item; shallow hybrid schemes at the surface navigation layer are fine, but deep hybrid schemes are not.
exception: shallow hybrid schemes limited to top-priority topics and tasks in surface or global navigation are acceptable

statement: When multiple organization schemes must appear on one page, preserve the integrity of each by presenting them separately, so each retains its power to suggest a mental model for users.

The major organization structures for information architectures are the hierarchy, the database-oriented model, and hypertext; each has unique strengths and weaknesses, and in many cases it makes sense to use all three in a complementary manner.

A well-designed hierarchy is the foundation of many good information architectures because its mutually exclusive subdivisions and familiar parent-child relationships let users quickly build a mental model of the structure and of their own location within it.

Start the information-architecture process with a hierarchy, because the top-down approach lets you grasp the scope of the environment quickly—identifying major content areas and candidate organization schemes—without first performing an extensive content inventory.

Be aware of, but not bound by, the rule that hierarchical categories should be mutually exclusive: balance exclusivity against inclusivity by cross-listing ambiguous items into two or more categories (polyhierarchy) so users can find them, but do not cross-list so many items that the hierarchy loses its value.
exception: if too many items are cross-listed the hierarchy loses its value

statement: The tension between exclusivity and inclusivity exists within a single organization scheme, not across different schemes: independent facets such as topic and format are simply two different ways of looking at the same set of items.

Balance breadth (options per level) against depth (number of levels): a hierarchy that is too narrow and deep forces users through an inordinate number of clicks, while one that is too broad and shallow overwhelms the main menu and disappoints users with too little content behind each option.

Constrain the breadth of a level by users' visual scanning ability rather than by short-term-memory limits, so do not blindly follow the seven-plus-or-minus-two rule; instead recognize the danger of overloading users with options, group and structure information at the page level, and subject designs to rigorous user testing.

Be even more conservative with depth than with breadth: if users are forced to click through more than two or three levels they may give up and leave, or at least become frustrated, and a balance of breadth and depth tends to give the best results.

For new information environments expected to grow, lean toward a broad-and-shallow rather than a narrow-and-deep hierarchy, because adding content to secondary levels is less disruptive and less expensive than changing the prominent, carefully designed main page.
condition: for new environments expected to grow

statement: Do not become trapped by the hierarchical model: certain content areas invite a database or hypertext-based approach, and the hierarchy—though a good place to begin—is only one component of a cohesive organization system.

Metadata is the primary key that links information architecture to database schema design: by tagging documents and information objects with metadata you apply the structure and power of relational databases to heterogeneous, unstructured web content, enabling powerful searching, browsing, filtering, and dynamic linking.

You need not be an expert in SQL, XML schema, entity-relationship diagrams, or relational-database design, but you must understand how metadata, controlled vocabularies, and database structures enable automatically generated indexes, dynamic 'see also' links, fielded searching, and advanced filtering and sorting—often working with a professional database designer and relying on a content management system.

The database model is particularly useful within relatively homogeneous subsites such as product catalogs and staff directories, while enterprise controlled vocabularies can provide a thin horizontal layer of structure across a whole site, with deeper vertical vocabularies created for particular departments, subjects, or audiences.
condition: within relatively homogeneous subsites

statement: Hypertext structures information nonlinearly as chunks connected by links, which gives great flexibility but also substantial potential for complexity and user confusion, because links reflect highly personal associations that may not be apparent to others and users can get lost without a mental model of the environment.

Hypertext is rarely a good candidate for the primary organization structure; use it to complement hierarchical or database structures, first designing the information hierarchy and then identifying where hypertext can complement it.

Social classification, driven mainly by user-generated free tagging (folksonomy), is an important tool for organizing information in shared environments; the tags are public and serve as pivots for social navigation, letting users move fluidly between objects, authors, tags, and indexers.

Free-form tagging does not eliminate the need for top-down, centrally defined information structures—pure tag-driven systems such as Delicious largely fizzled and most tag systems operate within centrally defined structures—but free tagging remains a valuable tool in specific situations.

All information-retrieval systems work best when applied to narrow domains of homogeneous content, so decompose the content collection into narrow homogeneous domains to identify opportunities for highly effective organization systems.

Break a complex information environment into its components so you can tackle one organization question at a time, but do not lose sight of the big picture, because a cohesive organization system requires mixing the right schemes and structures for that specific environment.

Use exact schemes for known-item searching (when users know precisely what they want) and ambiguous schemes for browsing and associative learning (when users have a vaguely defined need), and whenever possible use both types of schemes.

Providing multiple ways to access the same information helps deal with the core challenges of organizing information on the Web—ambiguous language, heterogeneous content, differing perspectives, and politics.

Large systems typically require several types of organization structure: the top-level umbrella architecture will almost certainly be hierarchical, collections of structured homogeneous information are excellent candidates for the database model, and less-structured creative relationships between items can be handled through author-supplied hypertext or user-contributed tagging.

Labeling is a form of representation: a label stands for a larger chunk of information and communicates its meaning efficiently, without taking up too much of a page's physical space or the user's cognitive space.

Because an information environment is a disintermediated medium with few visual cues and little or delayed feedback, communicating with users is harder, which makes labeling more important than in face-to-face communication.

Design labels that speak the same language as your environment's users while reflecting its content, provide clarification and explanation where a label may confuse, and use labels to educate people about new concepts and help them quickly identify familiar ones.
Successful labels are often invisible—they communicate without getting in the user's way.

Labels must be representative and differentiating: labels that do not represent the content they link to, or that fail to distinguish similar-sounding items (such as 'Menu,' 'Coffee,' 'Coffeehouse,' and 'Shop'), force users to click through to learn what they mean and create too much potential for confusion to be effective.

Avoid organizational jargon in labels and use user-centric language, because jargon labels are clear only to the tiny fraction of users who work for the organization and can lose customers—for example, labeling a product-ordering system an 'Order Processing and Fulfillment Facility' is a sure way to lose a sale.

Confusing labels waste money: whenever the architecture forces a user to pause and say 'huh?', there is a real chance the user gives up and goes elsewhere, negating the investment made to design, build, and market the site.

Labeling shapes the impression an information environment makes about the organization and its brand, so poor labeling can destroy a user's confidence, and labels are as integral to an effective web presence as brand, visual design, functionality, content, or navigability.

The meaning of a label can shift across channels—for example 'Menu' is often experienced in a mobile browser as the main navigation menu rather than a restaurant menu—so test labels in the context of each channel where they will be experienced.
condition: when labels are experienced across multiple channels

statement: Labels come in textual and iconic formats, and textual labels appear as several varieties—contextual links, headings, navigation-system choices, and index terms (keywords, tags, subject headings)—which are not mutually exclusive, so a single label can do double duty across them.

Contextual links are easy to create but are usually developed ad hoc rather than systematically, so their labels mean different things to different people; a contextual-link label draws its meaning from the surrounding text, and if the author fails to establish that context the label loses its representational value.

Before creating and labeling a contextual link, ask 'What kind of information will the person expect to be taken to?'—simply asking this improves representation—and study people's interpretations by giving them a page with the labels marked and having them write what they expect each to link to.

Because contextual links are usually authored by content creators and are often outside the information architect's control, prefer suggesting guidelines to content authors (for example, link employee names to directory listings when possible) over enforcing rigid rules.

Headings label the chunks of content that follow them and establish hierarchy within content, and the parent, child, or sibling relationships between headings are usually conveyed visually through consistent numbering, font sizes, colors and styles, and whitespace and indentation.
A visually clear hierarchy can take pressure off labels, because a set of labels that individually mean little can take on meaning once presented within a clear hierarchy.

Do not be too rigidly bound to showcasing hierarchical relationships in headings: apply heading emphasis where it helps users, but content that readers already recognize visually (such as a game schedule) does not need the same heading treatment as other sections.

Maintain consistency especially when labeling steps in a process: heading labels must be obvious and convey sequence, so use numbers to show progression and consistently frame the labels as action verbs that tell users where to start, where to go next, and what action each step involves.
condition: when labeling steps in a process users must complete in order

statement: Navigation labels demand consistent application more than any other label type, because a single inconsistent option introduces an 'apples and oranges' effect quickly in a small navigation set of fewer than ten choices, and navigation labeling problems are magnified through the repeated exposure a navigation system gets throughout the environment.

Navigation labels must not change from page to page—using 'Main' on one page, 'Main Page' on another, and 'Home' elsewhere destroys the familiarity users rely on—so apply each navigation label consistently, ideally in a consistent location and look as well.

Prefer common familiar navigation-label variants (such as Home, Search, Contact Us, Help/FAQ, and About Us) and apply one consistent choice, because these labels are already familiar to most web users.

The same label can represent different kinds of information in different systems, so if you use one label in different ways within your own system your users will be confused; one remedy is to add brief descriptions under navigation labels, at the cost of screen real estate.

Index-term labels (keywords, tags, descriptive metadata, taxonomies, controlled vocabularies, thesauri) represent a piece of content's meaning and support more precise searching than searching the full text, because a human has assessed the content's meaning and described it with those terms.

Index terms also make browsing easier and provide an alternative view that cuts across the grain of organizational silos, and they are often invisible to users—stored in content-management records or HTML meta and title tags—so a search on 'sofa' can retrieve a page even when the word 'sofa' does not appear in its text.

Using index terms from controlled vocabularies or thesauri gives a systematic way to describe a delineated domain consistently and predictably, which becomes more valuable when you need your pages to stand out from one another.

Iconic labels are a much more limited language than text, so use them for small option sets such as navigation or small organization labels rather than large sets like index terms, and avoid placing form ahead of function unless you have a patient, loyal audience willing to learn your visual language.
exception: when a patient, loyal audience will learn the icon language through repeated exposure

statement: Designing effective labels is perhaps the hardest part of information architecture: language is too ambiguous to ever perfect a label, labels will never be perfect, and measuring label effectiveness is extremely difficult, so seek guidelines rather than incontrovertible rules.
Content, users, and context affect all aspects of information architecture and are especially decisive for labels, because any of their variables can drag a label into ambiguity.

Narrow the scope of an information environment whenever possible, because a more defined audience and fewer subject domains reduce the number of possible interpretations of a label and yield clearer, more effective labels; too many environments take on too much and achieve broad mediocrity rather than nailing a few choice tasks.

If an environment must be a jack of all trades, avoid labels that address the entire system's content—except for global navigation, which necessarily does—and instead modularize content into audience-specific subsections with their own simpler, modular labeling systems.
exception: labels for global navigation systems, which legitimately cover the entire system

statement: Design consistent labeling systems, not just individual labels, because consistency means predictability and predictable systems are easier to learn: seeing one or two labels tells users what to expect from the rest, which benefits all users and makes the labeling effectively invisible.

Manage the dimensions that affect labeling consistency: style (use style guides for punctuation and case), presentation (consistent fonts, colors, whitespace, and grouping), syntax (choose one of verb-, noun-, or question-based form and keep it), granularity (labels roughly equal in specificity), comprehensiveness (no noticeable gaps), and audience (separate labeling systems where audiences use very different terminology).

Start designing labels from existing labeling systems—your current site and comparable or competitors' sites—rather than from scratch, which is prohibitively expensive for large vocabularies; a key benefit of existing labeling systems is that they are already systems, so study, learn from, and borrow what works.

Reuse your current environment's labels as a starting point and capture them in a single label table—walking the whole system and listing each label with the documents it represents—because arranging labels as a table gives a condensed, complete, accurate view of the system and makes inconsistencies easier to catch; this does not scale to large index-term vocabularies.
exception: index-term vocabularies are too large to table-ize unless you focus on small, focused segments

statement: Learn labeling systems from comparable and competitive environments: first determine your audiences' likely needs, then survey competitors' or best-in-class sites, borrowing what works and noting what does not.

Labeling patterns that emerge across multiple competitive or comparable environments can inform your label choices even before they become industry standards—for example a de facto label such as 'personal finance' may discourage you from choosing a synonym.

Existing controlled vocabularies and thesauri are a great source of labels because they were created by library or subject-matter professionals who have already done much of the work of ensuring accurate representation and consistency, are often publicly available, and are most useful for populating labeling systems used to index content.

Seek out narrowly focused vocabularies matched to your specific audience and content—for example a computer-science thesaurus for computer scientists—because they represent concepts the way your users understand better than a general scheme, and always check whether a useful vocabulary exists before building one from scratch.
When you must create labeling systems from scratch, your most important sources are your content and its authors, and the people who will use the environment.

Derive candidate labels through content analysis by reading a representative sample of content and noting descriptive keywords, but this is slow and does not scale to huge document sets, so speed it up by focusing on existing content representations such as titles, summaries, and abstracts.

Entity-extraction (auto-extraction) software can save time deriving terms from a huge body of content but typically only gets you about 80% of the way, so treat its output as candidate controlled-vocabulary terms that still need manual validation, and note the tools and their tuning can be expensive.

Content authors can suggest labels for their own content, but take those labels with a grain of salt and do not rely on them for accuracy, because authors do not realize their document is one of many in a broader collection, may not use sufficiently specific labels, and are rarely professional indexers—treat author labels as candidates, not final versions.

User advocates and subject-matter experts—such as librarians, switchboard operators, and reference staff who are familiar with users' information needs in a larger context—are a valuable source of labels, because their constant interaction gives them a good innate sense of what people want.

When no ideal controlled vocabulary exists and there is no content to draw from yet, use a top-down approach with knowledgeable advocates: determine users' major needs and categories, then generate terms appropriate to the audience—for a lay audience use everyday terms like 'leg' rather than 'femur.'
condition: when there is no matching vocabulary and no existing content to mine

statement: The actual users of a system are the best source of labeling there is if you can get the information from them, because they can tell you what the labels should be.

Card sorting is one of the best ways to learn how users categorize information: open card sorts have users cluster content into their own categories and name them, while closed card sorts have users sort content into your existing categories and define what each category label means—more similar user definitions indicate a stronger label—and both are most appropriate for smaller label sets such as navigation.

Card sorts do not present labels in the context of an actual product, so a label's ability to represent meaning is diminished; card sorting has value but should not be the only method used to investigate label quality.

Free-listing is an even lower-cost way to get users to suggest labels: pick an item and have representative participants brainstorm terms to describe it, optionally ranking them; three to five participants are not statistically significant but are far better than nothing.

Analyze the results of labeling exercises for patterns and frequency of usage—for example whether users prefer 'cell phone' or 'mobile phone'—because such patterns reveal both how to label an individual item and the overall tone and style (jargon, acronyms) of your users' language to adopt in the labeling system.

Search log analysis is one of the least intrusive sources of the labels your audience actually uses in their own language, so mine query logs (and Google AdWords term data) to tune labels—deciding whether to use jargon, choosing short or long labels, and connecting user-supplied terms like 'pooch' to preferred terms like 'dog' via thesaurus-style lookup.

Turn a raw list of labels into a labeling system by sorting the terms alphabetically, removing duplicates, and reviewing for consistency of usage, punctuation, and letter case while establishing conventions for punctuation and style.

Decide which terms to include based on how broad and large the system must be, and check for obvious gaps against all possibilities the environment may eventually need; if you are uncertain whether scope will expand, assume it will and devise labels for the additional content now.

For a topical labeling system, anticipate the topics not yet covered and add these 'phantom' labels during design, because failing to plan ahead leads to future content that does not fit or that ends up in cop-out categories such as 'Miscellaneous,' 'Other Info,' and 'Stuff.'

Balance planning for the future against what the labeling system must accomplish today: keep the scope narrow and focused enough to address your environment's unique content, its audiences' special needs, and the business objective, but be comprehensive within that well-defined scope.

A labeling system is never finished: because labels represent a constantly changing relationship between people and content, the system you launch will need tweaking shortly after, so be prepared to run usability tests, analyze search logs regularly, and adjust the labels as necessary.

A well-designed taxonomy reduces the chance that users get lost, but complementary navigation tools are often still needed to provide context and greater flexibility; structure and organization build the rooms, and navigation design adds the doors and windows.

Navigation systems have two kinds of elements: embedded global, local, and contextual navigation integrated within pages (providing context and flexibility—where you are and where you can go, and generally necessary but not sufficient alone) and supplemental systems outside content pages, where sitemaps give a bird's-eye view, A-to-Z indexes allow direct access, and guides offer linear navigation customized to an audience, task, or topic.

Navigation design sits in the gray area between information architecture, interaction design, information design, visual design, and usability engineering, so interdisciplinary collaboration is the ideal and works best when each expert understands something about the others' areas of expertise.

Because navigation is so important to the user's experience, designers must be judicious when experimenting with new and untested navigation schemes, since much research has gone into established browser and operating-system navigation features and users expect them to work consistently.

Transmitting a clear context—what the environment is and what you can expect to find and do in it—makes information more easily understandable, so creating a sense of place through language and giving users clear paths to explore are among the key roles navigation systems play.

Before a user can plot a course they must locate their position, so provide a 'You Are Here' indicator, because online environments lack the natural landmarks of the physical world and hypertext can transport users right into the middle of an unfamiliar system, bypassing the main page.

Ensure users always know which site or app they are in even if they bypass the front door and enter through a search engine or a deep link, by extending the organization's name, logo, and graphic identity throughout the environment.

The navigation system should present as much of the information hierarchy's structure as possible in a clear and consistent manner and indicate the user's current location, because this helps users build a mental model of the organization scheme, which facilitates navigation and makes them feel comfortable.

Run a navigation stress test on an existing site: ignore the home page and jump into the middle, and for each random page check whether you can tell where you are relative to the rest of the site, what section and parent page you are in, and whether the links are descriptive and distinct enough to show where they lead.

Pure hierarchies are limiting from a navigation perspective, whereas the Web's hypertext supports both lateral navigation across branches and vertical navigation between levels, so it is often desirable to let users move sideways, up or down, or back to the main page—getting anywhere from anywhere.

Balance the advantages of navigation flexibility against the dangers of clutter: too few lateral and vertical navigation aids is very limiting in a large environment, but too many bury the hierarchy and overwhelm the user, so design navigation to complement and reinforce the hierarchy by adding context and flexibility.

A global navigation system is intended to appear on every page of a site, often as a top navigation bar, giving users direct access to key areas and functions no matter where they are in the site's hierarchy.

A global navigation bar should link to the home page (usually via the logo) and to search, and should also reinforce the site's structure and indicate the user's current location; when it does neither it pushes the burden of providing context down to the local level and opens the door for inconsistency and disorientation, and because one size does not fit all these decisions must be informed by user needs and the organization's goals, content, technology, and culture.

Because the global navigation bar is often the single consistent navigation element on a site and therefore has a huge impact on usability, subject it to intensive, iterative user-centered design and testing.

Local navigation systems complement global navigation to let users explore the immediate area, and large sites often have multiple local systems called subsites, which exist because certain content and functionality merit a unique navigation approach and because decentralized organizations have different groups responsible for different content areas.

Variation between local navigation systems should be driven by user needs and the local content, not merely by different design groups choosing to run in different directions, so organizations must decide how much central control to exercise over the look and feel of their local navigation systems.

Contextual navigation links specific to a page or object (such as 'see also' or related-product links) support associative learning by letting users explore relationships you define, creating connective tissue that benefits both users and the organization through cross-selling, up-selling, and brand-building; defining these links is often more editorial than architectural, done by an author, editor, or subject-matter expert.

Inline contextual links are problematic when they are critical to the content, because usability testing shows users scan pages so quickly that they miss or ignore inconspicuous links, so give critical contextual links a dedicated area of the page or a distinct visual convention.
condition: when contextual links are critical to the content

statement: Moderation is the primary rule of thumb for contextual links: used sparingly they complement existing navigation by adding a degree of flexibility, but used in excess they add clutter and confusion, so let the nature and importance of the links determine the approach on each page.

When designing a contextual navigation system, imagine that every page on the site is a main page or portal in its own right, because once a user identifies a particular product or document the rest of the site fades into the background and that page becomes their interface—so ask where they might want to go from there.

Balance freedom of movement against the danger of overwhelming users: global, local, and contextual navigation coexist on most pages, and if designed independently they combine to monopolize screen real estate and drown out the content, so integrate them so they complement one another and revisit the number of options in each bar when needed.

Navigation implementation depends on the medium: desktop browsers place global navigation at the top with local navigation alongside the content and favor clear text labels, while mobile hides navigation offscreen behind a menu button or places primary navigation at the bottom within thumb reach and often uses icons; know the conventions and limitations of your medium and test any deviation from the norm with users before release.

Supplemental navigation systems—sitemaps, indexes, guides, and search—are external to the basic hierarchy and provide complementary ways of finding content; they are critical to usability and findability in large systems but are often not given the care they deserve.

The taxonomy and the embedded navigation systems will always fail for a significant percentage of users and tasks, so supplemental navigation systems give users an emergency backup; do not assume that getting the taxonomy right will address all users and needs.

A sitemap presents the top few levels of the information hierarchy to give a broad view and facilitate random access, and it is most natural for large systems that lend themselves to hierarchical organization; if the architecture is not strongly hierarchical use an index or alternate representation, and for a small environment with only two or three levels a sitemap may be unnecessary.
exception: a small two-or-three-level environment may not need a sitemap

statement: Design a sitemap to reinforce the information hierarchy so users grow familiar with how content is organized, to facilitate fast direct access for users who know what they want, and to avoid overwhelming users with too much information—the goal is to help, not scare.

An index presents keywords or phrases alphabetically without representing the hierarchy and is relatively flat, so it works well for users who already know the name of the item; large complex sites often need both a sitemap (which reinforces the hierarchy and encourages exploration) and an index (which bypasses the hierarchy and facilitates known-item finding), plus search.

A major challenge in indexing a site is the level of granularity (whether to index pages, paragraphs, or collections—often all three), but the more valuable question is what terms users will look for, which should guide index design and requires knowing your audience through search-log analysis and user research.

Build a small system's index manually using your knowledge of the full content collection, but for a large site with distributed content management use controlled-vocabulary indexing at the document level to automatically generate a two-step index in which the user first selects a term and then selects from the documents indexed with it.

Term rotation (permutation) lets users find a phrase in two places in the alphabetical index (for example both 'Abuse, Elder' and 'Elder Maltreatment'), supporting the varied ways people look for information, but apply it selectively by balancing the probability that users seek a term against the annoyance of cluttering the index with too many permutations.

Guides (guided tours, tutorials, and walk-throughs for a specific audience, topic, or task) supplement navigation and introduce new users; design them with linear navigation but also offer hypertext for flexibility, keep them short, always let the user exit, keep Previous/Home/Next navigation consistent, design them to answer questions, and use crisp screenshots—remembering a guide will not play a central day-to-day role.

Configurators and wizards help users traverse complex decision trees, and the best ones combine a linear process with the ability to jump between steps and keep global navigation always present for context; because users often do not understand the impact of their choices, provide contextual clues that show the effect of each option.

Search puts users in the driver's seat by letting them use their own keyword terms and enables great specificity—finding a phrase unlikely to appear in a sitemap or index—but the ambiguity of language causes huge problems, because users, authors, and information architects all use different words for the same things.

Master the integration of the fundamental navigation building blocks before attempting advanced navigation approaches, because advanced navigation is a minefield that only works on a solid foundation.

Personalization (the system guesses what the user wants from a behavior model) and customization (the user directly controls presentation, navigation, and content) typically play important but limited roles, require a solid foundation of structure and organization, are really difficult to do well, and can make metrics harder to collect—so treat them as refinements, not the solution to all navigation problems.

Personalization works well in limited contexts but fails when expanded to drive the entire user experience, because users often do not share enough information to teach the system and it is genuinely hard to predict what people will want to do, learn, or buy tomorrow.

Customization works only where users are willing to invest effort—a handful of most-important sites, and better on intranets with a captive audience of repeat visitors—and where needs are stable (such as tracking a favorite team or owned stocks), but works poorly for broad or changing news and research needs because even users do not always know what they will want tomorrow.

Visualization-based navigation has mostly failed—metaphor-driven physical-place displays and fly-through sitemaps looked impressive but proved not very useful—and has proven most useful only when the user must select among a result set of elements they recognize by their looks, as when shopping for physical goods.

Social navigation derives value for the individual from observing other users' actions—from simple popularity or voting systems to complex social-graph algorithms—but avoid over-tuning navigation to a user's social groups, which can devolve into echo chambers that downplay alternative viewpoints, and keep a consistent global structure because people need shared, stable structure for placemaking over time.

Think twice before making a product searchable and do not assume a search engine alone will satisfy all users' information needs, because there are other ways to support finding and some users are natural browsers who prefer not to use the search box.

There is no specific content-volume threshold that merits a search engine; what matters more is the typical information need of your users, so if your product is more like a library than a software application (users have specific information in mind) search probably makes sense, balancing setup and maintenance cost against the payoff.

Do not let a search engine become a Band-Aid for poorly designed navigation; if you are falling into that trap, suspend implementing search until you fix the navigation problems, because search performs better when it can leverage strong navigation such as controlled-vocabulary tags and users benefit most when both work together.
exception: when navigation cannot be fixed for political reasons, search may indeed be the best alternative

statement: Search engines are fairly easy to get running but difficult to implement effectively, and inscrutable search results usually come from installing an engine with its default settings and forgetting it, so if you do not plan to invest significant time configuring it properly, reconsider implementing it.

Consider alternatives to search and your users' preferences before committing: an index is easier to implement (typically manual) and, like search, helps users who know what they want, while a third-party search engine is cost-effective but separates search from other finding into a disjointed experience and cannot generate your own search-analytics data.

Implement search when you have too much information to browse, when the site is fragmented into content silos (do full-text indexing across silos as at least a stopgap that also reveals what content exists), to use search-log analysis as a learning tool, because users expect a search box as a default convention, and to tame highly dynamic content by automatically indexing it instead of cataloging it manually.

A search system comprises the search engine (indexing and spidering plus algorithms that process the query and rank results), query interfaces ranging from simple boxes to voice-driven ones, decisions about how to display each result and the whole set, and query-language and query-builder variations; the technical guts can be left to IT while the information architect focuses on factors that affect retrieval performance.

The information-architecture team must be part of the search-system selection and implementation, arguing for at least equal responsibility to choose the engine that best serves users rather than the one that runs on someone's favorite platform or is written in someone's favorite programming language.

Searching is often iterative—not only because users dislike the results they retrieve, but because it takes a few tries to get the query words right—since a user senses an information gap but is not always sure how to express what they are looking for.

Indexing the full text of every document makes search comprehensive and fast to cover a huge amount of content, but indexing everything does not always serve users well, because in a large heterogeneous environment unrelated content muddies the results.

Create search zones—subsets of more homogeneous content indexed separately—to reduce the apples-and-oranges effect and let users focus their searches for fewer, more relevant results; your organization schemes (content type, audience, role, topic, geography, chronology, author, department) can serve as the basis for search zones.

Search zones are a double-edged sword: narrowing a search through zones can improve results but interacting with them adds a layer of complexity, and many users ignore search zones on their first pass by entering a simple query against the global index, only using zones on a second, advanced pass—so do not force zones on users.

Distinguish navigation pages from destination pages, because a user who searches is looking for destination pages, so including navigation pages in the retrieval just clutters the results—in one example the right destination page came back alongside five navigation index pages, meaning 83% of the retrieval obstructed the user.

The navigation/destination distinction is an exact scheme that requires each page to be one or the other, but 'similar' is relative and some pages are both, so test the navigation/destination distinctions before applying them; ambiguous zone approaches such as by audience, topic, or recency are more forgiving of pages that fit multiple categories.

Audience-based search zones make sense when you already use an audience-oriented organization scheme and content is audience-specific; less overlap between the indexes improves performance, but if separate indexes only reduce retrieval by a small amount such as 10-20%, the overhead of creating them may not be worth it.
condition: when using an audience-oriented organization scheme with audience-specific content

statement: Chronologically organized content allows perhaps the easiest implementation of search zones, because dated materials are generally unambiguous and date information is easy to obtain, so you can create date-based zones and even let users generate ad hoc date-range zones.

Let users search specific content components of documents to retrieve more precise results, and exclude administrative or meaningless components such as navigation options, advertisements, disclaimers, and header/footer text; indexing numerous content components also makes search results more meaningful, and content management systems with logical markup make it easier to leave the unwanted content out.

There is a paradox in search design: even if users would benefit from advanced search functionality, they likely will not ask for it during initial user research because they do not understand the intricacies and capabilities of search systems, so rather than relying only on use cases, examine other search interfaces that your users already find valuable and decide whether to offer similar functionality.

A retrieval algorithm is essentially a tool, and specific algorithms solve specific problems, so there is absolutely no single search engine that will meet all of your users' information needs—remember that when a vendor claims a brand-new proprietary algorithm is the solution to all information problems.

Most retrieval algorithms use pattern matching—comparing the user's query against an index of, typically, the full text of documents and adding a document to the retrieval set when a matching string is found—but this matching process can work in many different ways to produce different results.

Recall and precision are the opposite ends of the retrieval spectrum and are inversely related, so you cannot have both at once and must decide which balance most benefits your users: high recall for exhaustive needs like legal, scientific, or due-diligence research, and high precision when users want just two or three really good answers.

Stemming expands a query to include terms sharing the same root and so raises recall, while weak or no stemming raises precision and lowers recall, so choose the degree of stemming based on the kinds of information needs your users have.

Structured content with fields the search engine can see enables higher precision, because searching for 'William Faulkner' in an author field returns books he authored rather than every full-text document that merely mentions him.

Document-similarity, citation (cited-by, active bibliography, co-citation), and collaborative-filtering algorithms expand results from a single relevant document, but because the main purpose of all retrieval algorithms is to identify the best pool of documents and 'best' is subjective, you must grasp what users hope to find before choosing an algorithm.

Query builders such as spell checkers, phonetic tools, stemming tools, natural-language-processing tools, and controlled vocabularies or thesauri soup up query performance and are often invisible to users, so select which ones make sense from your users' information needs and confirm whether your search engine supports them.
Spell checkers correct an almost universal problem among searchers—search logs show a preponderance of typos and misspellings in queries—so they are well worth considering for your search system.

Display less information to users who know what they are looking for—representational components such as title or author—and more to users who are unsure—descriptive components such as a summary, abstract, or keywords; you may let users choose, but set the default from their most common information needs.
When a commonly displayed field such as the title makes retrieved documents hard to distinguish, show more differentiating information such as a page number to help the user tell results apart.

Because many if not most users never venture past the first screen of results, do not go overboard displaying lots of content per result, since heavy first results can obscure the rest of the retrieval.

Which content components to display for each result depends on what components exist in the document and how the content will be used—phone directories should show the number in the result itself rather than behind a click—and when there is little structure or the engine searches full text, showing the query terms bolded within their surrounding sentence helps users quickly scan for the relevant part of each result.

How many documents to display depends on how much information is shown per result and on the user's screen resolution, connectivity, and browser, so err on the side of simplicity with a small number of results while offering settings, and let users know the total number retrieved and provide a results-navigation system.

The moment a user is confronted by a large result set is often the moment they decide it is too large, which is a golden opportunity to offer them the option of revising and narrowing their search, for example by repeating the query in the search box.

There are two common methods for listing retrieval results: sorting (chronologically by date or alphabetically by a content component such as title, author, or department) and ranking (by a retrieval algorithm such as relevance or popularity).

Sorting is especially helpful to users making a decision or taking an action (such as sorting products by price), so offer sorting on components that actually help accomplish tasks, whereas ranking is more useful when users need to understand or learn something; because users assume the top few ranked results are best, choose relevance-ranking approaches carefully.

Alphabetical sorting is a good general-purpose approach, especially for names, and it works best to omit initial articles such as 'a' and 'the' from the sort order; use reverse-chronological sorting for news and press releases and plain chronological order for presenting historical data.

Relevance-ranking algorithms are typically based on how many query terms occur in a document, how frequently, how close together, where they occur (a term in the title may outweigh one in the body), and the document's popularity; because most searched content is heterogeneous, the more heterogeneous your documents the more careful you must be with relevance ranking.

Human indexing establishes relevance through manually selected 'best bets'—preferred results coupled with a query in advance—but because best bets require an investment of human expertise and time they are not suitable for every query and are typically reserved for the most common queries (identified by search-log analysis) and combined with automatically generated results.

Popularity ranking such as Google's PageRank, which factors in the number and quality of links to a document, works well for large multisite environments with a wide scope of usage and a rich set of links, but small sites and nonlinked 'silo' environments do not have enough variation in document popularity or cross-linking to benefit from this approach.
condition: for large multisite environments with rich link structure

statement: User or expert ratings and pay-for-placement can also order results: ratings-based ranking requires a sufficient volume of motivated users that most sites lack (though displaying ratings with a document can still help), while pay-for-placement can put a paid result above more relevant ones and suits systems that aggregate content from multiple vendors for shoppers.

No single listing approach is perfect, and as result sets grow ideal results get buried beyond where users give up, so consider clustering retrieved results by a common aspect—studies show clustering by category alongside a ranked list improves performance—where clusters from manually applied metadata like topic, audience, and product family are far more useful than clusters from existing metadata like file type or date, though manual clustering can be prohibitively expensive and behaves like generating search zones on the fly.

Use contextual inquiry and task analysis to understand what users want to do with their results, and support common post-result actions: a call to action that lets users act directly from a result, a way to select a subset of results (a shopping-cart mechanism, useful in search-intensive environments like library catalogs), and the ability to save a search for re-execution over time in dynamic domains.

There is no single ideal search interface, because variables such as users' searching expertise and motivation, the type of information need, the type of information being searched, and the amount of information all preclude a single right way to design it.

Unless your users are librarians, researchers, or specialized professionals, they will not invest much time crafting well-considered queries, so the burden of searching falls on the search engine, its interfaces, and how content is tagged and indexed—therefore keep the search interface as simple as possible, presenting a simple search box and a search button while burying advanced features in an advanced interface or building them invisibly into the engine.

Users make assumptions about how a search interface works—that they can just type descriptive terms, need no Boolean operators, need not worry about synonyms or fielded searching, and that the query searches the whole site—so test for these assumptions, and if your users hold them and are not motivated to learn more, go with the flow and give them the simple search box.

A help page explaining advanced queries is rarely visited, so instead look for opportunities to educate users when they are ready to learn—best after their initial searches, at the point of indecision or frustration when they are ready to revise their search.

Keep search limited to a single box unless your functionality truly requires more than one field (as with many travel services), in which case label the fields clearly, and place the search box consistently alongside global navigation with a button labeled 'search' so users know where to type their queries.

Autocomplete and autosuggest present possible matches beside the search box from the first characters typed—culled from search indexes, controlled vocabularies, or manual match lists—and are useful because they help users identify matches from partial information and hint at how the system is structured, which has mostly supplanted dedicated advanced-search mechanisms.

Advanced search interfaces serve advanced searchers (librarians, lawyers, researchers) and frustrated searchers revising an initial search, so if your system could benefit from advanced search, expose the heavy-duty functions on an advanced page for the few who want them but design the search system so the vast majority never need to go there.

Support search revision by repeating the query in the results page so users can modify it without re-entering it, explaining where results came from (which content or search zones were searched), and explaining what happened behind the scenes—restating the query, the content searched, any filters, implicit operators such as a default AND, the sort order, and the number of results; both too many and zero results are good signals to revise.
Look for opportunities to integrate searching with browsing—thinking of them together as 'finding'—so users can easily jump back and forth between the search and browse systems.

Handle oversized result sets by providing instruction on how to narrow the search and by letting users search within their current result set, since winnowing an oversized set is a form of search revision and users often self-select when they are ready to stop reviewing results.

Adopt a 'no dead ends' policy so users always have another option even when they retrieve zero results: a means of revising the search, search tips or advice on improving it, a means of browsing such as the navigation system or sitemap, and a human contact if searching and browsing will not work.
