An interactive information environment is a collection of interconnected systems with complex dependencies—a single link can simultaneously be part of the structure, organization, labeling, navigation, and searching systems—so study the systems independently but also consider how they interact, because reductionism will not tell the whole truth.

In large metadata-driven products, controlled vocabularies become the glue that holds the systems together, and a thesaurus on the backend can enable a more seamless and satisfying user experience on the frontend.

Draw on the decades of thesaurus-design experience from libraries, museums, and government agencies, but do not copy indiscriminately, because the systems you design present new challenges and demand creative solutions.

Metadata tags describe documents, pages, images, software, and video and audio objects for the purposes of improved navigation and retrieval, and the metadata-driven model shifts the design question from 'Where do I place this document in the taxonomy?' to 'How do I describe this document?', letting the software and vocabulary systems handle the rest.

Controlled vocabularies form a ladder of increasing sophistication: a synonym ring (a list of equivalent terms), an authority file (a list of preferred terms), a classification scheme (terms with defined broader/narrower relationships), and a thesaurus (which adds associative see-also/see-related relationships and integrates all the simpler forms).

A synonym ring connects a set of words defined as equivalent for retrieval (often not true synonyms), built from the variations found in search logs and content by exploding a user's query to include all the equivalent terms; there is really no excuse for the absence of this basic capability on large information environments.

Synonym rings can dramatically improve recall—one 1980s Bellcore study raised recall from 20% to 80%—but can reduce precision and confuse users with results that do not contain their keywords, so strike the balance with good interface design, for example using synonym rings by default while ordering exact keyword matches at the top, or ignoring them for the initial search but offering to 'expand your search to include related terms' when there are few or no results.

An authority file is strictly a list of preferred terms, but in practice includes both preferred and variant terms (a synonym ring in which one term is marked preferred); defining preferred terms benefits the backend (authors and indexers apply approved terms consistently, and the preferred term is a unique identifier for managing variants) and the user (mapping variants and misspellings to the preferred term educates them, builds brand recognition, and nudges everyone toward shared language).

Preferred terms matter when users switch from searching to browsing: presenting all synonyms, abbreviations, and misspellings in taxonomies, navigation bars, and indexes would be overwhelming, so include only preferred terms to keep the index short—but where equivalent terms begin with different letters (such as aspirin and Bayer) create 'see' pointers (term rotation) selectively so users can still find them, balancing usefulness against index length.

A classification scheme (or taxonomy) is an arrangement of preferred terms that is not tied to a single view or instance: the same scheme can serve as a frontend browsable hierarchy that is a visible part of the user interface and as a backend tool that authors and indexers use to organize and tag documents.

The most important goal of a thesaurus embedded in an information environment is synonym management—mapping many synonyms or word variants onto one preferred term or concept—so that the ambiguities of language do not prevent people from finding what they need.

A thesaurus is a controlled vocabulary in which equivalence, hierarchical, and associative relationships are identified for improved retrieval, and each preferred term becomes the center of its own semantic network built from those three fundamental relationship types.

The core thesaurus terminology—preferred term, variant term, broader term, narrower term, related term, USE, USED FOR, and scope note—gives experts efficiency and specificity, but do not expect users to recognize these terms, because you cannot require users to take a library-science class before using your system.

There are no 'right' answers when selecting preferred terms and semantic relationships and no 'right' way to design a thesaurus; there will always be a strong element of professional judgment informed by research.

A well-integrated thesaurus is invisible to the untrained eye—users rarely realize a variant term such as 'African sleeping sickness' was mapped behind the scenes to a preferred term like 'Trypanosomiasis, African'—and it lets the system search rich metadata records (abstracts plus subject headings) rather than full text.

A key advantage of using a thesaurus is the power and flexibility to shape and refine the user interface over time: you cannot take advantage of all its capabilities at once, but you can user-test different features and adjust as you go, drawing on the rich network of semantic relationships as design and development continue.

Choose among three types of thesaurus based on how you intend to use it, a decision with major design implications: a classic thesaurus used at both indexing and searching, an indexing thesaurus used only to index documents with a controlled vocabulary, and a searching thesaurus that leverages a controlled vocabulary only at search time.

An indexing thesaurus (controlled-vocabulary indexing without search-time synonym mapping) is better than nothing because it structures indexing for consistency and efficiency and enables browsable indexes of preferred terms; for captive audiences such as intranet users who learn the preferred terms over time, indexing consistency begins to rival indexing quality in value, and it positions you to upgrade later to a classic thesaurus.
condition: when you can index documents but cannot map variants to preferred terms at search time

statement: A searching thesaurus leverages a controlled vocabulary at search time but not at indexing, which suits situations where document-level indexing is impractical (third-party or dynamic content, or content volume too large to index manually); it maps a user's query onto the vocabulary before running it against the full-text index, through equivalence explosion or by 'posting down' the hierarchy to include narrower terms, which enhances recall at the expense of precision.
condition: when document-level indexing is impractical

statement: A major advantage of a searching thesaurus is that its development and maintenance costs are essentially independent of the volume of content, but it places much greater demands on the quality of the equivalence relationships and mapping.

Thesaurus standards such as ANSI/NISO Z39.19 and ISO 2788 are guidelines for human thesaurus compilers, not computing specifications of behavior or interface: they present simple guidelines that are very difficult to apply and provide a valuable conceptual framework, but they absolutely do not remove the need for critical thinking, creativity, and risk-taking.

Traditional thesauri were designed for trained expert users of print in academic and library settings, whereas online information environments typically serve novice, untrained, infrequent users in a business context, so you must work out which old guidelines still apply—neither following them blindly (like using a 1950s map on today's highways) nor throwing out the decades of research they embody.

Staying close to a thesaurus standard has advantages—good thinking is baked into the guidelines, most thesaurus-management software is designed to be standard-compliant, and compliance improves cross-database compatibility for merging vocabularies—so read the guidelines, follow them when they make sense, and be prepared to deviate from the standard when necessary.

The equivalence relationship connects a preferred term with its variants—synonyms, near-synonyms, acronyms, abbreviations, lexical variants, common misspellings, and even retired or competitors' product names—to create a rich entry vocabulary that funnels users to what they seek; equivalence is a broader concept than synonymy.

The hierarchical relationship divides the information space into broader and narrower concepts through parent-child links, with three subtypes—generic (class-species), whole-part, and instance—but building a hierarchy is hard because any space can be organized many ways (by subject, product category, or geography), so a faceted thesaurus supports multiple hierarchies, granularity must be decided, and the work should be grounded in users' finding needs using methods like card sorting.

The associative relationship (Related Term) captures strongly implied semantic connections not handled by the equivalence or hierarchical relationships; it is the trickiest and most subjective and is usually developed after the other two, and in online commerce it provides an excellent vehicle for cross-selling by connecting customers to related products and services.

Default preferred terms to nouns, because users understand and remember nouns better than verbs or adjectives, but use verbs (task-oriented words) and adjectives (price, size, color) where there is a clear benefit; for spelling, singular versus plural, and abbreviations, the most important thing is to make a decision and stick to it, because consistency improves the lives of indexers and users.

Selecting a preferred term involves a tension between literary warrant (choosing terms that occur in the documents) and user warrant (choosing terms that serve the majority of users), which can be resolved only by reviewing your goals and how the thesaurus will be integrated with the site—for example, whether you will use preferred terms to educate users about industry vocabulary or as the sole entry vocabulary in the index.

Manage ambiguity in preferred terms with parenthetical term qualifiers for homographs—for example Cells (biology), Cells (electric), Cells (prison)—and with scope notes that deliberately restrict a term's meaning to one concept (unlike definitions, which suggest multiple meanings), which help indexers select the right term and can also assist users during searching or results display.

Balance the specificity of preferred terms to your context: as the volume of content grows it becomes increasingly necessary to use compound terms to increase precision (otherwise users get hundreds or thousands of hits per term), and the scope of content matters too—a narrow site may want a compound term like 'knowledge management software' while a broad site may prefer 'knowledge management' and 'software' as independent terms.

Choose between a strict hierarchy (each term in one and only one place) and polyhierarchy (cross-listing terms in multiple categories); in large information systems polyhierarchy is unavoidable, because growing document counts require more precoordination with compound terms to keep precision, and digital systems handle polyhierarchy easily by representing primary and secondary locations, unlike physical objects that can be in only one place.

Faceted classification recognizes that documents and objects have multiple dimensions, or facets, so instead of the old model's question 'Where do I put this?' (one place per item) the faceted approach asks 'How can I describe this?', building multiple pure taxonomies each using one principle of division at a time.

Common facets in the business world are topic, product, document type, audience, geography, and price, applied by giving heterogeneous web content the structure of a fielded database; embrace multiple taxonomies focused on different dimensions rather than a one-taxonomy-fits-all approach, noting that some facets are flat lists (like price) while others must be represented hierarchically (like type).

Decide how and when to leverage facets within the interface by balancing user needs (how people want to browse and search), business needs (how the site can maximize sales of high-margin items), and the creation of meaningful contexts.

Faceted classification provides great power and flexibility: with the underlying descriptive metadata and structure in place you can experiment with hundreds of ways to present navigation and refine the interface over time while the faceted classification provides an enduring foundation, which is why single-taxonomy solutions are giving way to more flexible faceted approaches.

Information architecture does not happen in a vacuum, so designing complex information environments requires interdisciplinary teams (interaction designers, software developers, content strategists, usability engineers) and agreement on a structured development process, and even for small projects tackling the right challenges at the right time is critical to success.

Information-architecture development follows a phased approach—research, strategy, design, implementation, administration—which is not in conflict with agile: agile works best when the team knows the goal it is reaching for, and following the process helps the team understand the big picture, while the architecture still must be refined and iterated as the product meets real-world conditions.

An information-architecture strategy defines, from a top-down perspective, the highest two or three levels of the environment's organization and navigation structures, and from a bottom-up perspective it suggests candidate document types and a rough metadata schema, providing a high-level framework that establishes direction and scope for the project.

Design shapes the high-level strategy into detailed sitemaps, wireframes, and metadata schema and is where most of the work is done, but quantity cannot drive out quality, because poor design execution can ruin the best strategy.

Administration—the continuous evaluation and improvement of the information architecture, including daily tagging of new documents, weeding of old ones, and monitoring of usage and user feedback—can make a good information environment great, and the dedicated in-house staff who protect and perfect the architecture over the long haul are the unsung heroes of the field.

Clear lines rarely exist between the development phases and few projects begin with a clean slate, because budgets, schedules, and politics inevitably force you off the path, so apply the process framework, tools, and methods selectively rather than as a paint-by-numbers guide.

Good research means asking the right questions, and choosing the right questions requires a conceptual framework of the broader environment—the three circles of users, content, and context—to decide where to shine the flashlight and to understand what you see; not every tool makes sense on every project.

Begin projects with a clear understanding of the business context—goals and the political environment—because ignoring business realities is as dangerous as ignoring users and a perfectly usable product that fails to support business goals will not last; 'user-centered design' usefully moves the pendulum away from executive-centered design, but do not let it swing too far, and remember that context also includes budgets, schedules, technology infrastructure, human resources, corporate culture, and legal issues (especially in regulated industries).

Research is not a one-way street: because most large information environments depend on interdepartmental collaboration and decentralized content ownership, success is impossible without broad buy-in, so build awareness and support and weave elements of presentation and persuasion throughout the research process.

Asking the right questions is not enough—you must ask them of the right people, in the right way, at the right time—so begin with a review of background materials such as mission, vision, goals, audience, and content documents, and organization charts, which capture internal users' mental model of the organization and help identify potential stakeholders and user groups.

Compare the vision that preceded the current product with the actual product, because a large gap between an ambitious vision and a poorly designed reality is a red flag signaling misunderstanding between the managers who produce the slides and the team who must build the product—great visions are useless without the time, money, and expertise to implement them, so rein in expectations quickly.

Kick off a project with an introductory presentation that gets authors, developers, interaction and visual designers, marketing, and managers on the same page about what information architecture is and why it matters, how it relates to the other components and the organization, and the major milestones and deliverables, because doing so identifies land mines and builds a common vocabulary.

Hold targeted research meetings with the strategy team, content managers, and IT, and keep the strategy meeting small (five to seven people is ideal) and informal, because if the group gets too large political correctness takes over and people will not talk; follow your nose to dig into the most important topics rather than rigidly sticking to a formal agenda—act as facilitator, not dictator.

Meet with system administrators and software developers early to learn the existing and planned technical infrastructure and build trust, and because IT groups are often swamped and lack time to support information-architecture and usability efforts, identify that problem early and develop a practical, realistic solution, or the whole effort can stall when implementation time arrives.

Stakeholder interviews with senior executives and managers across departments are often one of the most valuable parts of business-context research, using open-ended questions about their assessment of the current environment and their vision; take the time to explain your project to them, because their political support may matter more in the long haul than the answers they give.

Assess the IT environment at the very beginning of a project so your strategies and designs are grounded in reality, because you usually must work with the tools and infrastructure already in place; talk with IT up front, then perform a gap analysis of the disconnects between business goals, user needs, and technology limits and see whether commercial tools can close those gaps.

Findability precedes usability—users must be able to find content before they can use it—so to create findable objects you must study those objects, identifying what distinguishes one from another and how document structure and metadata influence findability, balancing this bottom-up research with a top-down look at the existing information architecture.

When redesigning an existing environment, do not throw out the baby with the bathwater by insisting on a clean slate; instead learn from the existing environment and identify what is worth keeping, since a redesign lets you stand on the shoulders of those who came before.

A heuristic evaluation is an expert critique that tests a product against a set of design guidelines, and it is usually best performed by someone outside the organization so they bring fresh eyes unburdened by political considerations, ideally before a review of background materials to avoid bias.

A single-expert heuristic evaluation, like a physician's diagnose-and-prescribe model, often provides a good balance between cost and quality, while a more rigorous multi-expert review tests the system against a written list of guidelines (such as providing multiple access paths, supplementing the taxonomy with indexes and sitemaps, giving a sense of context, using audience-appropriate language, and integrating search and browse) with experts reviewing independently and then reaching consensus to reduce the role of personal opinion.

Content analysis is the bottom-up review of the documents and objects that actually exist in your environment, and what you find may not match the vision, quantity, or quality articulated by the strategy team and opinion leaders, so identify and address the gaps between top-down vision and bottom-up reality.

Gather a content sample using the 'Noah's Ark' approach—a couple of each type—guided by intuition and judgment rather than an overly scientific formula, distinguishing content 'species' by format, document type, source (which mirrors the organization chart and is politically astute), subject, and the existing architecture, while being careful not to let the old architecture overly influence the analysis.

Balance content-sample size against time and budget by weighing the relative number of each content species against the importance of certain types (a few annual reports may be content-rich and vital to investors), and heed the law of diminishing returns—when you stop learning anything new, go with the sample you have rather than going through the motions.

Analyze each content object for structural metadata (its information hierarchy, title, and chunks users might access independently), descriptive metadata (the many ways to describe it, such as topic, audience, and format), and administrative metadata (who created and owns it, when it was created, and when it should be removed), but do not lock into a predefined set of fields—let the content suggest new ones by asking what the object is, how to describe it for people and machines, what distinguishes it, and how to make it findable.

Beyond individual items, look for the patterns and relationships that emerge across many content objects—apparent groupings, clear hierarchical relationships, and potential associative relationships such as disparate items linked by a common business process—which makes content analysis necessarily iterative, with the key insight sometimes arriving on the second or third pass.

Bridge the top-down understanding from heuristic evaluation and the bottom-up understanding from content analysis by developing one or more content maps—high-level, conceptual visual representations of the existing environment used as a tool for understanding rather than a concrete design deliverable.

Borrowing information-architecture features from competitors can be valuable but must be done carefully with consideration of context, because copycatting risks borrowing bad ideas along with good ones—people repeatedly mistake large financial outlays and strong marketing for good information architecture, and careful competitive benchmarking catches this misdirected copying (as when a client insisted on following Fidelity's site even though its architecture was a mess).

Before-and-after benchmarking forces you to tie the high-level goals in your mission and vision to specific, measurable criteria, which drives a better design and creates a reference point for measuring improvement and ROI, and it encourages the transition from broad generalizations like 'our navigation stinks' to specific, actionable definitions.

Users are the ultimate judges of an information environment—confuse customers and they go elsewhere, frustrate employees and they will not use it—so you cannot blindly apply lessons learned by one site (such as Amazon) to another (such as Pfizer.com); you must consider the unique nature of the environment and of the people who will use it.

No single approach is the one right way to learn about users and their needs, mental models, and information-seeking behavior; it is a multidimensional puzzle to be viewed from many perspectives, so it is much better to conduct five interviews and five usability tests than to run one test ten times, because each approach is subject to the law of diminishing returns.

Observe the golden rule of discount usability engineering—any testing is better than no testing—so do not let budgets or schedules become an excuse, and remember that users are your most powerful allies, because colleagues and bosses find it easy to argue with you but hard to argue with their own customers and real user behavior, making user research an effective political tool.

For a redesign, begin by looking at usage data showing how people have used the system and where they run into problems—content performance reveals what is popular and helpful, visitor information gives general referral and capability data, and the clickstream traces users' paths—but clickstream data is rich yet often hard to act on without feedback from users explaining why they came, what they found, and why they left.

Search log analysis is a simpler and extremely valuable approach that reveals what users are looking for and the exact words they use (fantastic for developing controlled vocabularies and prioritizing best-bets terms) and sensitizes you to how users really search—one or two keywords, often misspelled—so use it to answer which popular queries return zero or hundreds of results and take concrete steps like adding vocabulary terms, changing navigation labels, improving search tips, or editing content.

Look to customer and technical support departments for captured problems, questions, and feedback, because help desk operators, call center representatives, librarians, and administrative assistants are the people customers and employees turn to for answers, which means they are the people who know the questions.

Because you can rarely study every user, define and prioritize the intended and actual audiences and build a primary hierarchy for participant selection that balances the organization's traditional view of its customers (such as home users, business users, resellers) with the distinctions you care about (such as people familiar versus unfamiliar with the old site).

Surveys are a broad-and-shallow research tool that gathers input from many people quickly and inexpensively (limit the number of questions to keep a reasonable response rate, and consider anonymity and an incentive), and because there is little chance for follow-up they do not yield rich data on information-seeking behavior but are best for identifying which content and tasks users value most, what frustrates them most, their ideas for improvement, and their satisfaction level—while also providing a powerful political tool.

Benchmarking is the systematic identification, evaluation, and comparison of information-architecture features and can be quantitative or qualitative, taking the form of competitive benchmarking between different sites or before-and-after benchmarking between versions of the same site over time.
Contextual inquiry can reveal information-use behavior that lab or abstract research misses because work environment and behavior shape each other.

statement: Include a project plan in strategy-phase deliverables when the team needs to test how recommendations will be accomplished, by whom, on what timeline, and with what dependencies.
condition: moving from IA strategy to design execution

statement: A project plan grounds IA strategy in reality by forcing questions about feasibility, duration, ownership, deliverables, and dependencies.
condition: developing the plan alongside the strategy report

statement: The IA project plan should bridge strategy and design by integrating with plans from interaction design, content authoring, and application development.
condition: other teams contribute to overall site design

statement: Provide both short-term and long-term IA plans when stakeholders need visible progress and a path for fuller architectural development.
condition: there is pressure to show immediate progress

statement: A completed strategy report and project plan are insufficient without presentation and discussion, because important recommendations may otherwise be ignored.
condition: stakeholders are busy or unlikely to read detailed IA reports

statement: Tailor strategy presentations to each audience by selecting compelling recommendation highlights and organizing them into a clear sequence.
condition: presenting IA strategy to stakeholders

statement: Use visuals and metaphors in presentations when they make abstract strategy options more memorable and easier for stakeholders to discuss.
condition: presenting complex IA strategy options

statement: The transition from strategy to design shifts stakeholder expectations from discussion toward concrete, well-defined IA deliverables.
condition: entering the design and documentation phase

statement: Research and strategy reduce design-phase uncertainty by giving architectural decisions stronger grounding than intuition alone.
condition: the project has time and resources for research and strategy

statement: Design decisions and deliverables are highly context-dependent and shaped by practitioner experience, project scale, collaborators, and domain complexity.
condition: working in the IA design phase

statement: Design-phase process remains important: concrete artifacts such as vocabularies, wireframes, and prototypes should still be tested and refined.
condition: moving from research and strategy into design

statement: When a project bypasses research and strategy, deliverables become especially important because they force review, reveal design problems, and can trigger belated research or design work.
condition: a project is pushed directly into design

statement: Information architecture diagrams should be understood as partial representations of abstract, multidimensional systems rather than complete visual models.
condition: documenting an information architecture visually

statement: Use multiple diagram views because no single diagram can communicate every aspect of a complex information environment.
condition: representing a complex IA

statement: Design each architecture view for a specific audience and need instead of reusing one diagram for all communication contexts.
condition: creating IA diagrams for different stakeholders

statement: Determine what recipients need from IA diagrams before creating them, because assumptions about diagram use can be wrong.
condition: diagram consumers include clients, managers, designers, or programmers

statement: Present IA diagrams live when possible so the architect can explain intent, resolve ambiguity, and defend choices.
condition: the audience is unfamiliar with the diagrams or visual language

statement: Prefer timely, useful diagrams over polished deliverables when the audience needs rapid working artifacts.
condition: stakeholders request simple sketches or fast iteration

statement: Sitemaps and wireframes communicate structure better than semantic meaning, so semantic questions may need other documentation.
condition: using sitemaps or wireframes as primary IA diagrams

statement: IA diagrams should clearly show content components and the connections that enable navigation or other actions between them.
condition: diagramming structural elements of an information system

statement: Use a consistent visual vocabulary or template when it helps collaborators understand diagram symbols and syntax.
condition: creating repeatable sitemaps or wireframes

statement: Treat IA deliverables as communication tools; textual outlines, spreadsheets, or page descriptions are valid when they fit the creator and audience better than visual diagrams.
condition: visual diagrams are not the best communication style for the team or audience

statement: IA concepts eventually need to connect to visual and interaction design work, even when early IA documentation is textual.
condition: moving from IA concepts toward product design

statement: Sitemaps show relationships among pages or other content components and can portray organization, navigation, and labeling systems.
Creating a sitemap forces abstract architecture ideas into practical structure and can reveal concepts that do not work in a concrete product.
condition: turning brainstormed IA ideas into a sitemap

statement: Use high-level sitemaps iteratively to explore primary organization schemes, major areas, and top-down navigation approaches.
condition: designing the broad structure of a site or product

statement: High-level sitemaps are useful discussion tools for content ownership, content management, and user access pathways.
condition: discussing architecture with clients or colleagues

statement: High-level sitemaps should provoke questions and challenges early, when design changes are cheaper and buy-in can still be built.
condition: presenting a high-level sitemap to stakeholders

statement: Augment sitemaps with live presentation, notes, or brief explanatory text because they rarely explain themselves completely.
condition: sharing sitemaps with clients or cross-functional teams

statement: Let sitemap form follow purpose; a sitemap may show the whole vision, one navigation mechanism, filtering behavior, task flow, or user engagement progression.
condition: choosing a sitemap format

statement: Use task-oriented sitemaps or process maps for transactional and task-centered systems, not only content-heavy sites.
condition: the product includes workflows or transactions

statement: Keep sitemaps intentionally selective; omitting page-level details and minor navigation elements can make the major structures clearer.
condition: creating a sitemap for strategic or design communication

statement: As projects move toward implementation, lower-level sitemaps should use a simple, condensed notation that multidisciplinary production teams can understand quickly.
condition: communicating IA to designers, editors, programmers, or developers

statement: Limit the sitemap object vocabulary to avoid overloading one diagram with information better carried by other views.
condition: building lower-level or production sitemaps

statement: Detailed sitemaps should evolve with the rest of the design as development exposes new conditions, incomplete assumptions, and changing requirements.
condition: working in agile, lean, or implementation-stage projects

statement: Before production starts, detailed sitemaps should map the full hierarchy from main page to destination pages and specify area-level labels and navigation systems.
condition: preparing implementation guidance for the production team

statement: Assign unique identifiers to sitemap components to support organized production, database population, and traceability across pages and content chunks.
condition: a production process must coordinate many components

statement: Distinguish content chunks from page containers when the production process or design layout needs reusable, independently meaningful content units.
condition: content may be assembled into pages in multiple ways

statement: Use sidebars, legends, or notes to describe global and local navigation when arrows would be confusing or easy for production staff to miss.
condition: a detailed sitemap must communicate navigation systems

statement: Modularize large sitemaps into linked subsidiary diagrams, using shared identifiers to connect parent and child diagrams.
condition: the full architecture is too large to view or print reasonably as one diagram

statement: Shared component identifiers can bridge content inventories and sitemaps, making production population more systematic.
condition: content inventory and architecture work need to align

statement: Wireframes depict page or template structure from an architectural perspective and connect IA decisions with interaction design.
Wireframes can reveal navigation overload or placement problems early enough to revise the sitemap before implementation becomes expensive.
condition: testing IA ideas in page context

statement: Because screens are constrained spaces, wireframes force choices about which architecture components should be visible and accessible.
condition: laying out IA on a page or screen

statement: Use wireframes to clarify content grouping, ordering, and priority on important pages or templates.
condition: designing page-level IA

statement: Wireframe only pages that are important, complex, unique, confusing, or pattern-setting; do not attempt to wireframe every page by default.
condition: planning wireframe coverage

statement: Use wireframes to explore how page structure and architectural components reflow across phone, tablet, and desktop screen sizes.
condition: designing responsive products

statement: Label wireframes as architectural artifacts rather than final visual design so visual and interaction designers understand their intended scope.
condition: wireframes include visual layout choices

statement: Explain verbally how wireframes reduce labeling and structural work for designers while still leaving visual and interaction design expertise in play.
condition: collaborating with visual or interaction designers around wireframes

statement: Use wireframes as triggers for interdisciplinary collaboration rather than as one-way handoff documents.
condition: wireframes affect visual design, interaction design, and development

statement: Choose wireframe fidelity according to purpose and lifecycle stage, with earlier stages usually requiring less precision.
condition: selecting a wireframe format

statement: High-fidelity wireframes can make pages feel concrete and support paper-prototype testing, but they require more effort and can shift attention away from IA too early.
condition: using high-fidelity wireframes

statement: Wireframe fidelity tradeoffs should be explicit so the team uses wireframes as communication and collaboration tools without mistaking them for finished interface design.
condition: choosing among low-, medium-, and high-fidelity wireframes

statement: Maintain consistency across wireframes because colleagues may interpret them literally and production work depends on stable patterns.
condition: presenting or handing off multiple wireframes

statement: Use reusable backgrounds, templates, stencils, or shared drawing objects to keep repeated navigation and page-layout elements consistent.
condition: creating multiple wireframes for one product

statement: Use callouts to document page-element functionality, leaving space around the wireframe so explanatory notes remain readable.
condition: wireframes need functional detail

statement: Treat wireframe sets as professional deliverables with page numbers, page titles, project titles, and revision dates.
condition: wireframes circulate among clients or production teams

statement: When multiple team members create wireframes, establish shared procedures, templates, stewardship, and synchronization time to maintain functional and visual consistency.
condition: wireframing is distributed across a team

statement: Content mapping connects top-down IA structures with bottom-up content collection and analysis during design and production.
condition: moving from research and strategy into design and production

statement: Define a content chunk as the smallest portion of content that merits or requires individual treatment, not as a fixed sentence, paragraph, or page size.
condition: chunking content for architecture or production

statement: Separate content from its source and destination containers because source pages and destination pages rarely map one-to-one across formats.
condition: mapping existing content into a new digital environment

statement: Separating content from containers enables reusable content chunks when paired with database-driven content management.
condition: content chunks may appear in multiple contexts

statement: Content mapping remains necessary for newly authored content, especially when multiple authors create source documents that must be tracked into destination pages or systems.
condition: new content is created outside the final publishing system

statement: Chunking decisions should consider whether users need separate access, whether the section needs independent indexing, and whether it will be repurposed.
condition: defining content chunks

statement: Document each content chunk's source and destination systematically so production teams can implement the mapping reliably.
condition: content chunks have been defined and mapped to pages, feeds, or another medium

statement: Assign unique identification codes to content chunks when source-to-destination mapping must be coordinated across inventories, sitemaps, and production work.
condition: content mapping involves many chunks or production staff

statement: A content inventory should describe available content, its source locations, and gaps that must be filled.
condition: preparing content for production or audit

statement: Choose a content inventory tool according to site complexity and production workflow, ranging from spreadsheets to database-backed content or document management systems.
condition: planning a content inventory

statement: Use a content inventory to support a content audit that identifies new content, missing mockups, and designed pages needing review before integration.
condition: content inventory exists

statement: Content models are architectures of small interconnected content chunks that support contextual navigation deep within a product.
Content models depend on consistent content objects and logical connections; omitting important objects or disrupting expected order can make the model fail.
condition: designing a content model

statement: Use content models to let users move horizontally across related content based on their current specific need rather than forcing them back through top-down hierarchy.
condition: users are deep in the product and have expressed a specific information need

statement: Content models are especially valuable for large sets of high-value, similar, poorly linked content chunks that technology can connect automatically.
condition: there are many homogeneous valuable content chunks and a CMS or comparable system can automate links

statement: Model only the most valuable content when resources are limited, using both user needs and organizational needs to define value.
condition: content modeling effort cannot cover everything

statement: Validate proposed content-object links with user research when the natural connections between objects are not obvious.
condition: designing a content model with uncertain link logic

statement: A content-modeling card-sort variation should remove existing navigation cues, ask users where they would go next, and capture desired link direction between content objects.
condition: researching contextual navigation between content objects

statement: Use content-modeling research to perform gap analysis by asking which missing content objects users would want included.
condition: evaluating a candidate content model

statement: Content modeling can identify missing content objects, logical entry points, useful external connections, and candidates for future content models.
condition: developing a content model

statement: Automated links between content chunks usually require metadata or behavioral data that can express the linking logic.
condition: content links are generated rather than manually curated

statement: Use unique identifiers as connecting metadata when names or titles are ambiguous.
condition: linking content objects with non-unique names or titles

statement: Content modeling helps prioritize metadata investment by revealing which attributes are required to support valuable links.
condition: metadata creation resources are limited

statement: Build a content-object linking table that lists each object, target object, and shared metadata attributes needed to create the connection.
condition: designing or implementing a content model

statement: Prioritize metadata attributes that appear repeatedly across content-model links when resources are constrained.
condition: metadata creation or acquisition resources are limited

statement: Content modeling is both a deliverable and a prioritization exercise that clarifies which content and metadata matter most.
condition: large content and metadata problem spaces need simplification

statement: Controlled-vocabulary work should include metadata matrices for prioritizing vocabularies and tools for managing terms and relationships.
condition: developing controlled vocabularies

statement: Use a metadata matrix to weigh vocabulary value for user experience against development and administration cost under time and budget constraints.
condition: choosing which vocabularies to develop

statement: Choose vocabulary-management tooling according to vocabulary complexity: thesaurus software for rich term relationships and simpler tools for basic preferred and variant terms.
condition: building or maintaining controlled vocabularies

statement: Even modest controlled vocabularies can strain simple document-based management, so tool limits should be considered before scale grows.
condition: managing several vocabularies and hundreds of accepted terms

statement: Design collaboration requires integrating IA concepts with the visions, vocabularies, and constraints of visual designers, developers, content authors, and managers.
condition: moving from IA deliverables into product development collaboration

statement: Use shared collaboration tools and an open-minded process to turn competing interdisciplinary ideas into a stronger shared vision.
condition: multiple disciplines are shaping the product

statement: Design sketches can pool visual-design, technical, and IA knowledge into an early interface-design attempt for key pages or screens.
condition: teams need to combine research, platform, and architecture knowledge

statement: Use wireframes as guides for sketching sessions so layout, navigation, architecture, and technical feasibility questions can surface together.
condition: running interdisciplinary sketching sessions

statement: Prefer rough sketches over code or finished graphics for early interdisciplinary design because they support cheaper, faster iteration.
condition: the team is still exploring interface design options

statement: Start interdisciplinary meetings with a sketch or wireframe because it gives participants a shared focus and shared terminology.
condition: holding cross-functional design discussions

statement: Avoid ownership disputes over sketches; the important outcome is useful contribution to the design, not which role controls the drawing tool.
condition: sketches describe architecture, function, or design across role boundaries

statement: Interactive prototypes make the product concrete enough to reveal IA problems or opportunities that sketches and scenarios may miss.
condition: architecture and navigation are embodied in an interactive system

statement: During production, the information architect should remain involved to ensure the architecture is implemented as planned and to address issues that could not be anticipated.
condition: the product has entered production

statement: Production-stage IA decisions should balance client requests, production effort, budget, timeline, usability, and the intended architecture.
condition: production raises questions about chunks, labels, pages, or navigation

statement: Major architectural decisions should be resolved before production; research, strategy, documentation, content mapping, and detailed sitemaps reduce the risk of late major flaws.
condition: preparing for production

statement: Treat information architecture as ongoing because content, people, and context keep changing after launch.
condition: maintaining an information environment

statement: Educate colleagues that IA evolves over time rather than framing the work as a quest for a perfect final architecture.
condition: maintainers or collaborators expect a final static answer

statement: Use an information architecture style guide to reduce architectural drift and help maintainers extend organization, navigation, labeling, and indexing systems responsibly.
condition: an information environment will continue changing after launch

statement: An IA style guide should explain how the environment is organized, why it is organized that way, who it serves, and how it should be extended.
condition: creating an IA style guide

statement: Begin an IA style guide with mission, vision, intended audiences, user assumptions, and content development policy.
condition: creating an IA style guide

statement: Document research, strategy, and design lessons and decisions because their rationale guides future maintenance and organizational change.
condition: the product may face new markets, new leadership, mergers, spin-offs, or other major changes

statement: A documented IA rationale helps prioritize requests for prominence or special treatment and supports saying no when requests conflict with the architecture.
condition: stakeholders request higher priority for features, departments, or content

statement: Distinguish mandatory standards from interpretive guidelines in an IA style guide so maintainers know what must be followed and what requires judgment.
condition: documenting maintainable IA rules

statement: Document maintenance procedures for recurring IA tasks such as adding controlled-vocabulary terms or ensuring content is indexed.
condition: the environment requires ongoing IA maintenance

statement: Include a pattern library when reusable navigation or interaction patterns can reduce reinvention across the product.
condition: the product has reusable design elements

statement: Reuse and explain design-phase artifacts such as sitemaps, wireframes, and vocabulary documentation in the style guide because maintainers may not have the architect available.
condition: style-guide users must interpret previous IA deliverables independently

statement: Provide explicit guidance for adding content so organization, labeling, navigation, and indexing systems remain coherent as the environment grows.
condition: maintainers will add or change content after launch

statement: Design the IA style guide for its own audiences, giving different maintainers the level of rationale, rules, or practical constraints they need.
condition: the style guide will be used by authors, designers, managers, or other maintainers

statement: Integrate IA guidance into existing brand, content, or online-presence style guides when that is the most usable maintenance path.
condition: the organization already has relevant style guides

statement: Where humans are concerned, context is everything, so a design must be evaluated by how it fits real usage conditions and needs rather than judged as an isolated innovation.
Evaluate a source's credibility before relying on it, because finding information is easy but assessing its trustworthiness is the hard part.

Applied research may relax the methods of pure science, such as revising questions partway through a study or accepting an imperfect sample, and is judged successful to the extent it contributes to its stated goal.
condition: when time or resources are constrained

statement: In design practice, research means inquiry that is integral to the design work itself and centered on understanding the people being designed for, making it a core part of user-centered design.
For a design to succeed it must serve the actual needs and desires of real people, not the preferences or assumptions of the designer.
Approach familiar people and situations as if they were unknown, deliberately setting aside your assumptions, in order to see them clearly during research.
Asking your own research questions and knowing how to answer them is essential to designing well; ceding the inquiry agenda to others leaves design decisions to focus groups or arbitrary algorithms.

Investigating how and why people actually behave, and the opportunities that reveals, produces more innovative and appropriate designs than asking people how they feel or merely tweaking a design from analytics.
Truly knowing your constraints through research yields stronger arguments, clearer purpose, and greater freedom to innovate.
Do not treat what people say they like or dislike as research data, because liking is subjective, self-reported, and disconnected from actual behavior.
People routinely do things they claim to hate and avoid things they claim to like, so self-reported preference is an unreliable predictor of behavior.

Do not choose research methods to appear rigorous or to match someone's image of research; select methods by fit to the question, since a well-run interview is valuable regardless of whether it happens in a usability lab.
condition: provided the interview is conducted with method and purpose

statement: Use the external, real-world facts gathered in research to bring an outside perspective to internal debates and power struggles, and prevent interpersonal dynamics from influencing the findings.
Stay alert to stakeholders who would use information-gathering for political ends or as a popularity contest, and protect the integrity of the findings from them.

When challenged on statistical significance or sample size, avoid arguing about statistical validity and keep the focus on gathering useful qualitative insights, because applied research is not science.
condition: when facing sample-size or statistical-significance objections

statement: A skeptical, questioning mindset is more valuable to a practitioner than mastery of any specific research methodology.
Everyone on the design team should participate in the research, not only a dedicated researcher.
Involve team members in doing the research from the start, because people who help gather insights are far more likely to apply them than people who merely receive a finished report.
Designate a research lead who keeps the team on protocol and holds ultimate responsibility for the quality of the work.
Ensure everyone involved in the research knows its purpose or goal, their own role, and the process before it begins.
Because every design project reduces to a series of decisions, include only the research activities that support the specific decisions you anticipate making.
Match research openness to problem definition: use more open-ended research when only an audience or goal is identified, and more focused research when the design problem is already well defined.
condition: when only an audience or goal is identified versus a well-defined design problem

statement: It is premature to fine-tune specific solutions while you are still searching for ideas and the problem is not yet defined.
condition: while the problem is still undefined and you are still seeking ideas

statement: Choose a research approach from the decisions in play (the purpose) and what you are asking about (the topic), rather than from academic classifications of research.
Use generative or exploratory research, such as interviews, field observation, and reviewing existing literature, to produce ideas and define the problem before the solution is known.
exception: not limited to the earliest stage; also applies when seeking enhancements to an existing product

statement: After generative research, synthesize the findings to identify the most commonly voiced unmet needs, which reveal useful problems to solve and can be framed as a testable hypothesis.
Use descriptive research to understand the full context of an already-identified design problem so that you design for the audience rather than for yourself.
condition: once a design problem has been identified

statement: Use evaluative research, most commonly usability testing, iteratively and continuously throughout design and development to check that proposed solutions work and meet the identified requirements.
Use causal research, including analytics review and multivariate testing, to explain why a live product is being used the way it is.
condition: after a solution is implemented and live
exception: establishing a genuine cause-and-effect relationship is difficult

statement: Do not over-worry about categorizing the type of research; stay clear about your questions and expectations and remain open to learning at every stage of the process.
Assign the interviewer and the notetaker to two different people so the interviewer can give full attention to the participant, and keep both written notes and a recording to make analysis easier.
exception: if one person must both interview and take notes, record the session as unobtrusively as possible

statement: Allow clients or teammates to observe research in progress only when their presence will not change what happens; otherwise give them raw recordings instead of live access.
condition: only when the observers' presence will not influence the research itself

statement: Ensure everyone collaborating on a study shares an understanding of how the work will proceed, even if that shared plan is only a simple checklist.
Secure approval and organizational buy-in and advocate for the research before starting it, because if a higher decision-maker later overrides the findings the effort is wasted.
condition: before the work begins

statement: Answer the no-time objection by weighing the large cost of redoing work built on wrong assumptions against the smaller cost of upfront research, which speeds the rest of the project and can start small.

Treat limited budget or expertise as no barrier to research: you can usually find related studies online, recruit a few representative users, and run light usability testing, while questioning your assumptions costs nothing.
There is no universally superior research methodology; what you need to find out determines whether qualitative or quantitative research is appropriate.

Good applied research requires wanting to find out more than wanting to be right, so as to avoid confirmation bias, depersonalizing the work so there are only findings, and being a clear communicator and analytical thinker.

Learn the highest-risk unknowns, such as what the audience already does, whether people want the product, and what the organization must do to support it, before you start designing or coding rather than deferring them to beta.
Take a fresh look at users and the problem even when the team feels it already knows them, because familiarity breeds unexamined assumptions and blind spots.
exception: unless the existing knowledge comes from recent inquiry specific to the current goals

statement: Adjust a project's scope intentionally at the start rather than being surprised by new information later, treating research as a safeguard against unexpected complexity.
Let your professional environment, whether freelance, agency, in-house, startup, or agile, inform which research activities you choose and how you conduct them.
Leverage being external to an organization by asking naive questions that cut straight to hidden assumptions, which insiders often cannot get away with asking.

For an existing product, mine customer service conversations and inbound support requests as a rich source of real user needs and language, and look past what people say they want to what they actually need.
At a startup, document and review your assumptions to find where research would help most, get early team agreement on research's role, keep tracking assumptions, and maintain a skeptical stance.

Decouple research planning from the development process: instead of answering every research question before coding, set up reusable observation guides, interview guides, and equipment and fill in the actual questions and prototypes on the fly.

For continuous research alongside development, aggressively prioritize the highest-value users, analyze and model data quickly and collaboratively, and defer less urgent research to run while the software is being built.
Prioritize studying the user types whose acceptance is critical to the product's success and who least resemble the developers on the team.
Because recruiting and scheduling participants is the hardest part of research, always be recruiting and keep a pipeline of participants scheduled.

Accept that every study contains bias that cannot be eliminated, and instead note potential and obvious bias explicitly so you can weight the results appropriately, using a bias checklist and grading hard.
Counter unavoidable sampling bias in quick qualitative work by being mindful and modest about the general conclusions you draw.
Keep interviewers as neutral as possible, especially early on while establishing rapport, and develop a neutral style through practice interviews and critiques.
Reduce sponsor bias by describing the organization and study goals in general terms and not naming the sponsoring company until it appears in the materials being evaluated.
Counter social-desirability bias by emphasizing the need for honesty and promising participants confidentiality.
Counter the Hawthorne effect, where people change behavior because they are observed, by blending into the background and encouraging participants to go about their normal routine.
Conduct all research involving people and their personal information ethically and conscientiously, without deceiving or injuring participants.
Refuse to take part in research whose overall project goal is unethical or would harm others, because designers act as gatekeepers and an above-board study does not make a harmful goal right.

Obtain informed consent: participants must understand and agree in advance to the study goals and to how their data will be recorded, used, and shared, unseen observers must be disclosed, and minors require a parent's consent.
Protect participant safety and privacy, and never conduct a phone interview with anyone who is driving; end the call immediately and reschedule by another means.
Cultivate habitual skepticism by questioning your assumptions and checking your facts, since awareness of what you do not know makes you and your products stronger.

Consider hiring a trained professional researcher rather than doing it yourself when the project or organization is large or complex, the subject is sensitive, the users are specialized, the politics are heavy, or no team member has the capacity.
condition: for large or complex projects or organizations, sensitive subject matter, specialized or challenging users, heavy organizational politics, or when no team member has time or inclination

statement: As an amateur researcher, maintain rigor through discipline and checklists and do not deviate from the checklists.
exception: until you have gained sufficient experience of your own

statement: Phrase the core question clearly: unless you can state plainly what you are trying to find out and why, applied research is a pointless exercise.

Set realistic expectations up front with everyone involved about the questions to be answered, the methods to be used, and the decisions the findings will inform, especially when requesting time or budget.
Prepare your process and materials before starting the research and set them up so they are easy to reuse.
Allow sufficient time for analysis to let insights click into place instead of rushing straight from data-gathering to solutions.
Record everything and report the results clearly, in a form informative and clear enough for anyone who must make decisions based on the research.

To do just enough research, identify your highest-priority questions by finding the assumptions that carry the biggest risk, asking what bad thing would happen in six months if each assumption turned out to be wrong.
If an assumption carries no real-world risk, do not spend time investigating it.
exception: for example, a technical proof of concept that genuinely does not have to satisfy any real users

statement: There is no fixed answer to how much research is enough other than the point at which you feel sufficiently informed and inspired to start on the solution; learn to listen for the click of the pieces falling into place.
Because human brains are pattern-recognition machines that can see patterns that are not there, interpret data collaboratively with a team to reduce overly optimistic interpretation.
Follow a six-step research process regardless of scale or timing: define the problem, select the approach, plan and prepare, collect the data, analyze the data, and report the results.
A useful study depends on a clear problem statement that names the topic and the goal, because in research you are solving for a lack of information.

Base the research problem statement on an outcome verb such as describe, evaluate, or identify, and avoid open-ended words like understand or explore, because you must be able to tell when you are finished and exploration is potentially infinite.
Let the problem statement point to the general type of research and let the available time, money, and people determine the specific approach, remembering that every approach carries tradeoffs.
Name a single point person responsible for the research plan and its checklist, whether or not they take part in the study, to keep tasks from falling through the cracks.
Sketch a quick initial plan, go with your best guess where you do not yet know, and expect to change the plan once you have facts, since research constantly surfaces new situations.

Decide your trade-offs and fallback plans in a cool moment before starting; for example, if recruiting runs long you can push out dates, relax participant criteria, or talk to fewer people now and more later.
A research plan should include the problem statement, the study duration, who performs which roles, how you will target and recruit subjects, and any incentives, tools, and materials.

Good recruiting is what puts quality into qualitative research: with a small sample the participants must genuinely represent your target, because talking to the wrong people makes the study useless no matter what you ask.

A good research participant shares your target users' concerns and goals, embodies key characteristics such as age or role, can articulate their thoughts clearly, and is about as familiar with the relevant technology as your target users.
Invest in getting good at recruiting, because although it is time-consuming it makes all of your subsequent research faster and easier.
Use a screener, a short survey, to identify good participants and filter out anyone who would waste your time, and keep it as short as possible so people do not abandon it.
Screen primarily for behaviors, because current behaviors determine whether a design, even a novel one, has a chance of being relevant and intelligible to participants.
Screen realistically for the tool knowledge, access, and domain knowledge your target users actually have, so that you test the product rather than the participant's unfamiliarity with the device.
Keep the screener vague about the actual contents of the test to prevent professional participants from gaming their answers to win the incentive.
For in-person testing, follow up by phone with everyone who passes the first cut, using a couple of quick questions to weed out poor matches and avoid awkward encounters.
Move research files onto a shared drive as fast as possible and carry a small backup drive in the field, because losing good data is common and irreversible.
Use a consistent file-naming convention and, between sessions, verify that files are named and saved correctly while noting your initial impressions while they are fresh.

Use tools you already have and are familiar with first, because technical difficulties and equipment learning curves cause the trickiest research problems; choose the tools and documentation that work for your team.
Set up a ready-to-go research kit, or at least a grab checklist, so you can start a study at a moment's notice.

Use a semi-structured interview, with prepared questions and topics but no rigid script, as the most effective way to see the world as another person does and to follow up useful topics you would not have thought to ask.
Treat preparation, structure, and conduct as the keys to a successful interview, aiming for a comfortable interaction that yields the information you were looking for.

Usability testing is a directed interview with a representative user attempting specific tasks on a prototype or actual product, to determine whether the design is usable to a predetermined standard and to surface serious, resolvable issues.
Start usability testing sooner and more often and involve more of the team, treating it as just another review alongside business, design, and technical review rather than a separate activity.

Usability is necessary but not sufficient: testing shows whether people understand and can use a product and surfaces problems in labeling, structure, mental model, and flow, but it cannot supply vision, predict market success, rank which tasks matter most, or replace QA.

Do not test in a controlled usability lab; go to where the people are and embrace real-world distractions, because you want to learn how your ideas work in the wild rather than under an illusion of control.
exception: testing mobile devices ironically requires more in-person testing

statement: Recognize that good participants, good facilitation, and good analysis, not a perfect recording setup, make a good usability test, and aim to identify the most significant issues in the least time.

When you cannot talk to representative users directly or need background, use documented studies by other researchers to inform your understanding, validate general assumptions, and complement your work.

When using third-party literature, note how well their questions align with yours, how well their sample maps to your users, the biases of whoever conducted and funded it, and the date to see whether anything significant has changed.

Analyze data by gathering it all together, looking for meaningful patterns, turning those patterns into observations and then recommendations, and continually referring back to your original problem statement.

Involve as many team members as possible in the analysis, because a group generates more insights faster and internalizes them far better than circulating a report, including people who can contribute and excluding those who would only distract.

Give analysis-session participants advance access to the notes or recordings so they arrive prepared, and expect the session to take from half a day to a few days depending on the number and length of the interviews.

Follow an explicit analysis structure even with a two-person team: summarize the goals and process, describe who you spoke with and how you gathered the data, pull out quotes and observations, group them into themes, summarize the findings and their design implications, and document it all in a shareable format.

Enforce analysis ground rules: focus only on understanding user context and needs, respect the session structure by not naming larger patterns before going through the data, clearly separate observations from interpretations, and propose no solutions yet.
Group observations around the patterns that actually emerge from the data rather than groupings imposed before analysis, and if needed set a time limit and take a vote when time is up.
When examining the data, look for quotes and observations that reveal participants' goals, priorities, tasks, motivators, barriers, habits, relationships, tools, and environment.

When a participant turns out to be an outlier who would never realistically use the product, note the fact and circumstances for future recruiting and set their data aside rather than accommodating them in your model.
condition: when a participant does not match the design target and reveals no previously unknown user type

statement: Match the formality of your reporting to how decisions will be made, documenting informally within a small close-knit team and more formally when results must influence executive decision-making.

Always write a brief, well-organized summary covering goals, methods, insights, and recommendations, since given good data a quick persona sketch or a photo of sticky-note findings beats a lengthy written report that gets ignored.
Accept that the only dependable way to design systems that work for imperfect people in a chaotic real world is to go out and talk with those people where they are.

The nature of an organization matters to the design process, because budgets, approvals, timing, and resources all depend on navigating it, and a product's ultimate success depends on how well it fits what the organization is doing and how well the organization will support it.

Research the organization, including what drives the business, how its pieces fit together, and its capacity for change, using the same methods as user research but talking to current stakeholders instead of potential customers.

Interview client stakeholders, meaning people whose roles will be directly affected by the outcome, as part of requirements gathering, which is essential when you are coming in cold to an unfamiliar organization.

In organizational research the observer effect can be a force for good, because asking hard questions forces reflection, asking the same question of different people reveals differences in motivation and understanding, and listening to people who feel unheard builds goodwill.

Treat as a stakeholder anyone without whose support the project would fail, including executives, managers, subject-matter experts, and staff, and be generous in your selection to avoid an overlooked stakeholder surfacing too late.

Interview executives to learn mission and vision fit, managers for resource and incentive concerns, subject-matter experts for background in your weakest areas, and front-line staff, especially customer service and salespeople, for knowledge of the end users.

Stakeholder interviews expose areas of misalignment between an organization's documented strategy and stakeholders' actual attitudes and daily decisions, and can surface organizational disconnects alongside domain insights.

Use organizational research to surface hidden politics; when you learn why someone opposes your work you can often win them over, and stakeholder conversations let you sell the value of your work in terms that matter to each person.

Gather clear business requirements before proceeding, because without them you cannot tell whether the work has succeeded, and work that does not support the business has failed no matter how good the design; inquire into technical requirements too.
Gauge how genuinely important the project is to the organization, because Mule has repeatedly observed that projects an organization treats as more important tend to succeed more often.
Ask stakeholders about the typical workday and how decisions get made, and adapt your design process to the organization's existing work styles rather than trying to change ingrained habits.
condition: especially when the project brings together cross-functional teams, teams that have never worked together, or internal teams and outside vendors

statement: Ask influential people for their input before you start, because the fundamental human need to be consulted makes early consultation a peerless safeguard against those people rearing up late with insurmountable objections, and inviting participation empowers them.
Do not wait for people inside the organization to come to you or rely on a higher-up to name your contacts; based on the project goals, it is up to you to determine whose input you need.

Inform the organization how much work your project will require to accommodate, so you find out early whether you actually have the organizational support you assumed and can make decisions accordingly.
Account for workflow by identifying how your design and development decisions will affect operations and whether similar, complementary, or competing work is already underway in the organization.

Build a wide list of interviewees and then prioritize it, expecting to talk with some purely for political reasons, and cap the number at what you actually have time for while sticking to that time budget.
Research each interviewee beforehand as you would for a job interview to inform your line of discussion, but avoid leading with any private detail the person would not expect you to know.

As a rule, interview stakeholders individually, because the more political the organization the more important private conversations are, and assure interviewees their answers will not be directly attributed while assuring others they will get what they need in an aggregated report.
exception: a manager who insists on sitting in should be resisted by explaining the observer effect

statement: Use group interviews to save time only among people of roughly equal influence who work closely together, watching for anyone reticent and following up with them privately.
condition: only for a group of roughly equal influence who work closely together and share the project's benefits and risks; use email interviews only as a last resort for a remote or unreachable stakeholder

statement: Keep each stakeholder interview to thirty to sixty minutes in a private place, with a calm, genuinely interested interviewer and a separate notetaker, recognizing that recording may make subjects less candid, so prioritize their comfort speaking honestly.

Send an agenda and the key questions, though not all questions, ahead of time so participants are not ambushed; open by restating the purpose and how information will be shared, promise non-attribution, and get written assurance from the sponsor that people can speak without fear of reprisal.

Keep the stakeholder interview informal rather than an interrogation and let the conversation follow its natural course, then close by restating how you will use the information, confirming the person's ongoing role, and getting permission to follow up.

Ask each stakeholder a baseline set of questions covering their tenure, duties, typical day, key working relationships, their own definition of project success, concerns, the greatest internal and external challenges, and how their interactions will change, plus system-usage questions where they are also users.

When a stakeholder turns hostile, remain calm, restate your goal, ask a broad open-ended question about what they think matters most, and cut the interview short if needed, but never let them take control of the interview or bully you.

Anticipate which stakeholders might react with hostility, whether from being unprepared and suspicious, making a power move, or being under performance pressure, and pre-empt it by explaining why their participation matters, how to prepare, and how long it takes, and practice hostile scenarios with your team.

For each stakeholder, record their attitude toward the project, their stated goal, how well their incentives align with the project's success, the amount and type of influence they hold, who they communicate with regularly, how much and in which role they must participate, and whether their view harmonizes or conflicts with others.

You have interviewed enough stakeholders when you confidently know who they all are, their roles, attitudes, influence, and availability, how they benefit or suffer from success or failure, who could block the project, the workflow changes required, the resources available and needed post-launch, all business requirements and constraints, whether the team agrees on goals, whether the stated goals are the real shared goals or hide agendas, and how outsiders view the project.
