Write a clear statement of what must be accomplished for the organization to consider the project a success, treat these as the business requirements that design and development exist to satisfy, and get everyone who cares about the project to agree on them.

Make business requirements cohesive, complete, consistent, current, unambiguous, feasible, and concise, aiming for no more than two or three pages, so they are actually read, understood, remembered, and used.

Keep specific solutions and design requirements out of the requirements document, and tailor its level of detail and distribution to the organization, potentially maintaining a fuller version for the core team and a summarized version for broad distribution.
Hold the business strategy constant while a project is underway.
condition: for the duration of a single project

statement: Document the problem statement and assumptions, the reconciled goals gathered from every individual's differing view of success, and success metrics, both qualitative and quantitative, that support those goals.
Define and validate completion criteria so you can tell when the project is done, even when the answer seems obvious.

Prevent scope creep by documenting in as much detail and plain language as possible what is included, noting who is responsible for what, and explicitly recording what stakeholders might assume is included but is actually out of scope.

Increase the odds of success by acknowledging risks, concerns, and contingency plans for anything you uncover that might cause failure or unmet expectations, collaborating closely with project managers to do so.
Address conflicting concerns from different groups head-on and seek a solution that satisfies both, often by focusing on the highest-priority features identified through user research.
Capture verbatim quotes, shared without identifying information, because a person's specific words are highly valuable in revealing their personal perspective and attitudes.

For internal or workflow-changing projects, diagram both the current and the proposed workflows and use the diagrams throughout the project to track whether the organization is changing enough to accommodate the new design.
Do user research to identify patterns and develop empathy, since empathy is the most useful condition a designer can acquire and it comes only from interacting with the people you are designing for.

User research, as distinct from usability testing, means ethnography, studying target users as people in their cultural context to understand how and why they behave, which is fundamentally different from gathering opinions through surveys, polls, or focus groups.

Talk with or observe representative users directly in their own regular context, including their physical environment, mental model, habits, and relationships, to reduce the risk of bad assumptions based on your own experience, hopes, or preferences.

Understand the user's existing mental model of a system, because interfaces that strive for novelty with no hooks into an existing mental model are often unusable and force people to figure everything out from scratch.
Learn how users already solve the problem you address, because habits are hard to change but inserting a new hook into an existing habit is much easier than creating a wholly new habit.

Designing for yourself or your team risks embedding wrong assumptions, and even discrimination based on age, gender, ethnicity, sexuality, or ability, that alienates people and builds unintended barriers not serving your business goals or ethics.

Make each design decision deliberate and welcoming to your intended users instead of alienating them, and treat identifying and genuinely empathizing with the target audience as the most important research you do.

Never ask people directly what they want, because they tend to answer with what they think you want to hear or with how they like to see themselves, and because people cannot want what they cannot imagine.

Assume that people are poor reporters and predictors of their own preferences and behavior, so the researcher's job is to get the needed information by asking the right questions and observing the right details rather than trusting self-reports.

Recognize that the questions you ask directly and the questions you actually want answered are two different sets, and get people to tell stories about relevant real situations instead of asking the underlying question directly.

Ask about concrete past or typical situations, such as walking through a typical day or describing a specific misunderstanding, rather than speculative or self-assessment questions that invite rehearsed or useless answers.
Deep-dive to know a small but sufficient number of representative users very well rather than running a large, shallow survey of many people.
Get into the messy, unpredictable field and conduct participant observation in the user's actual environment, because behavior changes with context and no one acts naturally in your conference room.

Systematically analyze field observations with your team to work out what they mean and build useful models, since systematic analysis is what separates real ethnography from merely meeting interesting people.

Turn real observations into lively narratives, personas as fictional protagonists with goals, and scenarios, which keep the team honest by designing for the user rather than for yourself or your boss.
Understand that good interviewing is about shutting up and listening rather than being a good talker, treating the participant as the foremost expert on themselves.

Prepare an interview guide containing the study description and goal, the basic demographic or factual questions that give context, a couple of icebreaker warm-up questions, and the primary focus questions, and gather background on any unfamiliar domain beforehand.

Structure an interview in three acts, the introduction and warm-up, the body, and the conclusion, and in the introduction thank the participant, describe the purpose and topic without giving so much detail that you bias the answers, explain how the information will be used, and obtain explicit permission to record.

Ask open-ended questions that encourage the subject to talk rather than yes-or-no closed questions, use probing follow-ups such as tell me more about that, allow uncomfortable pauses without rushing to fill them, and use your questions as a checklist rather than a verbatim script.

Close an interview by inviting anything else the person wants to add, thanking them, and covering administrative matters like incentives and next steps, and do not be afraid to shut down an unproductive interview early.

Play the dual role of host and student: put the participant at ease, then become a nearly invisible, neutral presence that soaks up what they say and intervenes only to redirect back on topic or get clarification.

Practice active listening with attentive sounds, eye contact, and nodding, remember to breathe because your tension is contagious, stay alert for vague answers and probe for specifics, and avoid turning the conversation to yourself or your own experiences.

During field research note the exact phrases and vocabulary participants use so you can reflect the way they think and talk in the actual interface, and keep paying attention even after you stop recording, because a valuable revelation often comes then.

Treat the interview as the basic unit of ethnographic research: analyze all interviews together to find themes such as needs, priorities, behavior patterns, and mental models, and cluster the user types into personas you can use for the life of the product.

Use contextual inquiry, entering a participant's actual environment to watch them perform the activity you are studying, to see real behaviors and unconscious habitual workarounds that you would never hear about in an interview.

Run a site visit in stages: allow plenty of travel and setup time, get situated in a spot that does not interrupt the routine, interview first to build trust and learn when interruptions are least disruptive, observe and note everything in detail, and conclude by summarizing what you learned and asking the participant to verify it.
When a participant disagrees with your summarized observation you may still be correct, and the contradictory description is itself a very interesting data point.
Enter contextual inquiry ready to discover that people do not need what you assumed but need something entirely different, and joyfully release your preconceived plans and notions.

Avoid focus groups, because they create an artificial environment unlike any real use context, give no insight into behavior or habitual context, and invite social-desirability bias where participants proclaim or conceal behaviors for the benefit of the group, and a single bad recruit can tank the whole session.

Accept no substitute for listening to and observing the real people who need to do the things you are designing to help them do, since that information keeps paying dividends and grounds design decisions in real human needs and behaviors.

Define your competition broadly as everything anyone uses to solve or avoid the problem you address, not just the top market-share players and search results, including inertia, habit, and simply doing nothing.

Recognize that the hardest competitor to beat is the one your potential customers use right now, because switching to you incurs a cost, so your target customers must love you more than they hate change.

Identify who competes for your target users' attention, not only your obvious business competitors, because attention is the rarest resource you need to survive and you must convert attention into habit.

Do competitive research frequently and quickly, habitually asking what matters to your customers, how you serve that need better than any competitor, and how you show target customers that your product is the superior choice.
Treat knowledge as a competitive advantage: if you do competitive research and your competitor does not, you hold an advantage.

Use a SWOT analysis, arranging strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a simple grid, to grasp your competitive position and identify the user-experience aspects that amplify strengths, exploit opportunities, mitigate weaknesses, and counter threats, focusing your research on opportunities and threats.

Remember that you can see only the external surface of competitors, which is what users see too, so use critical thinking and extrapolation to infer why a competitor does things a certain way rather than relying on user research to reveal it.

Conduct a competitive audit by assembling competitors from your own list plus a web search plus products repeatedly mentioned in user interviews plus admired leaders solving a similar problem, then for each analyze how they position themselves, who they target, their key differentiators, how they embody your positive and negative attributes, how the needs they serve overlap yours, what they do well or badly, and where there are conventions or clear opportunities to be superior.

Audit your own brand, meaning your reputation and identity signals, to check it sets the right expectations, recognizing that for many interactive products the brand experience is the user experience, the interface visual design is the brand identity, and the interface voice is the brand personality.

Assess a brand through its attributes, meaning the associations you want and want to avoid, its value proposition of what it offers that others do not, and the associations real customers actually report in ethnographic interviews.
Recognize that the importance of branding varies tremendously with the marketplace, so compare like with like when analyzing competitive brands.
condition: depending on the marketplace: minimal for an essential local monopoly, and greater with a wider audience, stronger competition, or a premium product

statement: Treat the name as the single most important aspect of a brand, requiring at minimum that it be unique within the competitive field, unambiguous, and easy to spell and to say.

Assess a logo's importance by listing all the contexts in which target users will encounter it and reviewing competitors' logos in those same contexts, since how much a logo matters depends on where it must do its work.
condition: depending on the contexts in which users must identify and distinguish the product, and whether the logo ever appears on its own

statement: Usability-test your competitors' products with task-based testing to understand their strengths and weaknesses from the user's point of view, spot opportunities to develop your advantages, and learn how target users conceptualize core tasks and key features.
Assess how well your design works for its intended audience and purpose before staging a public launch, treating evaluation as research you never stop doing.
Assess a functional design with a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, because the numbers tell you what is going on and the individual people help you understand why it is happening.

Use heuristic analysis, in which at least two or three evaluators independently go through a site or application against a checklist of usability principles and score it, as a quick and cheap way to catch obvious issues in early prototypes without recruiting users.

Evaluate an interface against Nielsen's usability heuristics: visible system status, a match between the system and the real world, user control and freedom with undo and redo, consistency and standards, error prevention, recognition rather than recall, flexibility and efficiency with shortcuts, aesthetic and minimalist design, help recognizing and recovering from errors, and available task-oriented help.
Treat heuristic inspection as a good sanity check but not a substitute for usability testing with real users.
exception: heuristic analysis focuses on the system rather than the relationship between the user and the system and may miss issues that arise in context

statement: Treat usability as the absolute minimum standard for anything designed to be used by humans, so that a design which thwarts its intended users attempting the intended use is a failure from a user-centered standpoint.

Recognize that the easier it is for customers to switch to an alternative the more important usability is to your success, since barriers to usability are barriers to sales while a more usable product earns better word of mouth and lower support costs.
Accept that the harder a system is to design and build, the more effort its usability demands, that this effort is always worth spending, and that this is also a reason to keep feature sets simple.
Assess usability across Nielsen's five components: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, and satisfaction.

Run cheap tests before expensive ones: learn everything you can from paper prototypes and sketches before building a prototype, in your own office before going into the field, and with a general audience before harder-to-find specific ones, and test a competitor's product before you even start designing.

Test as often as significant design decisions are being made, because the most expensive usability testing is the kind put off until very late, and the costliest of all is what customers do for you through customer service after launch.
exception: never run usability testing right before launch

statement: Build usability practices into your workflow from the start like internal reviews, create a testing process and checklist covering the information and equipment you need, always be recruiting and maintain a database of potential participants, and designate a point person to keep it running smoothly.

Assemble everything a usability test requires: a plan, a sketch or prototype, four to eight participants for each target user type (drawn from personas or marketing segments), a facilitator, an observer, at least one way to document, and a timer.

Build a usability test around tasks, deriving the tasks and scenarios from the personas and their core tasks you have used throughout design, and for each feature write a brief story giving background on how the user arrived and what they are trying to accomplish.

Recognize that not all tasks are equal, so go into a test knowing which failures matter most and treat the deal-breaker task, such as completing a purchase or finding a location's address and hours, as one that must succeed.

Make a checklist test plan covering objectives, the subject and its state, methodology, participants and recruiting, procedure, tasks, usability goals, completion rate, and error-free rate, and keep planning time low to save your energy for analyzing the results.

Treat usability-test participants as single-use fuel and keep a good supply, since participants brought back are tainted by prior exposure and will not show how someone approaches the system for the first time.
Select usability-test participants who share some key goals with your target users, because otherwise they cannot immerse themselves sufficiently in the scenarios you give them.

Choose a facilitator with the right temperament, personable and patient enough to warm participants up yet able to dispassionately observe them struggle, because a bad facilitator tanks the whole test no matter how well-targeted the participants are.

During a usability test avoid leading the user or helping them when they get lost and embrace the uncomfortable silences, and be especially wary that the system's own designer or developer is most tempted to inject hints and leading questions.
When a participant blames themselves for a usability issue rather than the system, ask them to describe the behavior they expected from the system and the reason behind that expectation.
Have a second person observe and take notes even when you are recording, so the facilitator can stay responsive to the participant and the observer can create the fewest distractions.

Audio-record sessions with informed consent as a reliable, low-overhead backup for imperfect memories and notes, while treating video as often less valuable because its usefulness depends on time-consuming editing and it consumes large amounts of storage.

Have the observer, working from a copy of the test script with room for annotations and approximate time codes, note the participant's reaction to each task, how long it takes, whether they failed, and any terminology that was a stumbling block, prioritizing nonverbal frustration, verbatim quotes, and features that were notably successful or unsuccessful.
Avoid paying for eye-tracking in most cases, because the equipment and specialists are expensive and it is rarely worth the cost.
condition: only when testing populations who have trouble articulating what is drawing their attention on the page

statement: Aim usability testing at identifying specific significant problems to fix, producing a ranked punch list with rationale focused on the issues, their severity, and recommended fixes, and keep the source materials organized for anyone interested or skeptical.
Rate each problem users encountered on both severity and frequency, because you must consider both to prioritize real obstacles rather than chasing a fluke.

Use defined severity levels, where high prevents completing the task, moderate causes difficulty but the task is still completed, and low is a minor problem, together with frequency bands of high at thirty percent or more, moderate at eleven to twenty-nine percent, and low at ten percent or fewer.

Sort usability issues into three tiers combining severity and frequency and weighted by how core the related task is: Tier 1 high-impact frequent blockers that pose high risk, Tier 2 moderate problems, and Tier 3 low-impact rare problems that pose low risk.
Act on usability results immediately by starting with Tier 1 issues, identifying the fixes with the lowest technical effort, implementing them, and then testing again.

To convince decision-makers to make changes, arrange for important people to watch real users struggle, which is more convincing than a report, and pair verbatim quotes and video clips of failure with the report, always connecting the tested tasks and found problems to high-priority business goals.

Run a benchmark usability study by testing a small common set of tasks across your site and your competitors' with a common scoring system to see who is most usable overall and per task, and re-run it after a redesign to verify improvement relative to competitors.

Analyze qualitative data collaboratively by closely reviewing the notes, writing each interesting behavior, emotion, action, or quote on a sticky note coded back to its source user, grouping the notes on a whiteboard, watching the patterns emerge, and rearranging as you assess them.
Use an affinity diagram to extract general design mandates from interviews, which if time is short may be your only analysis pass, and then prioritize those mandates based on business goals.

Write down as an observation only a direct quote or objective description of what the user did or said, flag quotes that represent each user type's needs for your personas, and note the vocabulary participants used, especially where it differs from your organization's.
Name each emerging pattern and the user need it reveals, then translate it into an actionable design mandate or principle.

Treat a persona as a fictional user archetype, a composite model built from data gathered by talking to real people, that represents a group of needs and behaviors and lets designers advocate for users' needs against business, marketing, and engineering voices.

Keep design targets separate from marketing targets, because market segments do not translate into archetypes and the user type with the highest business value may not be the best design target; designing for users with less expertise can also meet the needs of those with more.
Create as few personas as possible while still representing all relevant behavior patterns, reducing the number by creating relationships among them and assigning multiple roles to a single persona.

Base a useful persona on firsthand user research and collaborative pattern-finding rather than invention, keeping the documentation brief enough to build a vivid individual from a few key details that can be reused over time.

Construct a persona from a real non-stock photo of someone unknown to the team, a memorable pronounceable name, realistic non-stereotyped demographics derived from real users, a role matching both an interviewed participant and a target type, an actual revealing quote, three to four key goals, defining behaviors and habits, a realistic skill level you do not merely assume, the relevant environment, and the relationships that affect use.

Treat a scenario as the story of how a persona interacts with your system to meet a goal, and use scenarios to flesh out requirements, explore and validate potential solutions, and seed usability-test scripts, keeping them close to real research data while allowing the format and details to evolve.

Distinguish scenarios from use cases and user stories: a scenario is told from the perspective of the individual human user represented by the persona, whereas a use case is a list of system-user interactions that captures functional requirements.
Judge your personas to be working when they become the first people you check any new idea against, replacing does this work for me or my boss with does this address the persona's concerns.
In design, intuitive means matching the user's mental model, so the closer an interface fits that internal image the easier it will be to learn, use, and navigate.
To design an application or website, study the mental models of the activities you want to support, such as the mental model of getting to work when designing a transit app.
Remember that as a designer you hold your own mental model of what you are building plus assumptions about users, and it is easy to overestimate how well your view matches their reality.

Document the user's mental model to get it out of your own head and visible to the team, using the diagram to collaborate, prioritize features, organize information, find needs that are not being served, and resolve divergences between user types or between proposed and actual design.

Create a mental-model diagram by doing user research, making an affinity diagram, stacking the affinity clusters of actions, beliefs, and feelings to represent the user's cognitive space, and grouping the stacks around the tasks or goals they relate to.
Translate the mental model into a conceptual map that relates content and functionality from the target user's point of view, which becomes the basis of the information architecture.
For an existing product, use the mental model to run a gap analysis of mismatches between what you offer and what users need or expect, and design features that fill those gaps.
exception: drop planned features that do not fit the users' mental model at all

statement: Use task analysis to break one task into the discrete steps required to accomplish it and map real-world behavior to functionality, using contextual inquiry as the best prelude or sufficiently detailed interview data.

Break down a task by noting the initial state, the event that prompts the user to begin, the information or tools needed at each step, and any steps where the task is likely to be interrupted or resumed, then reassemble the steps as a workflow.
Use task analysis to identify where specific content can support the user along their task path, remembering that users may take very different paths than you anticipated.

Treat communicating the meaning and value of research as a design activity itself, because a clear, economical, visually appealing diagram helps promote the value of research among skeptics in your organization.

Recognize that optimizing a design is the chief aim of quantitative research but that what is optimal is always subjective and involves trade-offs, so you must define what you are optimizing for and watch for optimizing one thing causing other harms.

Use qualitative methods like ethnography and usability testing to design for likely success, then use the quantitative data from the live product to see how right you were, accepting that you will not get everything right up front.

Define conversion as any measurable action you have set as a goal of the site and measure the conversion rate of each path, while treating how much each type of conversion matters to the organization as a business decision.

Use analytics, the collection and analysis of actual usage data, to identify where the site is not as effective as you want, make changes, and then check the metrics again to see whether the changes had an effect.

Track basic analytics such as visits, pageviews, pages per visit, bounce rate, time on site, and percentage of new visitors, and interpret them against your goals rather than in isolation, since more pageviews can mean either engagement or people unable to find what they need.

Define quantitative goals if you lack them, starting from averages for your type of site or industry as the numbers to beat, and when you are not making your numbers review the data and prioritize changes, starting with bounce rate.

Use analytics to find the most frequent entry pages and review them for clarity, making sure the design and content convey what you want visitors to do, then follow up with usability testing or split testing.

Understand that a split test serves the current design as a control to some visitors and a variation to others, with the variation that performs significantly better on a specific metric being the winner, which can then face further challengers.
Run a split test only with a specific, quantifiable goal, knowing the current conversion rate or metric and how much you want to change it, because there is no room for interpretation.

Ensure a split test has sufficient traffic and sample size, because small incremental changes matter more on high-traffic sites and a small change measured in a small sample is likely just the result of chance.

Run a split test until you reach a ninety-five percent statistical confidence level, ideally over a holiday-free period of about two weeks to rule out chance and confounds like day of the week or traffic outliers, since less patience opens you to more false positives and false negatives.
Reserve split testing for the parts of a design suited to it rather than applying it everywhere.
condition: for aspects of the design where users might expect to see variation and where there is a single clear user behavior to elicit, such as search-marketing landing pages for new users, and not for stable elements like global navigation

statement: Design and run split-test experiments so as not to disrupt what is already working well, because a consistent online experience builds trust and habit while split testing by nature introduces inconsistency.

Treat split testing as an incremental optimization tool rather than a source of high-level strategy, and beware that focusing only on small positive changes can breed a culture of incrementalism and risk aversion.
Beware the local maximum, since you can only optimize so far within an existing design system, and weigh larger innovations against incremental optimization of what you already have.

Always answer why before asking how, because the best response to a user-interface question is not necessarily a test and it is understanding context and qualitative factors that lets you see opportunities beyond the current best.

Build teams that embrace data while inspiring everyone to look beyond what can be measured to what might be valued, because you can optimize everything and still fail if you optimize for the wrong things.
Value questions over answers, recognizing that asking hard questions often takes more courage than sticking with comfortable assumptions.
Always inquire into the real-world context surrounding your work, because when blue-sky thinking meets reality, reality always wins.

Cultivate a desire to be proven wrong as quickly and as cheaply as possible, since in a fail-fast culture there is no faster way to fail than testing an idea still on the drawing board, or checking your assumptions before you even start drawing.
Treat research as a means to develop useful insights within your existing process rather than a burden or a luxury, following one basic sequence of forming questions, gathering data, and analyzing.

Conversational design is more than building interfaces that talk or text; it means applying the deeper principles of how humans interact so systems succeed on human terms regardless of the interaction mode.
A conversational approach treats every interaction as human-centered design at every step, rather than as a novel feature bolted onto a product.
Words and language are a design material and should be considered from the start of the design process, not treated as content added at the end.
Organizations that form teams around the artifacts people produce (visual design, code, copy) rather than around the shared problem fragment the work and isolate writers.
Interface copy should be treated as iterable and changeable like the rest of the interface, not as a fixed contract that must survive a heavyweight approval process before it can appear.
An interface that appears conversational on the surface (exchanging text with a bot) is not necessarily conversational in practice or easier for people to reach their goals.
Designing the visual container first and adding meaning afterward is backwards; what each view should contain cannot be known until the user's needs are considered.
The compelling pull of texting comes from always-available social connection and language, not from high production values, rich media, or feature complexity.
Conversation is the oldest human interface, so the principles of human conversation can be reused to make digital systems intuitive.
A good conversation amounts to far more than trading phrases; it rests on an unspoken agreement between the participants and works only when they cooperate toward a goal they both accept.
Nothing is more valuable simply because it is new; a technology is valuable when it delivers more of what is already meaningful to people.
Conversational interfaces built well amplify the human-computer bond and promote trust, while those built poorly produce mistrust.
A designer's core job is to listen to people's real needs, feelings, and stories, grounding empathy in reality rather than in artifacts that only appear to serve users.
Digital communication has returned to the values of oral culture (immediate, social, participatory, collaborative, anti-authoritarian), a state Ong called secondary orality.
Oral traditions used formulas, repetition, and concrete vivid imagery to make knowledge memorable, a technique still useful for making language stick.
Collaborative, conversational contribution can be more powerful than top-down authority, as shown by Wikipedia outcompeting authority-governed encyclopedias.
Designing for internet-based culture requires shifting from thinking about how information occupies space (documents) to how it occupies time (events).
A text-based interaction with a machine that stands in for a human should feel like a text-based interaction with a human.
Verbal design should be approached as a conversation, not as a literary work, because literary writing is inherently non-interactive.
Approaching communication as an assembly of content pieces rather than as an interaction leaves customers feeling handed a manual when they expected a conversation.
Interactive systems should evoke the best qualities of living human communities (active, social, simple, present) rather than being passive, isolated, complex, or closed off.
The ideal interface is one that is not noticeable at all, collapsing the distance from thought to action.
Making customers learn an unfamiliar interface before they can get value is bad for business; it is better to reward the expectations they already bring.

Because people simultaneously occupy multiple contexts and roles across connected devices, any single system contributes only a fraction of the overall experience, so being context-aware is essential.
An interface is effective to the extent that it helps both parties in an interaction get what they need from each other; value must flow both ways.
Interfaces should be as simple, intuitive, and similar to one another as possible, because conversation is the interface most people already know how to use.
It is not the mode of interaction but the meaning of the exchange that makes it valuable.
Regularly conversing does not automatically make someone good at designing conversational interactions; designing them requires understanding how conversation works.
Grice's cooperative principle holds that for conversation to work, every participant must contribute what is required, when required, to keep it on track toward the accepted purpose.
Maxim of Quantity: make a contribution as informative as required and no more informative than required.
Maxim of Quality: do not say what you believe to be false or that for which you lack adequate evidence; be authentic and transparent about your agenda.
Maxim of Relation: contribute in a way relevant to the conversation's purpose; skilled communicators are appropriate, not merely relevant, which demands higher-order context awareness.
Maxim of Manner: be brief, orderly, and unambiguous; brevity is necessary but insufficient, so aim for expression that is both succinct and clear.
Lakoff's politeness principle adds three rules to Grice's maxims: don't impose, give options, and make the listener feel good.

A system should manifest conversational qualities at a deeper level rather than a superficial conversational facade, because a facade forces people to focus on the limits of the technology instead of their goals.
Grice's maxims can be reformulated into design principles that apply to any interaction or interface regardless of mode or medium, including systems that use no verbal language at all.

Cooperative systems actively support the customer and require no special knowledge or computer literacy; without a deep commitment to stay on the customer's side, the technology dictates the range of interactions.
condition: only when the organization deeply commits to remaining on the side of the customer

statement: A successful interaction helps both parties meet their goals pleasantly and efficiently; nothing can be designed in the absence of a clear goal.
Only user research reveals what a customer needs in different times, places, and circumstances; device signals such as location and time zone alone are insufficient for true context-awareness.
Prioritize the subjective sensation of speed and keep ambiguity out of systems; precision is a machine's chief advantage, so do not undermine it with human imprecision.

Conversation happens in turns, so set the right expectations and provide progress cues (such as a visible 'thinking' indicator) when processing will take time, to prevent users thinking something is broken.
Request or provide the right information at the right time and validate input before acting on it, especially when a misunderstanding carries a penalty or the action is non-trivial to undo.
condition: especially when a misunderstanding carries a penalty or the action is hard to undo

statement: Functional conversations require shared clarity about whose turn it is at every moment.
Being truthful in an interface means setting the right expectations so that what the user expects strongly correlates with what the system offers, not merely avoiding technically false statements.
Nielsen Norman Group research found that unexplained 'Get Started' links are no better than login walls that trick users into creating accounts before understanding the service.
Polite design respects the user's time and meets business goals without interrupting the customer's pursuit of their own objectives; interrupting ads that obscure content are rude.

A truly conversational interaction is fault-tolerant: it anticipates errors and recovers seamlessly, whereas superficial natural-language interfaces overpromise cooperation and can deliver a less human experience.
Rather than simulating human minds, designers should capitalize on the complementary differences between humans and computers instead of forcing people to conform to the technology.
A conversational interface need not use natural language; voice or text can be a burden when the application is complex or the system cannot reliably guess the user's intent.
exception: unless the application is simple enough and the system robust enough to correctly guess intent

statement: Google Search has embodied core conversational principles since 1998 and has needed only cleanup rather than redesign, showing that a sound conversational model endures.

Aim for interactions that flow like conversations regardless of medium, letting users switch modes seamlessly by context; with the right framework in place, new capabilities can be layered in without breaking the model.
The experience of speed is subjective, and presentation alone can change it: identical results felt slower on Yahoo than on Google despite Yahoo licensing Google's engine, because of a busier layout.
The better a system matches the user's intent, the better the outcome for both the user and the business.
Design to tolerate messy, imperfect human input and interpret intent rather than putting the work of supplying clean input onto the user.
Making query revision and repeated turns feel effortless, with natural turn-taking, makes users perceive the system as reliable and unbreakable.
Following conversational design principles is only part of the job; they must also be applied in the right way at the right time.
Interactions occur in a series of key moments (Introduction, Orientation, Action, Guidance), and each moment should support the success of the overall interaction.
In just seconds, a successful introduction should convey who the product is, capture attention, show what it is worth, forge an emotional connection, earn trust, and point to an obvious next step.

New users arrive with unspoken questions about who the product is, what it does for them, why it should matter, how they ought to feel, whether it can be trusted, and where to go next; unless the design answers these deliberately, the system will leave them unanswered for the user.
If you cannot distill what you offer into a single introductory sentence, you are pushing the work of understanding it onto the customer.
The more complex the product or service, the more powerful its first impression needs to be.
Treat every page as a potential homepage and entry point, continually asking, 'What if someone who doesn't know what we do ends up here?'
Lead with concrete details rather than abstract promises.
Overexplaining erodes credibility and wastes time; match the amount of explanation to what the social context already conveys.
condition: when the social context of the interaction already conveys the proposition

statement: Evoke emotions and physical sensations rather than speaking in abstractions, and be persuasive as well as descriptive, because it is not an interaction unless the person answers.
Creating awareness is not enough; move people from awareness to action without requiring effort on their part.

A product becomes forgettable when it has a generic or hard-to-spell name, says too little or too much, looks or sounds like other products, lacks a clear pitch, offers too many options, or uses terms meaningless to the target customer.
Deliberately imitating other products to benefit from customer confusion is a dark pattern.
A spatial metaphor makes information easier to retain and process, so use language to build a vivid mental map, ideally one that fits a pre-existing mental picture and requires no learning.
Navigation labels should be as straightforward as possible, and navigation is not the place to try out novel concepts, because unclear 'mystery meat' labels fail users.
People interacting with information systems perform a continuous cost-benefit analysis (information foraging) and want to know as quickly as possible whether they are on a path to success.
Orient a service around the user's intention rather than forcing users to reorient themselves as they move between devices.
A device-centered perspective is a pitfall; ask how a device can provide more value to both the customer and the business, not merely how to extract more purchases from the customer.

Provide cues, prompts, and suggestions to reveal capabilities, because without them users must be highly motivated to discover features, as shown by sharp Amazon Echo usage drop-off after basic tasks (only 32% reported buying anything).
Hick's Law: the more choices a person faces, the longer a choice takes, so determine the smallest number of the most appropriate choices to reach the goal.
Offer the right choices at the right time rather than all up front, and order them so the most consequential or meaningful choices come first.

An open input field represents a nearly infinite set of choices and is appropriate only when the system offers a large response set relative to possible requests; otherwise menus are faster and friendlier.
condition: only when the system offers a large set of potential responses relative to the set of possible requests

statement: Orienting a user means presenting the full range of possibilities and then eliminating nearly all of them, because a user with a goal only wants to know whether they can accomplish that specific thing.
A system that remembers past behavior can offer timely, appropriate choices (such as reordering) without blocking the user from making new choices.
When a system makes decisions on behalf of users, it must preserve at least the illusion that the human is still in control.
The most fundamental design decision is what actions (verbs) the product lets customers take, because the verbs are the point of the conversation and part or all of the goal.
To reconcile human mental models (habit, feeling) with machine precision, break a single customer action into its component parts and rebuild it piece by piece.
Every action must be goal-oriented and context-aware and must provide feedback on whether it succeeded or failed and what to do next, with its implications clear and apparent.
All actions must be reversible or give a very clear warning when they represent commitments; any interface that omits or misrepresents an action's full consequences is failing to be truthful.
For each action, communicate its prerequisites, encouragement, instructions, consequences, and level of commitment, and present users only with actions they can actually take.
Ambiguity decreases trust and increases cognitive overhead, creating anxiety and work; even a soft word like 'especially' can introduce unsettling uncertainty.
The wording of an action defines it even in graphical or icon-based interfaces, and no amount of styling can overcome misleading wording.
Design choices carry an ethical dimension, not only a cognitive one, and a system working in true cooperation with a user will not lead them down a bad path even though each minor choice adds up.
A limited menu of choices can create the illusion of greater freedom while actually manipulating the user and distracting them from their true needs.
Because users rarely question what is absent from a menu or whose goals it serves, designers should recognize a duty to minimize distraction from customers' higher-order life goals.
Action labels define the range of human agency within a system, and the more people rely on that system, the more consequential those labels become.
Aim for a system in balance: transparent about the business goals it represents while encouraging actions that provide value to both the business and the customer.
Habits are feedback loops of cue, routine, and reward formed through repetition, and nothing that requires conscious thought will ever be as usable as something used out of habit.
Design the interaction as a learning loop where system feedback helps users build mastery over time, because that growing mastery is a powerful reward that aligns customer goals with system goals.

Attempts at 'delight' commonly fail by underestimating the cognitive effort an unfamiliar interface requires and overestimating the pleasure of the reward, yielding novel interfaces that frustrate or delight only once before grating on repetition.
Even a well-designed system often needs to explain itself to help customers succeed; avoiding verbosity may look refined, but leaving users confused is worse.
Practice progressive disclosure: offer just what is needed for the task at hand, and combine an unambiguous action with additional guidance rather than relying on a label or icon to do all the work.

Computers should perform all information storage and retrieval in the relationship, and any system that relies on human memory to function has failed its human, which is why password-based authentication is a major failure.
Use stored information to benefit customers, but avoid creeping them out; a system that refers to itself as a watching 'we' concerned about 'you' destroys the illusion that it is a neutral utility.
Place detailed guidance after the user's choice, not before it, because presenting too much information at the wrong time (as in a password-recovery flow) violates conversational maxims.
Notifications should require affirmative consent, so establish trust and offer value before prompting a customer to receive them, and maintain a holistic strategy across all messaging channels.
Helpful notifications are well-timed, concise and clear, personalized and relevant, and deliver value that enables action while rewarding the customer's trust.

Notifications are appropriate only when the customer is likely to welcome the interruption and can take action in response; they should not be used for advertising, messages with no customer value, or situations with no action to take.
Creating a sense of urgency in a notification when there is no possible action for the customer only creates anxiety.
Demonstrate context-awareness in messaging by routing notifications only to the customer's active endpoint rather than every signed-in device.

The amount and type of onboarding a system needs depends on how different it is from systems the customer knows, its conceptual complexity, and the effort required before the customer gets something useful.
The best onboarding is the least intrusive: lightweight and integrated into the experience rather than a long up-front tutorial, focused on getting the user to value in support of business goals.
To design effective onboarding you must know which customer actions deliver the greatest value, and if you do not know what constitutes value, you must do user research before designing the system.
Treat the entire interaction as a cooperative endeavor in which misconceptions can arise on either side, rather than as a simple dichotomy between error and correct behavior.
Expecting people to behave 'correctly' produces fragile interactions, because humans are improvisational, not precision systems.
When a user makes a mistake, the humane response is to gently correct, redirect, and help prevent the error from recurring; how a machine handles human error is the best test of how human it seems.
When the system itself fails, do not be glib about serious setbacks (especially loss of personal data); offer a sincere apology and a quick path to setting things right.
condition: especially when the failure causes a serious setback or loss of personal data

statement: Set expectations for a learning system so it does not overreach ('be as smart as a puppy'), but remember that endearing failure is unacceptable when the user is pursuing an important goal like booking a flight or transferring money.
exception: except when the user is trying to accomplish an important or high-stakes goal, where failure is not endearing

statement: Apply poka-yoke (mistake-proofing) by constraining user input within boundaries, such as offering a menu of options instead of open text input.
Run through every scenario in which a customer using the system as designed could end up harming themselves, and design to prevent it.
Preventing customers from embarrassing or harming themselves (for example, warning about a missing email attachment) earns lasting loyalty.

Start with the right concept that matches the user's existing mental model; since you cannot control user expectations, you must understand them and assume users are on autopilot, drawing unconscious inferences from the barest cues.
Interface cues set expectations: open-ended input implies any answer is acceptable, and a voice that sounds too human sets expectations too high.
Never require users to retain information in their memory, always confirm ('Are you sure?') before dangerous or consequential actions, and gently warn users when they approach a risky boundary.

Before adopting a chat or natural-language interface, verify it will actually make life easier, because such interfaces often lack context-awareness, take more time than a button click, are unpredictable, and are not error-tolerant.

The same conversational principles apply across all interaction moments with different emphases, and designers should avoid assumptions about what users want in favor of understanding real-world contexts.

Conversational principles need a unifying personality to come to life; a distinctive, appropriate, and consistent personality is the animating spirit of conversational design, and it matters more as interactions grow more sophisticated.
If you do not craft a system's personality intentionally, customers will assign one in their minds, and it will not be as good as one you design and control.
The fewer senses a service engages, the more of the product design the voice must carry, so text-based chatbots depend almost entirely on their personality.
A voice interface forces assigning a gender (or offering a choice), and users may connect with or be repelled by the system based on associations between its capabilities and its gender presentation.
Naming and persona choices carry social implications, so choosing whether an assistant is a named human-like servant or represents the whole company requires a nuanced approach.
To make an emotional connection you must understand the people and what they are emotionally connected to; otherwise you build the personality you would like rather than the one they want.
Conducting user research before design work and continuously throughout it is not optional for creating interfaces meaningful to real people.

Listen to how real users talk about your service, their day, and their problems in order to be intelligible to them (not to mimic them), and rid yourself of internal phrasings in favor of ones natural to users.
Understand and anticipate users' negative emotional states, such as anxious, confused, overwhelmed, skeptical, bored, and frustrated, to find the right balance of clarity and humanity.

Extract your interface vocabulary from users by interviewing about half a dozen representative customers, letting them speak, then pulling the nouns and verbs from your notes to guide labels and action phrases.
Liking and valuing customers is a discipline required to design well for them; a cynical view of people (as 'eyeballs' or 'uniques') produces impersonal, system-centered design.
Liking customers means appreciating that they have a different perspective, not identifying with them; you must care about them or you cannot expect them to care about you.
Clear values are needed to create a personality with integrity, values are implicit in the business model, and you cannot adopt values that run counter to how you make money.

Define values collaboratively with key stakeholders in the context of real interactions, because personalities go wrong when abstract core values are written at the top and handed down for a design team to interpret.
State company values in human terms that sound like something a real person would say in conversation, because that is where the energy and life are.
After clarifying values, list the adjectives you want customers to use and those to avoid, then narrow to three positive adjectives unique to you and three to avoid, and use them to guide all work.
Focus on what you have to say before how you sound, drawing the right style out of the subject matter rather than applying authenticity like a veneer.
Lead with the functions and flow that reflect what customers already care about, so you inhabit existing mental pathways rather than carving new ones.
Being conversational does not mean being informal or unserious; doctors, bankers, and funeral directors all have conversations within professional propriety.

Match a system's personality to the human analog of the role it plays in users' lives (for example, a reliable banker or a compassionate funeral director) rather than to a celebrity or an abstract metaphor.
Keep the fundamental characteristics of a personality stable while allowing its tone to adapt to subject matter and context.

Define a system's personality along the dimensions of identity, expertise, mood and attitude, and relationship, since the degree to which it exhibits its own identity sets expectations for functionality and familiarity.
An overly human personality can backfire (as parodied by Marvin the Paranoid Android), and most effective interfaces are neutral and slightly positive.
A robust personality makes the most difference in the mundane, repeated details of interactions, so design copy as real, recurring customer interactions rather than abstract descriptors.

For an international audience, adapt the personality to the local language and culture through transcreation (evoking the same emotions and implications), because translating only for meaning is ineffective.

At every point and in every role, the interface should come across as supportive and on the customer's side, even during less positive interactions, and should never adopt an inappropriate role such as a clingy romantic partner.
Humor depends on context and timing and can backfire, since what is funny to one person may be incomprehensible or offensive to another.
The easiest way to avoid being unfunny is to not try to be funny; deeply understanding your audience reveals what actually gives them pause or tickles their fancy.
Lead with the crucial information the customer needs (such as when food will arrive) rather than burying it beneath canned cheer.
The best humor plays against expectations and works because it is unexpected, so it loses effect if it appears constantly.

Language is imitative, so borrowing from bureaucratic sites or clickbait will make you unconsciously parrot their mush; understand domain conventions but seek inspiration from a wide range of voices of verbal excellence.
Get out into the real world where customers go, listen to how people in different roles actually talk, and collect and catalog both good and bad voice samples for reference.

Use concrete, precise language with no superfluous words and go in fear of abstractions, because spare, evocative language lodges in the mind precisely because it is conversational and needs no embellishment.
Clarify a system's voice and values by making an explicit list of 'avoidably ugly words' that must never be used because they are imprecise or empty.
Start defining a voice from the negative space: articulate what you do not want to sound like first.

Avoid meaningless filler and clichés that any product could use (such as 'helpful', 'compelling', 'innovative', or 'world-class'), because if you have to say it, you probably are not it; let customers judge those qualities.
Stop using 'Submit' as a button label and instead describe the specific action the button triggers.
Avoid generic calls to action like 'Click here', because they break down as interfaces increasingly support switching between voice and text.

Use second-person pronouns for the user's things ('your' profile or cart) and first-person plural for the company's things ('our' policy), address customers as 'you', and drop possessives for anything that is just part of the experience, since awkward possessive labels sound even worse spoken aloud.
Words convey only a fraction of human communication, so because digital systems lack body language they must lean heavily on well-chosen language and seek supplemental social cues.
Small textual cues change perceived tone; research found that text messages ending in a period seem less sincere, and absent explicit positive signals readers default to a negative interpretation.

People can react more strongly to perceived unfairness from a computer than from a human (shown in Ultimatum Game fMRI research), and computer-mediated interaction can be less stressful because people get less emotionally involved.

Choose nonverbal or emotional embellishment (such as emoji) according to context and the system's personality, since it can be inappropriate (for example a bank sending a sad face about an overdraft) and always requires a personality clearly defined in words.
condition: depending on the context of the communication and the personality of the system

statement: Tacking a friendly face onto a system in bad faith will not make the underlying system more meaningful or sustainable; genuine personality comes from valuing customers and knowing your values.
To create conversational, human-centered systems, a team must work in a more conversational, human-centered way.
Conway's Law holds that any organization designing a system produces a design whose structure copies the organization's own communication structure.
How human and goal-oriented a system feels reflects how well its creators interacted with each other; visible seams in an interface are the result of handoffs and unresolved arguments.
'Process' is just a business word for habit, and changing an organization's habits requires tremendous effort in the absence of a crisis, even when the current way causes pain.

Verbal (writing) design must not run on a separate track from visual and interaction design, because splitting it disserves the whole experience and produces an interface of boxes filled in with language.
Writers and designers need a feedback loop telling them how successful their work was, because without it they can never learn and improve.
Process change begins with a perceived problem; if no problem is perceived, there will be no change.
Decisions about verbal language and nonverbal cues belong within interaction and interface design, made together in a single process rather than on separate tracks.
The greatest barrier to innovation is comfort with the current way of doing things, because an artifact-based process makes it easy to repackage familiar thinking while feeling like progress.
Do not confuse polish for value, because once an artifact exists it is easy to invest it with value and become unwilling to discard the weak idea it represents.

Agile and Lean risk conflating features with value; the goal of conversational design, like any good design, is to create the most value with the fewest features, favoring more thinking and less building.
Get people to talk together early rather than passing documentation around, because an organization cannot solve a problem holistically if different groups work from different information sets.
A conversational work culture applies the same principles as conversational interfaces: cooperative, goal-oriented, context-aware, quick and clear, turn-based, truthful, polite, and error-tolerant.

Listening is an underrepresented workplace skill, so everyone must wait their turn and truly listen, treating the work as an interactive collective process rather than the sum of individual contributions.
Build an error-tolerant team culture that is a safe environment in which people can offer ideas that may be wrong or fail, treating that as a productive part of the process.
Some authority and documentation is a fact of organizational life rather than a flaw, but every organization should still have clear goals and a willingness to continuously reflect and improve.
As soon as you start drawing screens you stop being truly human-centered, so do not begin the design by drawing screens.

Use the Concept-Script-Sketch model: begin with a strong, device-independent concept (a weak idea cannot be saved by delightful styling), then script the exchange of information, and only then sketch the supporting interface.

Before building, step back from Minimum Viable Product to a 'Minimum Meaningful Conversation' to understand the exchange of value from the customer's perspective, treating it as the thought experiment before the experiment.
Start from the customer's intent, questions, and expressed needs, and design how and where you answer at the moment they have a problem, rather than leaving that moment to marketing.

Work through the value exchange by asking how the customer expresses need, what exchange occurs, what they must give, what choices they get, how to close while conveying value, and how to leave the door open to future interactions.

Design early prototypes to separate the polish of production from the value of the idea, because it is easy to become defensive about labor-intensive artifacts that are merely shiny vessels for weak ideas.
The best way to design, prototype, and test interactive systems is to interact with people, and you can test more interactions faster by doing less.

Use the Wizard of Oz method, having a human simulate the system to test flow and conversation without technological constraints, which reveals genuine customer expectations and tests the core interaction from both sides.
Reiterate the project's goals and principles regularly and use checklists to ensure adherence, because forgetting is easy and repetition is powerful.
Work in real time by including all perspectives at once rather than passing an artifact around for commentary, using real-time collaboration tools and eliminating internal email as much as possible.
Encourage candid feedback and have everyone practice giving, receiving, and responding to it, because feedback and critique are the essence of a lively, iterative process.
Include decision-makers directly in the design process, even remotely, because their participation saves significant time later.
Frame design conversations around decisions and the experience being created (an exchange of information in time) rather than around artifacts and the arrangement of elements in space.

Never permit lorem ipsum or placeholder language, because language and meaning belong at the center of the experience and specific wording is part of the design subject to continuous iteration, not a separate 'writing' process.

Read aloud every word intended to be customer-facing, because it is an essential test of meaning and timing, ensures the interface works across text and speech, and reduces the perceived permanence of the written word.
Significant change to how an organization designs and collaborates happens incrementally over time, with everyone involved contributing to the practice.
The true purpose of process is to make humans more efficient, not to eradicate humanity or to avoid dealing directly with one another.
When approaching a design problem, look past the surface components and code to what it means for the human beings involved.
Cultivating direct, honest communication and mutual respect is what enables a team to collaborate on meaningful interactions.
Advancing technology will not change anything fundamental about human nature, so to invent the future it helps to understand the long history of how humans communicate.
Begin design work by knowing your goal, listening before you speak, and starting the conversation with the question 'What are we here to do?'
To solve new problems in new ways, look beyond the typical design reading list to build historical perspective and an understanding of the nature of language.
Keeping a few key usability principles in mind gives designers more leverage than memorizing long checklists of specific do's and don'ts.
Most usability questions have no single correct answer; the honest answer is usually 'it depends', so usability guidance should be treated as guiding principles rather than hard-and-fast rules.
The greater the time investment a task requires, or merely appears to require, the less likely people are to undertake it.
Judge usability by whether a person of roughly average or lesser skill and experience can work out how to accomplish their goal with the thing, without it being more bother than it is worth.

Usability is fundamentally about people and how they understand and use things, not about technology; because human capabilities change very slowly, usability insights retain their value even as technology changes quickly.
Usability principles apply to the design of anything people must interact with (websites, mobile apps, appliances, ATMs, even ballots), not only web pages.
Designers can learn more from studying good designs that have minor flaws than from mocking badly designed ones.

Krug's First Law of Usability is 'don't make me think': a page or screen should be self-evident, obvious, and self-explanatory so users grasp what it is and how to use it without expending conscious effort.
'Don't make me think' is the overriding usability principle and the ultimate tie-breaker for deciding whether a design works.
When designing, treat your job as eliminating the 'question marks' (moments of unnecessary thought) from every page.
Avoid cute, clever, marketing-driven, company-specific, or unfamiliar technical names for things users must find or click, because such names force needless thought.
When naming things, bias the tradeoff further toward 'obvious' than instinct suggests, since names fall on a continuum from obvious to obscure.
Make links and buttons unmistakably clickable; users should never have to spend even a millisecond deciding whether something is clickable.

Every 'question mark' (moment of uncertainty) adds to the user's cognitive workload and distracts from the task; individually slight, these costs accumulate, especially for frequently repeated actions such as deciding what to click.
Making users puzzle over how to use a site erodes their confidence in the site and in the organization behind it.
Aim for each page to be self-evident; when that is impossible it must at least be self-explanatory (understandable with only a little thought).
condition: when a page cannot be made fully self-evident, e.g. for original, groundbreaking, or inherently complex tasks

statement: Achieve self-explanatory pages by coordinating visual appearance (size, color, layout), well-chosen names, and small amounts of carefully crafted text to create near-effortless understanding.
The main reason to minimize required thinking is that people spend far less time looking at pages than designers assume, so pages must do their work at a glance.

Users are not always free to abandon a frustrating site: they may have no alternative (an intranet, their bank, a sole supplier) or may endure the frustration while blaming themselves rather than the site.

In reality users do not read pages carefully; they glance at each new page, scan some text, and click the first link that catches their interest or roughly matches their goal, ignoring large portions of the page.
Design pages for the reality of a billboard going by at 60 miles an hour, not for the fantasy of readers savouring great literature.
People scan (skim) web pages looking for words or phrases that catch their eye rather than reading them.
exception: except document-style pages such as news stories, reports, or product descriptions, where people revert to reading, though often still alternating with scanning

statement: Users scan because they are usually on a mission to get something done quickly and because they know only a fraction of a page's content is relevant to their task.

Users focus on the page words and phrases that match their current task, their ongoing personal interests, or hardwired trigger words (such as their own name, 'Free', or 'Sale'), and perceive only a fraction of what is actually on a page.

Users satisfice rather than optimize: they choose the first reasonable option instead of weighing all options for the best one, so a link that merely seems like it might lead to the goal is very likely to be clicked.

Users satisfice because they are usually in a hurry (optimizing is slow), there is little penalty for a wrong guess (the Back button), extra effort often does not improve the outcome on poorly designed sites, and guessing is faster and more enjoyable.

Whether a user weighs options before clicking depends on their frame of mind, how pressed for time they are, and how much confidence they have in the site, so satisficing is a tendency rather than a certainty.
condition: depends on the user's frame of mind, time pressure, and confidence in the site

statement: Users muddle through: they use things without understanding how they work, or with mistaken ideas about how they work, and very few take time to read instructions.
Muddling through is not limited to beginners; even technically sophisticated users have surprising gaps in their understanding of how things work.

Users muddle through because understanding how something works is not important to them as long as they can use it, and because once they find something that works they tend to stick with it and seldom look for a better way.

Helping users truly understand a site matters because muddling through is inefficient and error-prone; when users 'get it' they are likelier to find what they want, grasp the site's full range, be guided where you want them, and feel smart and in control, which brings them back.
If users treat your pages like billboards glimpsed in passing, design great billboards for them rather than fighting that reality.

To serve scanning users, apply six billboard-design tactics: exploit conventions, create clear visual hierarchies, break pages into clearly defined areas, make what is clickable obvious, eliminate distractions, and format content to support scanning.

Following established design conventions (widely used or standardized patterns) is one of the best ways to make something graspable in a hurry, because users need not relearn what things are and how they work as they move between sites.

Respect the conventions users expect for where things are located (e.g., the site logo top-left and primary navigation across the top or down the left in left-to-right cultures), how things work (shopping-cart and checkout patterns), and how things look (standardized icons).
If you choose not to use an existing convention, the replacement must either be so clear and self-explanatory that there is no learning curve, or add enough value to justify a small learning curve.
condition: when replacing an established convention with something new

statement: Innovate only when you know you have a genuinely better idea; otherwise take advantage of existing conventions.
Be as creative, innovative, and aesthetically ambitious as you like, provided the result remains usable.
condition: as long as usability is preserved

statement: Clarity trumps consistency: although consistency is generally worth striving for, if you can make something significantly clearer by making it slightly inconsistent, choose clarity.
Give every page a clear visual hierarchy in which the appearance of elements accurately conveys their relationships: relative importance, similarity, and part-of structure.

In a clear visual hierarchy, more important things are more prominent (larger, bolder, distinctive color, more white space, or nearer the top), logically related things are visually related (grouped, shared style, or in a defined area), and nested elements visually show what is part of what.

A good visual hierarchy saves users work by pre-processing the page so its organization and priorities are grasped almost instantly, whereas a flawed or absent hierarchy forces the slower work of scanning and makes users think unnecessarily.
Break pages into clearly defined areas so users can quickly decide which regions to focus on and which they can safely ignore.
Users exhibit banner blindness, completely ignoring page regions they believe contain ads, so important content should not be placed where it looks like advertising.

Make it obvious what is clickable, because much of web use is hunting for the next thing to click and users judge clickability from visual cues such as shape, location, and formatting (color and underlining).
For reliable clickability, signal text links with a single consistent color (or with clear shape and location), and never give links and non-clickable headings the same color.

Visual noise (shouting, where everything competes for attention; disorganization, from a lack of aligning grid; and clutter, too much stuff yielding a low signal-to-noise ratio) is a major enemy of easily grasped pages.
Shouting pages usually result from failing to make the tough decisions about which elements matter most and to build a visual hierarchy that leads users to them first.
When editing pages, presume every element is visual noise (guilty until proven innocent) and remove anything that is not making a real contribution.
Use plenty of headings, more than you would expect, and invest time writing them, because well-crafted headings act as an informal outline that helps users decide what to read, scan, or skip.

When using multiple heading levels, make the visual distinction between levels obvious, and keep each heading closer to the section it introduces than to the one above it so headings do not appear to float.
Keep paragraphs short to avoid a daunting wall of words; online reading tolerates even single-sentence paragraphs, so break long paragraphs at a reasonable point.
Prefer bulleted lists: almost anything that can be a bulleted list probably should be, with a little extra space between items for readability.
Highlight key terms by bolding the most important words where they first appear to aid scanning, but avoid over-highlighting, which makes the technique lose its effectiveness.
The number of clicks matters far less than how hard each click is: a click is acceptable when it is a mindless, unambiguous choice.
What really counts in navigation is the thought and uncertainty each click demands, not the raw click count.
exception: although there are practical limits to how many clicks users will tolerate

statement: Users tolerate many clicks as long as each is painless and they retain confidence they are on the right track (the 'scent of information'); links that clearly and unambiguously name their target give off a strong scent, whereas ambiguous or poorly worded links do not.
As a rough rule of thumb, about three mindless, unambiguous clicks cost a user roughly the same as one click that requires real thought.
exception: the value of fewer clicks rises when users must repeatedly drill the same path or when pages load slowly

statement: Make hard choices easier through progressive disclosure: instead of confronting users with all details at once, let an initial selection lead to a screen showing only the questions or information relevant to that choice.

When a difficult choice is unavoidable, provide as much guidance as the user needs but no more, and make that guidance brief (the smallest helpful amount), timely (placed exactly where it is needed), and unavoidable (formatted so it will be noticed).
condition: when a difficult choice cannot be eliminated

statement: Krug's Third Law of Usability: cut roughly half the words on every page, then cut half of what remains.
Most words on a typical web page merely take up space because no one reads them, and their presence implies they must be read, which makes pages seem more daunting than they are.
Cutting roughly half the words from most web pages is a realistic goal achievable without losing anything of value.
Removing needless words reduces page noise, makes useful content more prominent, and shortens pages so users can see more at a glance without scrolling.
Eliminate 'happy talk': content-free welcome or self-congratulatory promotional text that says how great you are instead of conveying useful information.

Treat instructions as a major source of needless words: users rarely read them and only after muddling through has failed, so aim to eliminate instructions by making things self-explanatory and cut any truly necessary instructions to the bare minimum.
People will not use a site if they cannot find their way around it; when users cannot find what they want or understand how the site is organized, they are unlikely to stay or return.

Users differ in how they navigate: search-dominant users look for a search box immediately, link-dominant users browse first and search only when stuck, and others decide based on their frame of mind, their hurry, and whether the site appears to have decent browsable navigation.
