The web lacks the physical-space cues of scale, direction, and location, so users find it hard to tell whether they have seen everything of interest and when to stop looking.

Because moving around the web is teleportation via links rather than traversal of physical space, users cannot build a bodily sense of location, which is why the Back button is the most-used browser control and a persistent, fixed Home concept that lets users start over matters.
Navigation is not merely a feature of a site; it effectively is the site, embodying the hierarchy and creating a sense of place, so web navigation must be good.

Beyond helping users find things and showing where they are, navigation also reveals what the site contains (often its most important function), implicitly teaches how to use the site, and builds confidence in the people who built it.

Follow navigation conventions for the appearance and location of navigation elements, because standard placement lets users find them quickly and standardized appearance makes them easy to distinguish from everything else.

Provide persistent (global) navigation, the elements that appear on every page in the same place with a consistent look, so users get constant confirmation they are still in the same site and only have to learn how it works once.

On form pages such as checkout, registration, subscription, or feedback, reduce persistent navigation to a minimal version (Site ID, a Home link, and any helpful Utilities), because full navigation can be an unnecessary distraction there.
exception: form pages are the exception to showing full persistent navigation on every page

statement: Show the Site ID or logo at the top of every page (upper-left for left-to-right languages) because it represents the whole site; position it to frame the page rather than dominate it, and give it the distinctive, scalable look of a brand logo.
condition: logo placement in the upper-left assumes left-to-right reading languages

statement: Provide primary navigation (the Sections) linking to the top level of the site's hierarchy, and expose secondary navigation as the subsections of the current section.
Provide Utilities, the links to important non-content elements such as Sign in/Register, Help, Site Map, Cart, About, and Contact, and make them slightly less prominent than the Sections.
Persistent navigation can hold only about four or five Utilities (the most frequently needed ones); relegate less-used links to the footer so the important ones do not get lost.

Always give users a way back to the Home page from the persistent navigation; a visible Home reassures users they can start over, most users expect the Site ID to link Home, and Home should also appear among the main sections.
Unless a site is very small and very well organized, every page should include a search box, or at least a link to a search page.
condition: unless the site is very small and very well organized

statement: Keep search simple with a box, a button, and either the word 'Search' or the magnifying-glass icon; avoid fancy wording, avoid instructions such as 'type a keyword', and avoid scope or advanced options in the persistent search box.
Offer search-scope options only where they are useful, on the results page after an over-broad search returns too many hits, rather than in the persistent search box up front.
condition: provide scope-limiting options at the point of need, not up front

statement: Give lower-level (third-level and deeper) navigation the same attention as the top levels, because users spend as much time on lower-level pages as on top pages and consistent top-to-bottom navigation is very hard to graft on later.
Produce sample pages showing the navigation for every potential level of the site before debating surface details like the color scheme.

Give every page a prominent name that frames the content unique to that page (usually the largest text on the page), and never treat a highlighted item in the navigation as a substitute for a real page name.

Honor the implicit contract that a page's name matches the link or button the user clicked to reach it; mismatches force needless thought and erode trust, so when exact matching is impossible make the names as close as possible and the reason for any difference obvious.
exception: when space limits prevent exact matching, match as closely as possible and make the difference obvious

statement: Show users where they are by highlighting their current location in the navigation, and make that 'you are here' indicator stand out (for example, combine a distinct color with bold), because hurried users routinely miss subtle cues.
If a designer thinks a visual cue already sticks out like a sore thumb, it probably still needs to be about twice as prominent, because hurried users routinely miss cues designers consider obvious.
Use breadcrumbs to show the path from the Home page to the current page and to make it easy to move back up the hierarchy; they are most useful in large sites with deep hierarchies.
condition: most useful in large sites with deep hierarchies

statement: Implement breadcrumbs by placing them at the top of the page, separating levels with a greater-than character, and boldfacing the last item as the current page name (which is not itself a link).
Favor tabs as a navigation device: they are one of the few interface metaphors that truly work, being self-evident, hard to miss, and a clear division between navigation and content.
For tabs to work, make the active tab appear to be in front of the others by giving it a different color or contrasting shade and physically connecting it to the content area below.

Apply the 'trunk test' to navigation: dropped at random onto a deep page and viewing it only at a glance, a user should instantly be able to answer what site this is, what page they are on, the site's major sections, their options at this level, where they are in the scheme of things, and how to search.

Design every page for users who are dropped deep into the site from a search engine, social network, or email link and have never seen its navigation, rather than assuming they start at the Home page and follow neat paths.

The Home page must accommodate many competing demands at once: site identity and mission, an overview of the site's hierarchy, search, teases, content promos, feature promos, timely content or other signs of life, deals, shortcuts to frequently requested content, and registration or sign-in.

The Home page must also meet abstract objectives: show users what they are looking for, expose them to worthwhile things they are not looking for, show where to start, and establish credibility and trust.

The Home page is the contested 'waterfront property' of a site: prominently promoted items get significantly more traffic, so every stakeholder competes for space, and the limited area above the fold is fought over most fiercely.
The one thing that most often gets lost on a Home page, and the thing you can least afford to lose, is conveying the big picture of what the site is.

The Home page must answer, at a glance and unambiguously with very little effort, a first-time visitor's core questions: what this site is, what they can do and find here, and why they should be here rather than elsewhere.

The first few seconds on a new site or page are critical (the Big Bang effect): if it is not immediately clear what users are looking at, everything else becomes harder to interpret and misinterpretation and frustration grow more likely.
Users form snap judgments about a page within milliseconds, and those first impressions tend to be a reliable predictor of their later, more considered assessments.

Users' first impressions can be wrong, and they then force-fit new information onto that mistaken understanding, so orienting them correctly from the start is crucial because users who begin lost tend to get more lost.
Because people often enter a site by teleporting to a deep page from an email, blog, or social link, every page should orient visitors to who you are, what you do, and what the site offers.

Provide three explicit places that state what the site is: a tagline next to the Site ID, a Welcome blurb (a terse description in a prominent block, usually top-left or center of the content), and a 'Learn more' option such as a short explanatory video for novel propositions.

When conveying what the site is, use as much space as necessary but no more, keep the message short (just enough to make the point, not every feature), and never use a corporate mission statement as the Welcome blurb because no one reads them.

Whether the Home page conveys what the site is is one of the most important things to usability-test with outsiders, because the missing 'main point' is the one thing nobody inside the organization will notice is absent.
Give the site a tagline: a pithy phrase placed right by the Site ID that sums up what the enterprise is and what makes it great, positioned where users most expect a concise statement of purpose.

Make taglines clear and informative, just long enough (about six to eight words), and expressive of differentiation and a clear benefit (ideally one no one else could claim); keep them lively and only as clever as helps convey rather than obscure the benefit, and do not confuse a tagline (a value proposition) with a motto (an ideal).

After users know what the site is, the Home page must make obvious where to start to search, to browse, and to sample the best content; on process-based sites the entry point should leap out, and register or sign-in should be prominent.

Make entry points look like what they are (a search box looks like a search box, a section list looks like a section list) and label them clearly with words like 'Search', 'Browse by Category', 'Sign in', and 'Start here'.

Resist over-promoting on the Home page: because a prominent link reliably boosts an item's traffic, every stakeholder wants one, creating a tragedy of the commons in which each promo's gain is private while the resulting clutter degrades the whole page's effectiveness.

Protect the Home page from gradual promotional overload with constant vigilance: educate stakeholders about the cost of overgrazing and offer alternative ways to drive traffic, such as cross-promoting from other popular pages or rotating use of the same space.

Left to themselves, web teams decide usability questions poorly, wasting time in unresolvable 'religious debates' (clashes of strongly held personal beliefs about things that cannot be proven) that rarely change anyone's mind and erode team respect.

Beware the 'everybody likes' fallacy: because team members are themselves web users with strong preferences, they project their own likes and dislikes onto users in general and assume most sensible users are like them.

Recognize that professional passion divides teams (designers favor visually pleasing pages while developers favor complex, ingenious features), and each side struggles to imagine that others do not share its priorities, which fuels conflict over design decisions.

There is no 'Average User': all web users are effectively unique and web use is basically idiosyncratic, so describing users in terms of one-dimensional likes and dislikes is futile and counterproductive.

The Average-User myth is harmful because it feeds the false belief that good design is mostly about discovering what people like; in reality the important questions lack simple answers, and success comes from well-integrated design that meets a real need and is carefully worked out, well built, and tested.

Replace unproductive design debates (such as 'do most people like pull-down menus?') with the concrete, testable question: does this specific element, with these items and wording in this context on this page, create a good experience for most of the people likely to use this site?

Usability testing defuses arguments and breaks impasses by shifting discussion from what is right, wrong, liked, or disliked to what actually works, and by revealing how varied users are so the team stops assuming all users are like them.

Focus groups are not usability tests: a focus group has a small group talk about opinions and reactions, whereas a usability test watches one person at a time actually try to use something to do typical tasks so you can detect and fix what confuses them.

Use focus groups in the planning stages to learn what your audience wants and whether your idea and value proposition make sense, but use usability tests throughout the entire development process to learn whether the site works and how to improve it.
condition: focus groups suit planning-stage questions; usability tests belong throughout the process

statement: If you want a great site you must test, because after working on a site even a few weeks you can no longer see it freshly, and the only way to learn whether it really works is to watch other people try to use it.
Testing one user is a hundred percent better than testing none: testing always works, and even a poor test with the wrong participant reveals important improvements.

Testing one user early in the project beats testing fifty near the end; a simple test done early, while you still have time to act on what you learn, is almost always more valuable than an elaborate test done late.
Correct usability problems early, because changing a site once it is in use is often hard: some users resist any change and even apparently simple changes can have far-reaching effects.
When you have no time and no money, do usability testing yourself; hire a professional if you can afford one, but never let the lack of one stop you from testing.
condition: hire a professional if affordable, otherwise do it yourself

statement: Have every web development team do usability testing one morning a month: test about three users in the morning and debrief over lunch to decide what to fix before the next round (or, for Agile teams, a smaller cadence such as two users every two weeks).

Keep testing simple so the team keeps doing it: if testing is complicated or time-consuming it will be skipped when things get busy, and doing more rounds matters more than wringing everything out of any single round.

Fix a recurring testing day (for example, the third Thursday of the month) rather than tying tests to milestones or deliverables, because schedules slip and milestone-based testing slips along with them.

Use about three participants per round of do-it-yourself testing; the goal is not to prove anything (that requires quantitative testing) but to produce actionable insights by identifying and fixing usability problems.

Do not try to find every problem: in any short session you will surface far more issues than you have the capacity to repair in a month, so fix the most serious ones first, and three users will still hit many of the most significant problems.

Recruit loosely and grade on a curve: seek participants who resemble your audience but do not obsess over it; loosen requirements and, when someone hits a problem, ask whether your real users would hit it too or only because the participant lacked knowledge your users have.

For most sites you can do much of your testing with almost anybody, because recruiting a narrow profile costs more time and money and, especially early on, the site's flaws will trip up nearly anyone.
exception: sites that require specific domain knowledge need some participants who have it, though not all of them do

statement: Always include some participants from outside your target audience, because you should not design a site only your target audience can use, everyone is a beginner under the skin (experts often just muddle through at a higher level), and experts are rarely insulted by something made clear enough for beginners.
Pay participant incentives and offer a little above the going rate, because it signals that you value their time and improves the odds that they show up.

Encourage as many people as possible (team members, stakeholders, managers, and executives) to observe test sessions, because watching is often a transformative experience that makes observers finally grasp that users are not like them.

Make the facilitator's main job (beyond keeping the participant comfortable and on task) getting the participant to think out loud, since combining what they do with what they are thinking lets observers see the site through the user's eyes; almost anyone patient, calm, empathetic, and a good listener can facilitate.
Have each observer write down the three most serious problems they noticed after each session, because the debriefing's purpose is to identify the most serious problems so they get fixed first.

Start testing as early as possible and keep testing throughout development, from rough sketches through wireframes, comps, prototypes, and finished pages; it is never too early, so test competitive sites before you design and test an existing site before redesigning it.

Choose test tasks by listing what people need to be able to do with what you are testing, word each task carefully (including any information the participant needs but would not have), and pick enough tasks to fill the available time (about 35 minutes of a one-hour test).

Let participants choose some details of a task (for example, 'find a book you would want to buy' rather than a fixed title), because it increases their emotional investment and lets them draw on their own knowledge, yielding more revealing results.

During the task portion of a test, let participants work on their own and avoid influencing them: ask no leading questions and give no clues or help unless they are hopelessly stuck or extremely frustrated, and if they ask for help respond 'what would you do if I weren't here?', while prompting them to keep thinking aloud when they fall silent.

Tell participants clearly that you are testing the site and not them, that they cannot do anything wrong, and that you want their honest reactions, because this framing is what makes them comfortable enough to behave and speak naturally.

Do not over-react to individual reactions about a site's aesthetics during testing, because taste varies widely (one participant loves a color the next hates); watch behavior, not opinions about looks.

Expect three recurring types of usability problem: users are unclear on the concept (they do not get it, or think they do but are wrong), the words they are looking for are not there (you misjudged their vocabulary), or there is too much going on (what they need is present but not seen).
After each round of testing, debrief as soon as possible (ideally over lunch while observations are fresh) so the team shares what it saw and decides which problems to fix and how.

Focus ruthlessly on fixing the most serious problems first, because teams tend to defer serious problems or knock off many easy ones instead, which is why even large, well-funded sites keep serious usability problems.

Run the debriefing as triage: collect each observer's three most serious observed problems into a shared list without discussion, pick the ten most serious, rank them, and turn them into an ordered list with a rough fix, an owner, and required resources for the coming month.

You do not have to fix each problem perfectly or completely; often a small tweak is enough to move it out of the 'serious' category, and once you have allocated all the fixing time and resources available for the next month, stop.
Keep a separate list of 'low-hanging fruit': non-serious problems that one person can fix in under an hour without needing anyone's permission.

Resist the impulse to add things when users do not get something: the reflex is to add an explanation or instructions, but the right fix is usually to remove what is obscuring the meaning rather than add another distraction.

Take participants' 'new feature' requests with a grain of salt, because participants are not designers; ask them to describe how the feature would work and they usually abandon it, and when they do have a genuinely good idea you will recognize it immediately.

Ignore 'kayak' problems: momentary wrong turns from which the user recovers quickly on their own, without help and without being fazed, can be left alone, since if the user's second guess is always right that is good enough.
condition: only when the user notices quickly, recovers without help, and is not fazed

statement: Consider remote testing to expand your recruiting pool from people near your office to almost anyone, and unmoderated remote services for cheap, low-effort tests, accepting that you lose real-time interaction with the participant.
Mobile usability rests on the same basic principles as any other usability, except that people move even faster and read even less on small screens.

Treat design as fundamentally about constraints (what you must and cannot do) and tradeoffs (the less-than-ideal choices you make to live within those constraints), because wherever there are constraints there are tradeoffs to be made.

Recognize that many, if not most, serious usability problems result from a poor tradeoff decision that did not place enough weight on creating a good experience for the user, and that good mobile usability largely comes down to making good tradeoffs.

Use a Mobile-First approach, designing the mobile version first around the features and content most important to users and then expanding for desktop, because it forces you to determine what is truly essential.

Do not assume mobile users only want 'on the move' features: people use mobile devices everywhere, including at home, and expect to do everything, since everyone wants to do some things and together those amount to everything.

When you include everything on a small screen, prioritize even harder: keep things users want frequently or in a hurry close at hand, and let everything else be a few taps away as long as there is an obvious path to it.
Accept that small screens make more tapping and scrolling inevitable; that is fine as long as users stay confident that what they want is further down the screen or behind a given link or button.
Managing screen-real-estate challenges should never be done at the cost of usability.

Expect scalable and responsive design (one version that looks good across screen sizes) to be a lot of work and hard to do well, but treat it as mandatory now that small screens dominate: any site must be usable on any size screen.
Avoid maintaining separate versions of a site, because keeping 'two sets of books' at least doubles the effort and guarantees the versions fall out of sync or are updated less often.

As minimum mobile courtesies, make sure your site can be zoomed on a phone, send deep links to the actual content the user clicked rather than dumping them on the mobile Home page, and always offer a link or toggle to the full (non-mobile) site.

Understand affordances as the visual clues in a design that suggest how to use something; just as clearer link wording strengthens the scent of information, more distinct visual cues give a plainer signal about how an element works.
Make affordances noticeable enough that people can spot the ones they need to do their tasks; affordances are by definition the last thing you should hide, though they need not hit users in the face.

Remember that touch screens have no cursor and therefore no hover, so hover-dependent features (tool tips, buttons that change on pointing, and menus that reveal on hover) are unavailable on mobile and must be replaced by other means.

Beware that flat design removes visual distinctions while affordances depend on visual distinctions, so flattening interface elements can strip away the cues users rely on to tell what is interactive.

When using flat design, actively compensate for the visual distinctions you remove by using the remaining dimensions (such as position and formatting like reversed type or all caps), because flat design tends to strip away not just decoration but the information that textured elements conveyed.

Prioritize speed, especially on mobile, because slow performance frustrates users and loses goodwill; remember that mobile download speeds are unreliable, so avoid responsive solutions that load more code or larger images than the user's screen needs.

Center your usability effort on learnability, effectiveness, and efficiency (the heart of usability), and treat 'useful' and 'desirable' as marketing questions to settle before the project starts through methods like interviews, focus groups, and surveys.

Build delight into products by marrying something people would love to do but do not think is possible with a clever use of new technology; delight increasingly matters in competitive app markets, but never pursue it so hard that you forget to make the product usable.

Recognize that apps with more than a few features can be hard to learn, and that typical minimal onboarding (a screen or two, with help that is hard to refind) is often not enough once functionality grows or departs from familiar conventions, so you must do better than most and use usability testing to find out how.
Make things memorable by making them incredibly clear and easy to learn the first time (if it is easy to learn, it is easy to relearn), because poor memorability drives users to abandon an app.

Test mobile usability with essentially the same process as desktop testing (make up tasks, watch people try them, prompt think-aloud, stay quiet, and get stakeholders to observe); what differs about mobile is logistics, not the process.

For mobile testing logistics, use a camera pointed at or attached to the device rather than screen mirroring so observers can see the participant's gestures and taps, attach the camera to the device so the user can hold it naturally, and skip a face camera since it distracts and observers can read feeling from tone of voice.
Treat usability as having a second component beyond clarity: doing the right thing by being considerate of the user, so alongside 'Is my site clear?' also ask 'Does my site behave like a mensch?'

Treat every user as arriving with a limited 'reservoir of goodwill' that each problem lowers; if you exhaust it, users may leave, use your site less in future, think less of your organization, or criticize you publicly.

Account for the goodwill reservoir's properties: it is idiosyncratic (varies by person, so never count on a large reserve), situational (a hurry or a prior bad experience lowers it), refillable (you can replenish it by showing you look out for the user's interests), and sometimes emptied by a single mistake such as a huge registration form.

Avoid the behaviors that make users feel you do not have their interests at heart: hiding information they want (support phone numbers, shipping rates, prices), punishing them for not formatting data your way, asking for information you do not need, faux sincerity, putting marketing 'sizzle' in their way, and letting the site look amateurish.

Almost no one abandons a site merely because it does not look great, so ignore users' comments about colors during testing unless roughly three of four participants use a strongly negative word for the color scheme.
If you deliberately do something user-unfriendly for business reasons (for example, revenue-boosting pop-ups), make it an informed, intentional business decision rather than an inadvertent one.
condition: when a user-unfriendly choice is made deliberately for business reasons

statement: Increase goodwill by knowing the main things people come to your site to do and making those things obvious and easy, since teams can usually name the top three tasks but often fail to make them the top priority.

Increase goodwill through candor: be upfront about things you would rather hide (shipping costs, fees, outages), because you gain more in trust and in helping users compensate than you lose by disclosing.

Increase goodwill by saving users steps wherever you can, visibly putting effort into solving their problems, providing creature comforts such as printer-friendly pages, and making it easy to recover gracefully from unavoidable errors.
Anticipate the questions users are likely to have and answer them with genuine, up-to-date, candid FAQs (this week's real top questions), not marketing pitches disguised as FAQs.
When you cannot do what a user wants, apologize and at least let them know you understand you are inconveniencing them.
You cannot call a site usable unless it is also accessible, unless you have consciously decided that people with disabilities are not part of your audience.

Treat 'it is the right thing to do' as the primary reason for accessibility, because it dramatically improves some people's lives (for example, blind people with a computer can read almost any newspaper on their own); expect legal requirements to arrive as well.

The single most effective thing you can do for accessibility is to fix the usability problems that confuse everyone, because whatever confuses most users confuses users with disabilities even more and they recover less easily; fixing code without first making the site clear does not help.

Design for screen-reader users who 'scan with their ears': like sighted users they are impatient and do not hear every word, listening only to the first few words of a link or line before moving on, so put the meaningful words at the beginning of links, headings, and lines.

Capture the high-impact accessibility basics: add appropriate alt text to every image (empty alt for decorative ones), use real HTML headings in order (h1 for the page title, h2 for sections) styled via CSS, label form fields with the HTML label element, add a 'Skip to Main Content' link, make all content keyboard-accessible, ensure strong text-to-background contrast, and start from an accessible template.

Remember that what matters is not the label you use (Usability, Information Architecture, or UX) but the attitude and skills you bring: learning about users, testing whether people can use what you build, and getting changes to actually happen.

The most effective tactic for winning management support is to get your boss and higher-ups to watch a usability test in person, because seeing real users struggle live is far more persuasive than any presentation or recap; if they cannot attend, share short highlight clips.

Run your first usability test on your own time without asking permission: keep it simple and informal, use volunteers so it costs nothing, pick an easy target with a quickly fixable serious problem, then test it, fix it, measure the improvement if you can, and publicize the result.

Testing competitors' sites is a low-risk way to build support for usability work, because everyone enjoys learning about the competition and no one has anything personally at stake when it is not your own site being tested.
Approach management with genuine empathy for the position they are in and with humility, treating your role as sharing what you know rather than preaching the 'truth' to others.
Treat usability as fundamentally a user-advocate role: serve users' real needs rather than manipulate them.

Persuasion and influence are acceptable only when they are not deceptive; refuse to use usability skills for manipulation or dark patterns (such as pre-checked opt-ins, tricking people into installing toolbars, or phishing), because that is not part of your job and users are counting on you.
Do not rely on usability tests to judge whether something is desirable; desirability is a market-research question, and a test may give you only a vague sense of it.
Never use small, low-contrast type; if you must compromise, choose either large low-contrast type or smallish high-contrast type, but never combine small size with low contrast.

Avoid putting labels inside form fields unless every safeguard holds: the form is exceptionally simple, the labels disappear on typing and reappear when the field is emptied, the labels can never be confused with answers, there is no chance of submitting the label text, and the fields remain fully accessible.
condition: only acceptable if all the listed safeguards hold

statement: Preserve the browser's distinction between visited and unvisited text links (visited links shown in a different color), because it usefully tells users which options they have already tried and is tracked by URL rather than by link wording; any colors are fine as long as they are noticeably different.

Do not treat usability guidance as forbidding you from bending or breaking the rules; there are even cases where you want the interface to make people think, so long as you know which rule you are bending and believe you have a good reason.
Conversation-level design decisions can affect how users perceive a chatbot even when the underlying implementation technology differs.
Chatbot development should begin with conversational design before implementation details because users mainly experience the dialogue flow.
A chatbot should communicate in a way that fits its target audience to support satisfaction with the service.
Good conversational practice can strengthen user trust in the brand or organization represented by the chatbot.
Chatbot conversational requirements should be technology-independent, user-centered, and connected to business goals.
A conversational-design review should prioritize practices that users directly see in the dialogue or interface rather than hidden technical mechanisms.
condition: when the objective is conversational user experience guidance

statement: Natural interaction quality is important for reducing users' negative preconceptions or resistance toward chatbots.
Effective chatbot conversation design should include user observation, persona and goal definition, dialogue shaping, agent persona definition, message drafting, prototyping, and testing.
Conversational design work should involve designers, writers, developers, and business strategists with distinct responsibilities for flow, wording, platform support, and brand fit.
A system should be treated as an in-scope chatbot only if it processes natural-language input and can sustain a conversation rather than merely broadcasting messages.
exception: single-message social bots or non-conversational automation are out of scope

statement: Evidence for chatbot conversational practices may come from real chatbots, Wizard-of-Oz-style simulations, evaluated interaction examples, or user reactions to explained practice concepts.
Studies should be excluded from design-evidence synthesis when they do not report user impacts of the conversational strategy or practice under consideration.
Evidence synthesis for text-chatbot design should exclude spoken, embodied, machine-machine, social-media-bot, and other non-one-on-one human-chatbot interactions.
condition: when the target guidance is for text-based one-on-one chatbot conversations

statement: A static icon or image does not by itself make a text chatbot embodied; embodiment should require communicative body expression.
Studies focused on algorithmic accuracy or technical performance should be excluded when their user study does not measure user-centered outcomes such as satisfaction or trust.
condition: when building conversational-design guidance from user-experience evidence

statement: Evidence screening should require primary, full research studies rather than secondary, incomplete, or non-research publications.
Conversational practices retained for guidance should be pragmatic and replicable rather than abstract traits without concrete implementation examples.
A study should be accepted into a practice-impact synthesis only when its method, sample basis, results, impact analysis, and limitations are sufficiently clear to support scientific interpretation.
A quality checklist can protect a chatbot-practice synthesis from weak evidence by discarding studies that fail any required quality item.
The reviewed work produced chatbot conversational guidelines from forty selected studies and then evaluated practitioner perceptions of those guidelines through a survey.
Survey respondents strongly agreed that the proposed guideline set would support better satisfaction and engagement and that the web guide was usable, flexible, clear, and understandable.

When deriving chatbot guidance, concrete functional and interface practices are more operationally useful than broad subjective characteristics unless those characteristics are translated into implementable behavior.
The same conversational practice can have different impacts across chatbot domains, so the chatbot context should be treated as an indirect moderator.
Avatars can humanize a chatbot visually, but their gender and appearance can shape user impressions before any message is exchanged.
Emoji, emoticon, GIF, and meme use can increase emotional expressiveness by accompanying or replacing plain text.
Small talk can give a chatbot a social presence by covering casual out-of-domain content such as greetings, jokes, and fictional background.
Designers should decide explicitly whether and how the chatbot discloses its non-human identity because that choice shapes its background and user trust.
A chatbot can convey empathy by adapting responses to what the user has said, acknowledging negative user situations, or restating the user's message.
When a conversation breaks down, the chatbot should acknowledge the misunderstanding and offer a recovery path instead of leaving the user without repair guidance.
condition: when the chatbot fails to solve a problem or understand a message

statement: Chatbot recommendations, instructions, or information should include explanations or justifications so users understand why the content is being provided.
condition: when the chatbot gives advice, instructions, recommendations, or unexpected information

statement: The initial chatbot message should set a useful frame by introducing the agent, welcoming the user, naming capabilities, and optionally collecting the user's name for later personalization.
Chatbot language should combine politeness with restrained informality rather than relying on either extreme.
Language choices should fit the domain by adjusting features such as verbs, pronouns, conjunctions, and related phrasing patterns.
Typing cues and delayed responses can make a chatbot feel less instantaneous and more human-like, but they should be balanced against task efficiency.
Buttons and carousels can streamline input and reduce breakdowns by steering users toward messages the chatbot can handle.

The user impacts worth optimizing vary by domain: health chatbots often prioritize well-being, mental-health chatbots need closeness and trust for self-disclosure, and commercial chatbots often prioritize retention and satisfaction.
Because users often prefer human agents, revealing that an agent is a chatbot can immediately reduce trust.
A chatbot should not pretend to be human because discovery of deception can produce worse trust, anger, and frustration outcomes than transparent non-human disclosure.
Transparent identity disclosure works better when paired with capability statements and explicit limitations.
condition: when the chatbot discloses that it is non-human

statement: A decrease in perceived humanness after disclosure should be accepted when transparency prevents the stronger harms of perceived deception.
condition: when users may otherwise believe the chatbot is human

statement: Humanization, social-presence, and emotion-conveying elements generally improve perceived social presence and anthropomorphism.
For customer-service and recommendation chatbots, honest self-introduction and behavior justification are especially relevant transparency practices.
condition: when the chatbot serves customer-service or recommendation purposes

statement: Avatar effects are inconsistent across studies, so avatars should not be treated as a context-independent improvement.
Automatically activated chatbots may perform worse when paired with anthropomorphic avatars, so that combination should be tested carefully before use.
condition: when the agent opens automatically rather than being user-initiated

statement: Informal elements such as casual wording, emoji, GIFs, and jokes are more associated with joy, closeness, friendship, or motivation in health and learning contexts than with commercial satisfaction.
Informality should be moderated so it does not undermine politeness or the chatbot's professional image.
Intentional typing errors should be avoided because users may interpret them as developer incompetence rather than human-like informality.
Buttons can streamline conversations, but they should be used cautiously because they may reduce perceived humanness even when satisfaction is unaffected.
Designers should account for practice interactions, such as avatar activation mode, humor style, limitation acknowledgement, disclosure timing, and pretending to be human.
Human avatars can raise user expectations and increase frustration after chatbot failures, so avatar choices should be paired with transparency and failure-handling design.
condition: when using human-like avatars

statement: Demographic, personality, language-proficiency, technology-experience, conversation-duration, and usage-context differences can moderate practice impacts.
When deep target-user testing is not feasible, designers should avoid exaggerated use of conversational practices to reduce the risk of alienating user groups.
condition: when the team lacks sufficient target-user evidence

statement: Designers should pretest how users perceive intended practices because user belief can determine impact more than the designer's intended identity or effect.
For each recurring communicative function, designers should write varied response formulations so repeated use of a practice does not make the chatbot feel machine-like.
A chatbot's purpose should drive the desired user relationship, the target impacts, and the main conversational-design focus.
Information-collection and transaction chatbots should set expectations early by stating capabilities and limitations because they need attention, completion, and reliable user input.
condition: when the chatbot collects information or supports transactions

statement: Information and recommendation chatbots should emphasize credibility and trust, and recommendation chatbots may need intimacy-building practices to learn enough about the user.
condition: when the chatbot provides information or recommendations

statement: Well-being chatbots should emphasize companionship, intimacy, and encouragement rather than treating transparency as the dominant design focus.
condition: when the chatbot is meant to stimulate well-being

statement: Naturalness is a baseline concern across chatbot use cases, while transparency is most important for competent task performance and emotionality is most important for deeper user connection.
Emotionality and transparency can coexist, but designers should decide which one is foregrounded according to the relationship the chatbot must build.
A context-independent chatbot design guide should omit practices whose evidence is conflicting, weak, or tightly bound to audience-specific conditions.
condition: when producing general guidance rather than a domain-specific playbook

statement: A practitioner guide should use simple language, short explanations, and generic examples so designers with different experience levels can apply scientific findings.
The guide was evaluated with sixty-six practitioner survey responses, mostly in Portuguese, with respondents spanning diverse education and occupation backgrounds.
Although many respondents lacked chatbot-development experience, the sample still included a meaningful group with intermediate or advanced chatbot knowledge.
A large majority of respondents agreed that using the guide would help them design chatbots that improve user satisfaction and engagement.
Most respondents also agreed that they would use the guide when designing a chatbot.
Concerns about technical implementation difficulty can reduce perceived speed and ease of applying conversational-design guidelines.
Most respondents perceived the guidelines as clear, understandable, domain-flexible, and not dependent on extensive prior chatbot knowledge.
Concrete examples for each practice help practitioners visualize implementation and were a major perceived strength of the guide.
Objectivity and clarity increase practitioner acceptance of chatbot conversational-design guidance.
Excessive simplicity can become a weakness when practitioners need deeper process guidance, implementation detail, or richer examples.
A practical chatbot-design guide should include references to supporting studies or the synthesis source to increase credibility.
A practical chatbot-design guide should include extended examples, such as a flawed fictional chatbot and an improved version using the guidelines.
A conversational-practice guide should explain its objective and limitations early so users do not mistake it for a complete design-process or technical-implementation manual.
Practitioner responses support using the guide in both academic and industrial settings.
The lack of statistically significant response differences by prior chatbot experience supports using the guide for both novices and experienced designers.
Translating SLR findings into a ready-to-use guide is a distinct contribution beyond literature-review discussion alone.
An SLR-based practice list can be broader than a list elicited from a single user study because it aggregates many user studies and contexts.
Naturalness practices in the guide include self-introduction, addressing the user by name, small talk, echoing user responses, and casual language.
Emotionality practices in the guide include exclamatory feedback, graphical media, empathic messages, and humor.
Transparency practices in the guide include presenting capabilities, acknowledging limitations, making suggestions, and asking for clarification.
The guide identifies repetitive messages, exaggerated practice use, hidden chatbot identity, machine-like typeface, and forced errors as practices to avoid.
The findings should be applied within their scope because the work only covers text-based chatbots and speech interfaces may have different impacts.
condition: when applying the findings to non-text interfaces

statement: Because the search strategy focused on positive outcome terms, the synthesis may under-cover practices whose main evidence concerns negative outcomes.
The guide should not be treated as exhaustive because it summarizes selected studies and other beneficial practices may exist outside the reviewed set.
Automatic search, two-reviewer screening, and abstract-first exclusion can cause relevant primary studies to be missed or selection bias to enter the synthesis.
Survey-based validation remains limited by voluntary participation and unsupervised reading, even when consent and confirmation questions reduce low-effort responses.
Machine-like typefaces such as OCR-A reduce users' perception of a chatbot's humanness.
condition: user's familiarity with AI moderates the effect

statement: Anthropomorphic cues such as a human name and informal language increase users' perception of anthropomorphism while leaving perceived social presence largely unchanged.
Using emoji in chatbot messages increases positive user responses, including enjoyment, favourable attitude, confidence, perceived social attractiveness, competence, and credibility.
Dynamically delayed (time-adjusted) chatbot responses increase perceived humanness, social presence, and satisfaction.
When a chatbot acknowledges a misunderstanding and suggests solutions, users prefer that repair strategy for conversational breakdowns.
condition: user's social orientation and prior experience with chatbots and technology moderate the effect

statement: Sentiment-adaptive chatbot responses increase perceived empathy, humanness, social presence, and satisfaction.
condition: user's gender moderates the effect

statement: A reserved, calm, assertive, rational, counselor-like chatbot personality increases users' willingness to confide in and to listen to the chatbot.
condition: user's personality and the interaction context moderate the effect

statement: Code-mixing (mixing languages) in a chatbot's replies increases perceived conversational ability and humanness.
condition: user's language proficiency moderates the effect

statement: Adding a visual avatar alone does not significantly change users' perception of social presence.
Preset answer options and buttons reduce perceived humanness and social presence and do not improve satisfaction, though they can improve users' understanding of the task.
Disclosing that the conversational agent is a chatbot reduces user trust, perceived humanness, and perceived social presence.
condition: the size of the trust penalty is moderated by service criticality/failure setting and by whether the bot acknowledges its expertise or weaknesses

statement: A chatbot's use of small talk encourages users' self-disclosure.
condition: the effect grows with the passage of time in the interaction

statement: Racial mirroring — profile pictures and names implying a racial identity matching the user — increases interpersonal closeness but reduces disclosure comfort.
exception: the satisfaction gain holds only relative to non-mirroring, not relative to a neutral robot-avatar baseline

statement: A bundle of socio-emotional features (human name, empathetic and encouraging responses, active listening, using the user's preferred name, turn-taking, small talk) leaves trust and privacy concerns unchanged but reduces users' willingness to disclose data.
condition: perceived social presence moderates the effect

statement: A chatbot issuing a clarification request to repair miscommunication increases perceived anthropomorphism and adoption intent.
Persuasive inquiry by a chatbot lowers users' donation probability.
condition: the perceived identity of the chatbot moderates the effect

statement: A female avatar (gender cue) increases users' forgiveness in error conditions, satisfaction, and social disclosure.
Active-listening behaviours (paraphrasing, verbalizing emotions, summarizing, encouraging) increase engagement, interest, and overall chat experience.

An extraverted conversational style (covering many topics quickly, informal language, compliments, positive-emotion words) increases perceived social presence but leaves perceived humanness and communication satisfaction unchanged.
condition: user personality moderates the effect

statement: Simulated typing errors (dynamic, temporal, or spatial) reduce perceived humanness and social presence.
Chatbot humor (jokes, riddles, funny stories) increases user motivation and effort.
exception: self-defeating humour moderates the effect

statement: A social-oriented, informal style (small talk, exclamatory feedback, GIFs, emojis and memes, greeting users by name) increases perceived social presence, engagement, enjoyment, satisfaction, and brand likeability while leaving trust and intention to use unchanged.
Warm and polite conversational openers (a friendly initial message; polite greeting, thanks, and goodbye) increase user engagement.
condition: brand affiliation and the user's gender, age, and personality moderate the effect

statement: Mixed-modality interaction (buttons, sliders, checkboxes) increases enjoyability but does not change perceived supportiveness, efficiency, or precision.
A system-initiated, non-anthropomorphic assistant that starts the conversation increases user reactance.
condition: an anthropomorphic avatar and the user's gender moderate the effect

statement: An anthropomorphism bundle (human name, informal language, typing cues, dynamic delay, jokes) increases intention to buy, offer sensitivity, and likeability.
condition: chatbot disclosure moderates the effect
exception: dynamic delayed responses alone did not improve likeability in individual experiments

statement: Lexical and structural linguistic alignment of a chatbot's responses to the user increases user alignment.
Justifying or explaining why an item was recommended increases trust, perceived transparency, satisfaction, usefulness, and ease of use.
condition: user's age and experience with technology moderate the effect

statement: Supportive messages (attentional deployment, cognitive change, general emotional support, situation modification) increase emotional valence but do not change arousal.
condition: the effect holds for participants who believed they were interacting with a human

statement: A rich set of social and emotional qualities (politeness, small talk, humor, emojis, short exclamations, expressing feelings, using the user's name, asking questions) increases users' behavioral intentions.
condition: user's openness to technology, empathy propensity, and vulnerability moderate the effect

statement: Register compliance — matching linguistic features to the expected register — increases perceived appropriateness and credibility.
condition: the application domain moderates the effect

statement: Authenticity signals such as a female avatar increase perceived authenticity, engagement, satisfaction, and loyalty.
condition: avatar race congruence and professional dress moderate the effect

statement: Humanization techniques (self-introduction, addressing users by name, adaptive response speed, echoing users' answers) increase perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, satisfaction, and self-disclosure.
Conversational UX design requires formal attention to the mechanics of human conversation, because designers otherwise tend to focus only on message content rather than interaction structure.
condition: When designing interfaces that attempt to simulate or evoke natural conversation.

statement: Conversation Analysis is a useful source discipline for conversational UX because it documents systematic patterns in how people naturally organize talk across settings and languages.
condition: When a design problem depends on natural conversational sequencing rather than only language understanding.

statement: Transcript-based analysis helps designers inspect the details of conversational conduct instead of relying on impressions about topic or intent.
condition: When a conversational interaction can be recorded and represented as text for analysis.
exception: Face-to-face interactions may also require embodied action, setting, and artifact context.

statement: An agent can create an impression of listening by using generic follow-up requests that invite the user to rephrase, elaborate, or provide an example without requiring deep intent recognition.
condition: When the agent can place the follow-up after a broad range of user utterances.

statement: Repeating all or part of the user's prior utterance with appropriate grammatical transformations can signal that the agent heard the user and can support the appearance of limited understanding.
condition: When the repeat is tailored to the user's immediately prior wording or earlier relevant wording.

statement: Perceived conversational understanding can exceed a system's actual knowledge when users attribute background knowledge, insight, or reasoning to well-formed responses.
condition: When system behavior resembles listening or probing.

statement: Rule and template transformations can produce conversation-like responses without semantic understanding, but this mechanism limits what the agent actually knows or can provide.
condition: When the agent relies on keyword detection, minimal grammar, and response templates.

statement: Natural language interfaces remain prone to awkwardness and mutual-understanding troubles even when modern NLP, connectivity, and machine learning improve recognition capabilities.
condition: When the interface lacks robust conversational organization and context management.

statement: NLP can analyze units of language, but it does not by itself define how those units should be sequenced into recognizable conversational interaction.
condition: When the design problem is interactional rather than only linguistic.

statement: Conversational interface design must model the organization of natural conversation in addition to linguistic analysis.
condition: When the goal is a recognizably conversational interface rather than a command parser or search box.

statement: Designers should not assume a chatbot or voice assistant can support the same breadth of conversational complexity as a human interlocutor.
condition: When current technology constrains the agent's domain knowledge and interactional competence.

statement: Conversational interfaces are best treated as simplified simulations with limited rules and legal moves, not as full replicas of human conversation.
condition: When setting expectations for users, designers, or stakeholders.

statement: Users may need to learn how to navigate a conversational interface because each such interface has its own interaction mechanics and constraints.
condition: When the interface exposes a constrained conversation space rather than unrestricted human conversation.

statement: Because conversational UX is primarily made from utterance design and sequencing, visual GUI design conventions alone are insufficient for designing it.
condition: When the primary interaction channel is typed or spoken language.

statement: A mature conversational UX discipline should draw on formal knowledge from social sciences in a way analogous to how web design drew on graphic and interface design.
condition: When establishing design standards for conversational interfaces.

statement: Natural language classification expands the phrases a system can recognize, but it does not determine whether the resulting experience is system-centric, content-centric, visual-centric, or conversation-centric.
condition: When NLC is combined with agent responses and other UI elements.

statement: A system-centric style forces users to encode all request details into a single valid utterance because the agent does not retain sequential context across turns.
condition: When each user turn initiates an independent two-turn exchange.
exception: Slotted intents can preserve a limited intent while eliciting dependent details.

statement: System-centric conversational systems tend to provide little conversation management, such as repair or sequence closing, because they do not remember the prior utterance that such actions refer to.
condition: When the system lacks persistent sequential context.

statement: Voice control interfaces use a simple command-action interaction model and generally understand commands rather than broader social actions.
condition: When voice input is treated as an alternative to button or device-control input.

statement: A two-turn interaction model prevents agents from performing conversational activities whose natural structure requires multiple turns.
condition: When the activity depends on recipient participation, sequential placement, or prior-turn memory.

statement: Correct joke telling requires the agent to preserve the joke's sequential structure, not merely retrieve joke content.
condition: When implementing question-answer or knock-knock joke activities.
exception: One-line witty remarks can be delivered without the same multi-turn sequence.

statement: Natural language search interfaces make users repeat relevant keywords because each query is interpreted independently from previous turns.
condition: When the interface is built on a simple query-response information-retrieval model.

statement: Incremental follow-up utterances can fail in query-response systems because those systems lack the prior context needed to interpret what the user is building on.
condition: When the user refers back to a prior topic or partially specifies a new request.

statement: System-centric designs reduce authoring complexity by making users adapt to valid-query formats, but this comes at the cost of conversationality.
condition: When designers choose a familiar device-control or information-retrieval model.

statement: Content-centric agents use the same user-driven, two-turn interaction model as information search systems, but they return authored FAQ-like answers rather than database results.
condition: When the agent maps recognized questions to handcrafted topic responses.

statement: A content-centric answer can be accurate yet poorly conversational when it responds to a yes/no inquiry with a long monologue of contingencies instead of first resolving the user's immediate question.
condition: When the user asks a scoped question and only some details are relevant to that user.

statement: Verbose, thorough authored answers are poorly suited to voice interfaces and reduce opportunities for back-and-forth clarification on a single topic.
condition: When a system delivers many details in one extended response.

statement: Topic-based intents tend to route many distinct inquiries or requests to a single response, which makes the response less action-sensitive.
condition: When intents are organized by subject matter rather than by the user's conversational action.

statement: Visual-centric conversational interfaces solve some interaction problems by adding direct-manipulation elements such as buttons, menus, images, or emojis alongside language.
condition: When the interface is text- or screen-based and can expose graphical controls.

statement: Buttons can improve recognized-intent discoverability and speed input for constrained options, but only for the options the system exposes.
condition: When the user's likely next move is among a limited set of valid choices.

statement: Text-heavy chatbot interactions slow the rate of exchange when long responses are used in a chat-style interface.
condition: When response length grows while the interface remains chat-like.

statement: Displaying yes/no buttons adds little conversational value for a yes/no question unless the goal is to constrain the user to those choices.
condition: When the projected responses are already short and obvious.
exception: Buttons may still be useful when constraint is the intended design choice.

statement: Automatically asking for usefulness feedback after every answer can take over the third position where users would normally close the sequence, ask for repair, or provide their own feedback.
condition: When the agent immediately prompts after answering an adjacency-pair first part.

statement: Solving conversational UX problems with visual elements limits portability to voice-only systems and can shift the design closer to GUI or mobile interaction than conversation.
condition: When a design relies on buttons or other visual controls for core interaction.

statement: A conversation-centric interface must recognize and perform social actions that manage the conversation itself, not only domain requests or commands.
condition: When the product aims to behave like a conversational agent rather than a simple chatbot or voice-control system.

statement: Conversation-management actions operate on prior utterances, so an agent needs persistent sequential context to handle them.
condition: When supporting actions such as repair, cancellation, acceptance, refusal, or sequence closing.

statement: A conversational agent should handle preliminaries to inquiries or requests before the user supplies the fully scoped question.
condition: When users announce that they have a question or request before stating its contents.

statement: A conversational agent should support repeat and paraphrase requests about its own prior responses and about the user's prior turns.
condition: When the user displays trouble in hearing, understanding, or interpreting a prior utterance.

statement: A conversational agent should recognize common methods of closing a sequence or the whole conversation.
condition: When the user uses acknowledgments, thanks, goodbyes, or similar closing actions.

statement: Conversation-centric responses should be relatively short so the exchange can stay efficient in real-time voice or text conversation.
condition: When the interaction is intended to support natural back-and-forth exchange.

statement: For conversational delivery, content should be broken into smaller pieces, with the most relevant piece returned first and additional details unpacked as needed.
condition: When the source content contains multiple details or contingencies but the user's immediate need is narrower.

statement: Conversation-centric interaction should be mixed-initiative and nonlinear, allowing either party to lead and allowing the user to redirect the conversation.
condition: When designing a conversation-centric agent rather than an agent-driven script.

statement: A conversation-centric style is characterized by persistent cross-turn context, short responses with more exchange, nonlinear trajectories, and recognition of common conversational activities.
condition: When distinguishing conversation-centric systems from system-, content-, or visual-centric styles.

statement: Conversation-first design should start with verbal input and output alone, whether voice or text, before adding buttons or other visual aids.
condition: When the goal is a natural-language interface that can work across voice, text, and richer displays.

statement: Visual aids should progressively enhance an already functional conversation rather than carry core functionality that words alone cannot perform.
condition: When adding visuals to a conversation-first design.
exception: A visual-only product need not preserve voice portability.

statement: Conversation-first design supports multi-channel deployment by focusing on core functionality through words, while allowing each channel to offer different affordances.
condition: When the same agent may appear in voice-only, SMS/chat, desktop, or larger-display contexts.

statement: The four natural-language interaction styles are ideal types, so a real application may mix multiple styles when useful.
condition: When classifying or evaluating an implemented system.

statement: A system's ability to continue a conversation is not sufficient evidence that it understands the substance of the user's utterance.
condition: When assessing claims that a conversational system understands natural language.

statement: Understanding is practically attributable through demonstrated actions, explanations, and performances rather than through direct access to private mental states.
condition: When using a functional or social-practice account of understanding.

statement: Testing understanding requires eliciting definitions, explanations, examples, inferences, or other performances that reveal interpretation, not merely asking whether the person or system understands.
condition: When the interaction is intended to assess conceptual understanding.

statement: Ordinary conversation normally assumes understanding until there is evidence of trouble, rather than probing every expression for exact meaning.
condition: When participants are engaged in everyday practical activity rather than formal examination.
exception: Technical instruction or testing may warrant explicit probing.

statement: Over-clarifying ordinary expressions can breach conversational expectations and undermine social trust.
condition: When the user has not displayed a trouble source requiring repair.
exception: Clarification may be appropriate when misunderstanding would be consequential or when the user asks for precision.

statement: Conversational understanding may be assumed incorrectly, faked, partial, or demonstrated only for practical purposes, so designers should support later repair instead of treating understanding as final.
condition: When an agent proceeds after apparent user or system understanding.

statement: People maintain shared understanding by designing talk for recipients and repairing troubles only when those troubles emerge.
condition: When using conversation-analysis accounts of intersubjectivity.

statement: Third-position repair allows the initiator of an action to correct a recipient's displayed interpretation of the initiator's earlier turn.
condition: When the recipient's response reveals a different interpretation from the one intended.

statement: If understanding is defined functionally as an interactional outcome, a machine can be treated as understanding when it performs the relevant role adequately.
condition: When adopting a social-practice or performance-based conception of understanding.

statement: Evaluating whether a machine can imitate relevant human performances is more technically productive than debating whether it possesses human-like inner mental states.
condition: When framing research or design goals for conversational AI.

statement: Open-ended oral examination is useful for evaluating understanding because questions can be adapted in response to prior answers, making rote performance harder to sustain.
condition: When the evaluator can probe the respondent across unpredictable follow-up situations.

statement: A machine's level of understanding should be judged from performance across multiple situations and varying circumstances, not from a single convincing exchange.
condition: When assessing either topic understanding or understanding of conversational actions.

statement: The value of an imitation-style test is to compare computer performance with human performance, not merely to trick observers into believing the computer is human.
condition: When using Turing-style evaluation as a design or assessment frame.

statement: Computers may be able to understand in a functional sense without thinking in a human mental-state sense.
condition: When understanding is evaluated by adequate social performance.

statement: Current conversational systems may demonstrate limited understanding in narrow tasks while failing when probed in new contexts or with different phrasing.
condition: When systems are evaluated beyond the specific phrasings or situations they handle well.

statement: Human-comparable general or deep machine understanding remains a hard problem and may not be feasible for real systems.
condition: When the target is domain-independent conversational or conceptual competence.

statement: Narrow service encounters are plausible settings for practical machine understanding because their goals, requests, inquiries, and troubleshooting patterns are often repetitive and limited in domain.
condition: When the agent only needs to perform well enough for practical purposes within a constrained service domain.
exception: This does not imply domain-independent understanding.

statement: NLU is necessary but insufficient for conversational understanding because it only provides interpretations that still need to be tested and repaired in interaction.
condition: When the system must establish mutual understanding with users rather than only parse utterances.

statement: Conversational systems need natural conversation understanding: the ability to engage in repair practices when misunderstanding or partial understanding is displayed.
condition: When designers want the system to manage mutual understanding interactionally.

statement: Interpretation is analysis of language and action, whereas understanding is demonstrated correct or adequate interpretation of social action within interaction.
condition: When distinguishing what a system internally analyzes from what interactionally counts as understanding.

statement: An effective conversational agent should reveal its interpretation of the user's utterance, action, or topic so the user can recognize and repair misunderstandings.
condition: When the agent's interpretation affects the next action or answer.

statement: Designing for effective human-machine natural-language communication requires shifting from concealing misunderstanding to making misunderstanding available for repair.
condition: When the system risks maintaining only an illusion of understanding.

statement: Conversational agent UX demands design work on turn-by-turn utterance sequencing rather than primarily on buttons, menus, windows, or other visual manipulation.
condition: When designing natural-language interfaces such as chatbots, virtual agents, or voice assistants.

statement: UX designers who author dialog logic and agent utterances need formal knowledge of how human conversation is structured turn by turn.
condition: When the designer is responsible for the conversational user experience rather than only visual presentation.

statement: Current natural-language platforms provide substantial language analysis and knowledge retrieval capabilities but inadequate direct support for modeling conversational interaction.
condition: When comparing platform support for language recognition against support for conversation organization.

statement: The Natural Conversation Framework adapts Conversation Analysis into a systematic design framework with an interaction model, content format, pattern language, and navigation method.
condition: When using the book's proposed approach to design natural-language interfaces.

statement: A conversational UX design system should define a design philosophy, a pattern language for interaction, and a content format.
Conversational interfaces are designed mainly through ordered utterance sequences rather than through spatial arrangement of visual controls.
Conversational UX design needs working knowledge of human conversation, not only graphic design or general interaction-design conventions.
A design system scales a UX approach by reducing repeated design effort, supporting consistency, scaffolding learning, and improving cross-functional collaboration.
A design philosophy should give designers an overarching vision, interaction metaphors, and principles for consistency and novel design choices.
Interaction patterns should provide reusable components for designers and recognizable interaction types for users so both can focus on application content.
Conversational pattern languages can use recognizable human conversation mechanisms in a role similar to familiar GUI mechanisms in graphical interfaces.
A natural-conversation-style agent pattern language should cover activity structures, activity management, transitions between activities, and encounter openings and closings.
A content format should let content designers supply use-case utterances without requiring them to program intents, dialog nodes, or platform internals.
The Alma Design System uses natural conversation as its primary interaction metaphor and mutual understanding between user and agent as an overarching design goal.
Conversational agents should adapt recipient design, minimization, and repair from human conversation into automated-agent UX decisions.
Recipient design requires an agent utterance to be tailored for the particular user or recipient context.
Minimization requires an agent to use no more wording than is needed for the recipient to understand.
Repair practices should be available so either party can recover from trouble in speaking, hearing, or understanding.
The NCF organizes conversational patterns into three operational classes: primary conversational activities, sequence-level management, and conversation-level management.
Conversational-activity modules should cover simple inquiries or requests, complex requests, extended tellings, known-answer questions, and information-capturing questions.
Conversational-activity modules can be combined as building blocks to create larger activities such as troubleshooting workflows or tutoring sequences.
Sequence-level management patterns should handle agent understanding failures, user hearing or understanding trouble, successful completion signals, and user aborts.
User responses after an agent answer can function as fine-grained feedback about success, hearing trouble, understanding trouble, or failure of the sequence.
Conversation-level management patterns should support conversation openings, capability negotiation, topic introduction, topic transitions, last-topic checks, closings, and disengagement.
A practical conversational content format should include slots for user utterance, agent utterance, agent repeat, agent paraphrase, agent example, and agent definition.
User-utterance slots should contain multiple variants of the same user action to support intent training.
Agent-utterance slots may contain one response or multiple response strings selected sequentially or randomly.
Repair-oriented content slots should prepare repeat, paraphrase, example, and definition responses for likely user repair initiations.
An agent paraphrase should usually elaborate a short primary response when the user may need more context.
condition: When the primary agent utterance is short and assumes user knowledge
exception: When the primary utterance is long or potentially confusing, the paraphrase should instead be shorter and state the upshot.

statement: An extended telling can be built by repeating the content format across additional parts triggered by pauses or user continuers rather than unique user intents.
condition: When the agent needs to deliver a story, instructions, or another multi-utterance unit

statement: Conversation-first design avoids long agent turns by breaking paragraph-length material into interactive parts through an extended-telling structure.
condition: When designing for natural voice or text conversation

statement: The same utterance-sequence design can serve voice and text channels when the interaction is modeled as natural conversation and minimization is applied.
condition: When long display-only utterances are avoided and content is structured as conversational sequences

statement: A full conversation template reduces implementation effort by giving designers a working conversation space with predefined activity structures and conversation-management mechanics.
A conversation design system can improve collaboration by embodying conversation-science assumptions so teams do not have to renegotiate basic interaction mechanics.
The Elements model can be applied beyond websites to products and services whenever the work concerns how people experience what is being made.
UX authoring should emphasize asking the right framing questions before choosing methods, technologies, or implementation details.
A shared conceptual model and vocabulary for UX concerns helps teams educate one another and coordinate work more effectively.
A product can fail because of how people experience it even when its intended function exists.
User experience concerns the outward encounter between a person and a product or service, rather than the product's internal mechanics.
Every product or service that people use creates a user experience, including non-digital and everyday objects.
Small interaction details such as feedback, control layout, and discoverability can materially affect task success and customer trust.
UX design should look beyond aesthetic appeal and functional correctness to whether the user-facing form supports real use.
For user-facing parts of a product, appropriate form is shaped by users' psychology, behavior, and task context, not only by internal functionality.
UX design should evaluate whether controls and presentation work in the context of neighboring controls and the user's current goal.
