The more features, functions, or steps a product has, the more opportunities there are for the experience to break down.
condition: when product complexity increases

statement: Complex products need explicit UX design support because successful experiences are not automatically implied by the product category.
condition: when a product has multiple features, functions, or usage steps

statement: Web products should be designed as self-service experiences because users usually face them without manuals, training, or guided assistance.
condition: when the product is a website or web application

statement: A product that makes users feel incapable or confused is likely to drive them away even when the fault lies in the design.
condition: when users have trouble using complicated technology

statement: Adding features can create only temporary advantage if the resulting complexity makes the product harder for newcomers to use.
condition: when feature expansion increases complexity

statement: Quality user experience is a sustainable competitive advantage because it shapes customer impressions, differentiation, and repeat use.
Content-oriented products must present information so users can find, absorb, and understand it, not merely make the information available.
condition: when a product primarily communicates information

statement: Functionality fails as a product asset when users cannot understand how to operate it.
condition: when users cannot figure out how a feature works

statement: Customer loyalty depends more on the lived user experience than on technology sophistication or brand messaging alone.
Conversion rate is an appropriate UX return-on-investment measure when a site asks visitors to take a next relationship or purchase step.
condition: when the product has measurable user progression or transaction goals

statement: Small conversion-rate improvements can produce large revenue effects for commerce products.
condition: when the product monetizes visitor conversion

statement: Internal tools and intranets still need deliberate UX because their usability can determine whether they create organizational value or consume resources.
condition: when the audience is employees, partners, or other internal users

statement: UX improvements create efficiency by helping users complete work faster and make fewer mistakes.
Better usability can improve employee satisfaction and retention when the product is part of daily work.
condition: when employees repeatedly use the tool for work

statement: User-centered design requires taking users into account at every step of product development.
Every aspect of the user experience should result from conscious design decisions, including necessary compromises.
UX teams should analyze the experience by component elements and perspectives so they understand the consequences of design choices.
A successful experience should be cohesive and intuitive, and may also be pleasurable, because users will abandon products that do not serve them positively.
The five planes framework decomposes UX work into strategy, scope, structure, skeleton, and surface so design problems can be discussed at useful levels of abstraction.
Strategy defines both organizational objectives and user needs, and it should ground every later UX decision.
Scope decisions determine which features, functions, and content requirements the product will include.
Structure decisions determine how product features, interactions, and content categories fit together and how users move through them.
Skeleton decisions arrange interface, navigation, information, and content elements for effect and efficiency.
Surface decisions define the concrete sensory presentation of the finished product.
Design choices on each plane constrain and influence the choices available on the plane above it.
Misalignment between adjacent planes can derail schedules, raise costs, and produce an unsatisfying product.
condition: when upper-plane and lower-plane decisions do not naturally fit

statement: Project planning should allow upper-plane work to begin before all lower-plane decisions are final, while preventing any plane from finishing before its lower dependencies are finished.
Upper-plane design discoveries should be allowed to force reevaluation of lower-plane decisions.
condition: when later design work exposes a mismatch or missing lower-plane decision

statement: UX analysis should distinguish functionality-oriented concerns about tasks from information-oriented concerns about meaning, retrieval, and understanding.
condition: when a product contains both tools and information resources

statement: Most web products combine application-like functionality and information-resource qualities, so teams should avoid treating them as purely one or the other.
condition: when a web product has both task flows and content

statement: UX responsibilities do not require a separate specialist for every element, but the team must ensure that each element receives attention from someone.
Content availability, quality, manageability, and value strongly shape the final user experience.
condition: when content is a significant part of the product

statement: Technology capabilities constrain and enable the experiences a team can provide, even though the fundamental UX elements remain stable.
Product strategy should explicitly answer what the organization wants from the product and what users want from it before design execution begins.
condition: before implementation or visual production begins

statement: Product objectives should describe what the product itself is expected to accomplish, not the organization's entire mission or a prematurely chosen solution.
Effective objectives are specific enough to define success but broad enough to avoid prescribing implementation before the problem is understood.
UX decisions should be rooted in an understanding of their consequences against defined conditions for success.
Brand identity includes the conceptual associations and emotional reactions created by product interactions, not only visual marks and style.
Teams should make desired brand impressions explicit as product objectives rather than letting users form impressions solely by accident.
Success metrics should be defined before or during design so teams can later determine whether the product is meeting organizational objectives and user needs.
A good success metric must be tied to user behavior that design choices can plausibly influence.
Metrics can point in different desired directions depending on strategy, so teams must interpret measures such as time on site according to the intended experience.
condition: when choosing or interpreting success metrics

statement: Optimizing a metric in a way that frustrates users can damage long-term performance even if the short-term number improves.
condition: when a metric can be increased by adding friction or detours

statement: UX metrics should not be interpreted in isolation because marketing, competitors, press, and other external events can affect the same outcomes.
condition: when connecting product changes to measured outcomes

statement: User needs work should begin by identifying who the users are and researching their goals, behavior, and context.
Design teams must avoid assuming that users are like the team itself.
User segmentation makes diverse user needs manageable by grouping people who share relevant characteristics or needs.
condition: when the audience contains diverse users

statement: Useful segmentation can be based on demographics, psychographics, technology attitudes, domain expertise, social role, or professional role.
Segments should be revised after research and kept only where distinct user needs justify distinct groups.
condition: after research reveals similarities or differences among users

statement: When user segments have opposing needs, the team must strategically choose which segment to prioritize or provide separate approaches to the same task.
condition: when one solution cannot satisfy conflicting segment needs

statement: Research methods should be selected according to the kind of understanding needed: attitudes and perceptions, behavior, task performance, or contextual practice.
The more time a study spends with each participant, the more detail it can produce, but the fewer participants it can usually include.
condition: when project time and launch deadlines constrain research

statement: Surveys, interviews, and focus groups work best when the team first states exactly what information it needs from them.
condition: when using attitudinal research methods

statement: Contextual inquiry is appropriate when a problem requires deep understanding of users in their everyday environment, provided the project can afford the time and cost.
condition: when deep contextual understanding is needed

statement: Task analysis should examine the steps users take to accomplish a task through interviews, direct observation, or both.
condition: when designing around user tasks

statement: User testing should be understood as having representative users evaluate the product, prototype, or work in progress, not as evaluating the users themselves.
User tests can investigate both narrow task completion and broader effects such as whether a design supports the intended brand message.
Prototype testing can gather user input throughout the design process before a full product exists.
condition: when a complete product is unavailable or too costly to test

statement: Card sorting helps information-oriented teams understand how users naturally group and categorize content.
condition: when designing or revising information architecture

statement: Personas should be fictional but research-consistent representatives of real user needs, used to keep user perspectives present in design decisions.
Strategic discovery should gather perspectives from stakeholders and from customer-facing or operational staff who understand day-to-day problems.
Strategy documents should analyze relationships among objectives and connect them to the organizational context, rather than merely list goals.
Strategy documentation should be concise enough to be used, and should be actively accessible to designers, developers, and project managers making project decisions.
Product strategy may evolve during the project, but revisions should be systematic so the team is not chasing an uncontrolled moving target.
Scope translates user needs and product objectives into specific content and functionality requirements.
Defining scope is valuable because it exposes conflicts, rough spots, and deferable work while the product is still hypothetical.
A defined requirements set gives the team a shared reference point and common language for the work.
Requirements reduce ambiguity by making completion criteria and responsibility boundaries visible to the team.
Mapping the entire scope can reveal connections and overlaps between requirements that would otherwise appear separate.
Clear requirements provide a framework for evaluating new feature ideas against existing strategic commitments.
condition: when feature ideas arise during or after scope definition

statement: Out-of-scope ideas should be captured for future releases instead of silently expanding the current milestone.
condition: when a useful idea does not fit current requirements

statement: Requirements must be actively managed to prevent small additions from accumulating into schedule and budget failure.
Scope work turns the strategy question of why the product exists into the concrete question of what will be made.
Functional features and content offerings can be scoped with similar requirements practices even though they come from different disciplines.
condition: when defining the scope plane

statement: Content requirements often create functional requirements for systems such as content management, workflow, personalization, or device-specific delivery.
condition: when content must be produced, approved, managed, recombined, or delivered dynamically

statement: Functional requirements often create content requirements such as instructions, labels, and error messages.
condition: when a technology product exposes screens, states, or messages to users

statement: The detail level of requirements should match the project's scope, complexity, and content uniformity.
Users are the most productive source of requirements, but stakeholder requirements should also be elicited because stakeholders influence what enters the product.
Requirement elicitation should distinguish what people say they want from the underlying need their proposed solution is attempting to address.
condition: when users or stakeholders propose specific solutions

statement: Brainstorming can uncover requirements users and stakeholders did not know they wanted.
condition: when participants explore strategic objectives and possible ways to fulfill them

statement: Diverse cross-functional brainstorming can reveal possibilities that specialists immersed in an existing product may miss.
condition: when participants represent different organizational functions or user groups

statement: Generating requirements should look for ways to remove impediments between users and their goals.
Scenarios should place personas in short narratives of need fulfillment to identify possible requirements.
condition: when personas exist and requirements are being defined

statement: Functional specifications should stay lightweight enough to evolve with implementation rather than becoming a separate project.
condition: when technical uncertainty or implementation change is expected

statement: Specifications are valuable for clarity and accuracy, not for documenting every possible aspect of an idealized future product.
Requirements should be written positively by stating the intended system behavior rather than only prohibitions.
condition: when documenting requirements

statement: Requirements should be specific enough that the team can determine whether each one has been fulfilled.
condition: when documenting requirements

statement: Requirements should avoid subjective language unless the subjective quality is tied to objective criteria or an explicit reference standard.
condition: when documenting requirements

statement: Requirements should be falsifiable so non-fulfillment can be demonstrated.
condition: when documenting requirements

statement: Content requirements should identify all relevant content types, not just text.
condition: when defining content features

statement: Content requirements should focus on the purpose a content feature serves rather than treating a familiar format as the requirement itself.
condition: when stakeholders propose formats such as FAQs

statement: Content requirements should include approximate size information so designers can create appropriate vehicles for the content.
condition: when content scale, dimensions, or file size affects design

statement: Each required content element should have an identified owner for creation and maintenance early in the project.
condition: when a product depends on content features

statement: Effective content requires ongoing maintenance; treating content as publish-once can cause the product to degrade against user needs.
condition: when content changes over time or users expect currency

statement: Content update frequency should balance strategic goals, user expectations, and organizational resources.
condition: when defining content requirements

statement: Content requirements should identify intended audience segments when the product serves multiple audiences with divergent needs.
condition: when content presentation differs by audience

statement: A content inventory gives the team a concrete view of existing content that must shape the new user experience.
condition: when a project involves substantial existing content

statement: Requirements should be prioritized by strategic fit with product objectives, fit with user needs, and implementation feasibility.
condition: when deciding what enters scope

statement: Feature feasibility must account for technical possibility, available human and financial resources, and time constraints.
condition: when evaluating candidate features

statement: Conflicts between features should be resolved according to strategic objectives rather than by treating features as isolated wishes.
condition: when features impose trade-offs on one another

statement: A good out-of-scope feature suggestion can indicate that the team should reexamine strategy, but repeated strategy revisiting suggests requirements work began too soon.
condition: when a suggested feature is strategically attractive but outside current scope

statement: Stakeholder feature conflicts should be negotiated by returning to the underlying strategic goal and showing empathy for the needs each feature represents.
condition: when stakeholders champion conflicting features

statement: Structure work defines how scoped pieces fit into a cohesive whole after requirements have been prioritized.
condition: after scope has been defined and prioritized

statement: Interaction design and information architecture both define patterns and sequences of user options, but interaction design centers task completion while information architecture centers understanding information.
Interaction design and information architecture should be grounded in how people behave and think, not treated primarily as technical exercises.
Interaction design should describe possible user behavior and define how the system accommodates and responds to that behavior.
The technically efficient implementation path is often not the path that works best for the person using the product.
condition: when technical design choices affect user-facing behavior

statement: Interaction designs should use a clear conceptual model so related behavior, interface language, and functions stay consistent.
Familiar conventions make unfamiliar products easier to learn when the target users already know those conventions.
condition: when users have experience with comparable products or patterns

statement: Teams may depart from convention only when they have a strong reason and an alternative model users can understand.
condition: when considering an unfamiliar conceptual model

statement: Conceptual models do not always need to be explained explicitly to users; they should be inferable from consistent product behavior.
condition: when consistent behavior can communicate the model through use

statement: Designers should understand the models users already bring to a product before choosing the product's conceptual model.
Metaphors can help define interaction models, but taking real-world analogies too literally can make the product less functional.
condition: when using real-world analogs in interface design

statement: The best error-handling strategy is to design the system so important errors cannot occur.
condition: when the system can technically prevent an error

statement: When errors cannot be made impossible, the design should make them difficult, help users recognize and fix them, or recover from them.
condition: when user errors remain possible

statement: Automatic error correction should be used carefully because intrusive corrections can create additional user frustration.
condition: when the system attempts to correct user input or behavior on the user's behalf

statement: Irrecoverable actions should receive noticeable warnings, but excessive confirmations can make users ignore important warnings.
condition: when an action cannot be undone or recovered

statement: Information architecture matters in any product where users must make sense of presented information, including functionality-oriented products.
condition: when the product presents information users must interpret

statement: Information architecture should create organizational and navigational schemes that help users move through content efficiently and effectively.
condition: when designing content structures

statement: Information architectures may need to educate, inform, or persuade users, not merely help them locate items.
condition: when the product's content has communication goals beyond retrieval

statement: Categorization schemes should correspond to product objectives, user needs, and the actual content or functionality being incorporated.
condition: when defining information architecture categories

statement: Architecture work should balance top-down strategy-driven thinking with bottom-up analysis of content and functional requirements.
Pure top-down architecture can overlook important content details, while pure bottom-up architecture can become too tied to current content to handle change.
condition: when choosing an architectural approach

statement: A site structure should be judged by whether each step makes sense and follows naturally for users, not by minimizing clicks or steps alone.
condition: when evaluating navigation or task structure

statement: Effective structures should accommodate ordinary growth and change without requiring full redesign for each new requirement.
condition: when a site or product will evolve over time

statement: Teams should be prepared to rework structure when objectives or user needs change materially.
condition: when strategy or intended user needs change

statement: Using nodes as the unit of architecture lets teams choose the appropriate level of structural detail for the problem.
condition: when documenting or analyzing information structures

statement: Hierarchical structures fit content with parent-child relationships and are commonly understandable to users.
condition: when content can be grouped into broad-to-narrow categories

statement: Matrix structures can support multiple user needs by allowing movement across several dimensions, but they become hard to use as primary navigation when dimensions multiply.
condition: when users need multiple ways to traverse the same content

statement: Organic structures suit exploratory experiences with unclear or evolving relationships, but they make reliable return-finding harder.
condition: when prioritizing free-form exploration over reliable retrieval

statement: Sequential structures suit experiences where order is essential, especially smaller content flows or instructional material.
condition: when the order of presentation is necessary to meet user needs

statement: Organizing principles should group and separate content according to criteria that match objectives, user needs, and the level of the architecture.
The design challenge is to choose the right structure for user needs and objectives, because a body of information can support multiple plausible structures.
Designers should choose the facets most important to users instead of forcing users to sort through every possible attribute.
condition: when faceted organization is possible

statement: Nomenclature should use users' language consistently so users can understand and navigate the architecture.
A controlled vocabulary helps prevent internal jargon and inconsistent terminology from confusing users.
condition: when multiple people or teams create site content

statement: A thesaurus can map disallowed, internal, shorthand, slang, or acronym terms to approved terms and expose broader, narrower, or related concepts.
condition: when terminology variation affects findability or content architecture

statement: Detailed and consistent metadata increases flexibility in structuring, linking, and repurposing content.
condition: when content will be organized, recombined, or dynamically surfaced

statement: Metadata only enables reliable automation when the underlying vocabulary is consistent.
condition: when automated linking, grouping, or retrieval depends on metadata

statement: Search can become more relevant when metadata and thesaurus mappings help connect user terms to preferred concepts.
condition: when users search with terms that differ from approved nomenclature

statement: Architecture and interaction diagrams should communicate conceptual relationships and sequences rather than every link or page detail.
condition: when documenting complex structures for a team

statement: Structural responsibilities must be consciously assigned because a product will have a structure whether or not the team plans it.
A full-time UX specialist is most valuable when an organization has a steady stream of new content and functionality to manage.
condition: when deciding whether to staff a permanent UX design role

statement: A clear structural plan tends to reduce major overhauls and improve the product's ability to satisfy user and owner needs.
condition: when the site is built according to the plan

statement: Skeleton design makes structure concrete by defining the detailed form of components and their relationships.
Teams should distinguish interface, navigation, and information-design problems so they can judge whether the chosen solution addresses the actual issue.
condition: when working on skeleton-level design

statement: Interface design provides the means for users to act on product functionality.
condition: when the design gives users ability to do things

statement: Navigation design provides the means for users to see and move through an information structure.
condition: when the design gives users ability to go places in an information space

statement: Information design presents information so users can understand or use it effectively.
condition: when the design communicates ideas to users

statement: Designers should be cautious about deviating from interface conventions and should do so only for clear user-facing benefit.
condition: when users are likely to know the convention

statement: Internal consistency is more important than matching external conventions because it lets users transfer learning across the product.
Shared concepts such as start, finish, back, and save should receive consistent treatment wherever they appear.
condition: when the same action concept appears in multiple contexts

statement: Concrete metaphors should be used sparingly because users may interpret them differently or be misled by real-world constraints that do not apply on screen.
condition: when representing digital features through real-world objects

statement: Effective interface metaphors reduce user mental effort rather than merely adding novelty or cuteness.
condition: when considering metaphorical interface elements

statement: Interface design should select elements appropriate to the user's task and arrange them so they are readily understood and easily used.
Successful interfaces make important elements noticeable and reduce or remove elements users do not need for their likely tasks.
Interface design should not give rare edge cases the same visual and interaction weight as common user needs.
condition: when common and extreme cases compete for interface attention

statement: Default interface options should reflect the team's understanding of users' likely tasks and goals.
condition: when a default selection or state is needed

statement: Remembering users' previous choices can improve interface fit, but may be impractical when implementation complexity is too high.
condition: when persistence is technically and economically feasible

statement: Technical constraints can limit interface innovation while also helping users transfer knowledge across standard controls.
condition: when a platform or framework provides standard interface elements

statement: Interface element choices should be evaluated as trade-offs, such as space saved versus options hidden or system load versus user effort.
condition: when choosing among controls that can serve the same function

statement: Navigation design must help users move between points, understand relationships among navigation options, and understand how those options relate to the current page.
condition: when designing navigation for a site or multi-screen product

statement: Navigation links should be selected to support real user behavior rather than attempting to link every page to every other page.
condition: when choosing navigational access points

statement: Every page should clearly communicate where users are and where they can go next.
condition: when users can enter or move through pages independently

statement: Navigation should be designed as if users carry little or no structural memory from page to page.
condition: when the team lacks evidence that users maintain a reliable mental map

statement: Most sites should use multiple navigation systems, each serving a distinct role in different user circumstances.
condition: when one navigation mechanism cannot support all navigation needs

statement: Global navigation should provide access to the key site-wide destinations users need for broad movement across the product.
condition: when users need broad movement across site areas

statement: Local navigation should expose nearby parent, sibling, or child options in the architecture.
condition: when users need movement within a local section or hierarchy

statement: Supplementary navigation should provide shortcuts to related content that global or local navigation does not readily expose.
condition: when related content crosses the primary architecture

statement: Contextual navigation should be placed where users discover the need for related information, but only when the link clearly supports their task or goal.
condition: when embedding links inside content

statement: Courtesy navigation should provide convenient access to infrequently needed but commonly expected items.
condition: when users expect access to policies, contact details, feedback, or similar utility information

statement: Remote navigation tools such as site maps and indexes should support users when primary navigation fails or when content is too broad for simple browsing.
condition: when users need an independent overview or lookup tool

statement: A site map should usually show a concise architectural overview rather than excessive hierarchy detail.
condition: when documenting top-level navigation for users

statement: Indexes are most useful for sites or sections with a large, diverse range of content subjects.
condition: when alphabetical topic lookup fits user needs

statement: Information design should group and arrange information according to how users think and what their tasks and goals require.
Interface messages, instructions, and error explanations are information-design problems because they communicate what users need to use the interface successfully.
condition: when the system provides user-facing guidance or feedback

statement: Wayfinding should help users quickly understand where they are, where they can go, and which choices move them toward their objectives.
condition: when users move through a site or information space

statement: Wayfinding cues such as color, icons, labels, and typography should reinforce other location signals rather than carry the burden alone.
condition: when using non-navigation page elements to communicate location

statement: Wireframes should show the components of a page and how they fit together across interface, navigation, and information design.
condition: when documenting page layout or screen layout

statement: Wireframes should include annotations or references when behavior, source content, specifications, or architectural context is not obvious from layout alone.
condition: when a bare layout would leave implementation or design questions ambiguous

statement: A small set of standard wireframes can often cover recurring screen types without requiring one wireframe for every screen.
condition: when screens fall into functional or navigational patterns

statement: Wireframes serve multiple project roles by confirming expectations for strategy, scope, and structure and by answering build questions for implementation.
UX designers and visual designers should collaborate on wireframes when their responsibilities are separate.
condition: when skeleton and visual-design expertise sit with different people

statement: Documentation should be produced at the level needed by the team and project, because under-documentation and documentation for its own sake both create problems.
Wireframes are valuable because they integrate interface element selection, navigation system definition, and information component prioritization into one skeleton reference.
Surface design should present the logical arrangements of the skeleton through sensory design.
condition: when moving from skeleton to surface plane

statement: Visual design should be evaluated by how well it supports the objectives defined by lower planes, not by aesthetic preference alone.
Visual design can reinforce or undermine structure by clarifying or obscuring users' available options.
condition: when visual treatment affects distinctions between sections or choices

statement: Visual design should express brand identity in ways aligned with the intended strategic impression.
condition: when brand identity is a product objective

statement: Designers can evaluate visual hierarchy by asking where users' eyes go first and whether that first attention target supports user and product goals.
condition: when reviewing a visual design

statement: Informal attention checks can be sufficient for many visual fine-tuning tasks, although eyetracking provides more precision and nuance.
condition: when formal eyetracking is unnecessary or unavailable

statement: Successful visual flow should lead users smoothly through relevant possibilities without overwhelming them or distracting from goal-supporting information and functions.
Contrast is a primary visual tool for drawing attention, communicating relationships, and expressing conceptual groups.
Visual differences must be strong and intentional enough for users to recognize the intended distinction.
condition: when using contrast to communicate meaning

statement: Uniformity helps visual designs communicate without confusing or overwhelming users.
Grid-based layout can provide shared visual order across layout variations, but design standards should be revisited when they no longer meet product needs.
condition: when grids or standards constrain screen-based design

statement: Internal visual consistency should be built by identifying recurring design elements, designing them once, testing them in their contexts, and reworking them as needed.
condition: when the same element appears across multiple contexts

statement: A successful visual design system is a cohesive whole, not merely a collection of individually polished objects.
External consistency across media helps audiences perceive a clear brand identity for the organization as a whole.
condition: when the organization communicates through multiple products or media

statement: Color palettes should provide a coordinated range of colors suitable for foreground emphasis and background support.
condition: when defining visual design standards

statement: Colors used in the same context should be distinct enough for users to tell them apart and should be used consistently.
condition: when color communicates meaning or grouping

statement: Typography for extended body text should prioritize readability over ornate personality.
condition: when users must read longer text blocks

statement: Typefaces with more personality are better reserved for larger text or short labels where they do not undermine readability.
condition: when styling headings, labels, or navigation text

statement: Typography systems should use different styles only to indicate meaningful information differences and should avoid unnecessary variety.
condition: when defining type standards

statement: Design comps should show how chosen visual components work together and reveal where the visual system breaks down.
condition: when validating surface design

statement: Design comps should preserve the wireframe's relative importance and grouping even when the final visual layout differs from the wireframe arrangement.
condition: when translating wireframes into visual designs

statement: Style guides should document design decisions and standards so the rationale does not disappear as people forget or leave.
condition: when a design system will be maintained over time

statement: A style guide should cover global standards and, when needed, section-specific or component-specific standards at enough detail to support future decisions.
condition: when defining reusable visual standards

statement: Style guides are especially useful for enforcing design consistency across decentralized projects and teams.
condition: when independent teams contribute to the same product or brand experience

statement: The five-plane UX model can be applied regardless of product complexity, but the staffing and process needed to apply it should scale with the project.
Dedicated specialists can be effective for complex products because they can focus deeply on subsets of the user experience.
condition: when the product is too complex for a small team to cover well

statement: Small teams can produce strong UX results when they stay synchronized around a shared vision.
condition: when the team has limited resources but strong shared understanding

statement: UX work should treat design as many small problems that require identifying the real problem and the plane on which it occurs.
Every UX solution should be evaluated for consequences across the planes because decisions can ripple upward and downward.
Someone in the organization must think about each of the five planes, regardless of how responsibilities are distributed.
Teams should avoid design by default, where the user experience simply mirrors the underlying technology or organizational structure.
condition: when technology or departments suggest a structure that may not serve users

statement: Teams should avoid design by mimicry, where familiar conventions are copied without checking their fit for users or medium.
condition: when borrowing patterns from other products or media

statement: Teams should avoid design by fiat, where personal preferences override user needs and product objectives.
condition: when a decision is driven by authority or taste rather than strategy and evidence

statement: Designers should be able to answer why each UX decision was made in terms of the underlying user and product issues.
UX methods can be adapted to limited time, money, and staff by using lighter-weight evidence sources and informal tests.
condition: when formal research or testing resources are unavailable

statement: Teams should not defer fundamental UX evaluation to the end of the process because late findings may arrive after there is time or budget to fix them.
condition: when planning development and evaluation timing

statement: Late acceptance testing can miss or obscure the assumptions that shaped the user experience earlier in the project.
condition: when finished-product testing is the first serious UX check

statement: User testing is not a substitute for a thoughtful and informed UX design process.
User tests should be constructed around the specific UX element or problem being investigated so they do not answer the wrong question.
condition: when planning prototype or product tests

statement: Design teams cannot rely on users to articulate their own needs fully; the team must infer needs through multiple forms of understanding.
Development processes should alternate between fast forward motion and deliberate reflection, testing, integration, and refinement.
condition: when planning product development over time

statement: Deliberate attention to strategy, scope, and structure can cost time early but save more time later.
condition: when early planning tasks are at risk of being cut

statement: Cutting lower-plane preparation can leave later deliverables disconnected from the larger project context.
condition: when strategy, scope, or structure work is removed from a project plan

statement: Less visible lower planes such as strategy, scope, and structure play a central role in the overall success or failure of the user experience.
Failures on upper planes can prevent users from benefiting from good lower-plane decisions.
condition: when visual, navigation, or interaction problems block users from reaching deeper strengths

statement: Good upper-plane decisions cannot compensate for poor lower-plane choices such as an unusable strategy or structure.
condition: when surface or skeleton quality rests on weak lower-plane foundations

statement: A product becomes a stronger asset when everything users experience is the result of conscious decisions aligned with strategic goals and user needs.
